v1.224.0 = R341 Dynamic Test Intelligence cron - 8 new, machine-verifiable test cases from 2026-08-18 research. v1.224.0 mines the freshly-opened Chrome 157 stable surface via the chromestatuslite.com/?version=157 mirror (9,848 bytes - the same Chrome platform-status data that powers chromestatus.com/feature/<id>, listing 2 enabled-by-default features + 0 origin trials + 0 flagged features + 0 deprecations + 0 removals for Chrome 157 stable - a brand-new milestone that did not exist at the time of the v1.223.0 R340 cycle on 2026-08-17). v1.224.0 also re-mines the freshly-published Safari Technology Preview 250 release notes (released 2026-08-13, available at https://webkit.org/blog/18191/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-250/) for the 6 unmined contracts that v1.223.0 R340 deliberately deferred because the v1.223.0 budget of 8 cases was already full - the unmined surface covers CSS (ruby-overhang: spaces, ::marker content, white-space-trim, wrap-inside), Web API (Clipboard API image/svg+xml), and WebDriver (consume user activation extension command). The 8 fresh contracts cover: (1) the Approximate Geolocation API that extends the Geolocation API's PositionOptions dictionary with a new accuracyMode field accepting the values "precise" (default, preserves the high-accuracy contract) and "approximate" (the new value, requests city-level location data only) - the privacy-by-default contract that lets sites (news, weather, store-locators) request coarse location without triggering the high-accuracy permission prompt (W-456, Chrome 157 enabled-by-default, feature 5143609755828224, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/u/1/issues/495852854, spec at https://github.com/w3c/geolocation/pull/233); (2) the URL Standard spec-compliance fix that disallows space characters (and other forbidden host code points) in non-file:// URL hosts, closing the interop gap with Safari and Firefox on the Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket + URL focus areas (S-478, Chrome 157 enabled-by-default, feature 5083335148437504, spec at https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point); (3) the CSS ruby-overhang property's new "spaces" value that limits annotation overhang to adjacent spaces and punctuation characters, with "none" now an alias for "spaces" (B-278, Safari TP 250 WebKit commit 317569@main, bug 181808420, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-ruby-1/#ruby-overhang); (4) the CSS content property on the ::marker pseudo-element that lets authors customize list item bullets / numbers with arbitrary CSS content values (strings, images, counters, attr() references) (B-279, Safari TP 250 WebKit commit 317570@main, bug 182750380, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-pseudo-4/#marker-pseudo); (5) the CSS white-space-trim property from CSS Text Level 4 that controls whitespace trimming at the boundaries of preserved-whitespace contexts with values "none" (default), "start", "end", "both" (B-280, Safari TP 250 WebKit commit 317573@main, bug 182751076, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-text-4/#white-space-trim-property); (6) the CSS wrap-inside property (now renamed to text-wrap in the current spec draft) that controls whether text wrapping can occur inside a box, with values "auto" (default), "avoid", and "stable" (B-281, Safari TP 250 WebKit commit 317574@main, bug 182751559, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-text-4/#wrap-inside-property); (7) the Clipboard API extension that adds image/svg+xml MIME type support to navigator.clipboard.write / navigator.clipboard.read with markup sanitization on both read and write sides per the HTML sanitization spec (C-239, Safari TP 250 WebKit commit 317528@main, bug 137553836, spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/clipboard-apis/ and https://w3c.github.io/html-sanitization/); (8) the WebDriver BiDi "consume user activation" extension command that consumes the current browsing context's transient user activation and reports whether it was present - critical for test automation that needs to programmatically verify the user-activation-consumption contract (C-240, Safari TP 250 WebKit commit 317715@main, bug 102634281, spec at https://w3c.github.io/webdriver-bidi/). All 8 cases follow the v1.208.0-v1.223.0 case-body template with controlled-fixture acceptance criteria, per-engine control assertions, WPT fixture references, and the spec / commit / bug link triple for canonical evidence. v1.223.0 = R340 Dynamic Test Intelligence cron - 8 new, machine-verifiable test cases from 2026-08-17 research. v1.223.0 mines the freshly-opened Chrome 156 enabled-by-default surface via the chromestatuslite.com/?version=156 mirror (11,723 bytes - the same Chrome platform-status data that powers chromestatus.com/feature/<id>, listing 3 enabled-by-default features + 0 origin trials + 0 flagged features + 0 deprecations + 0 removals for Chrome 156 stable - a brand-new milestone that did not exist at the time of the v1.222.0 R339 cycle on 2026-08-16). v1.223.0 also mines the previously-unmined Chrome 155 enabled-by-default surface entry (the second of 2 enabled features) that v1.222.0 R339 deferred because the v1.222.0 budget of 7 cases was already full - the CSS margin-trim property. v1.223.0 also mines the freshly-published Safari Technology Preview 250 release notes (released 2026-08-13, available at the actual URL https://webkit.org/blog/18191/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-250/ - the older guessed URL https://webkit.org/blog/18183/ returns HTTP 301 to the real URL) - TP 250 ships 19 substantive new contracts spanning CSS, JavaScript, Media, Networking, Scrolling, Storage, Web API, Web Inspector, WebAssembly, and WebDriver, of which v1.223.0 mines 4 of the most relevant: TC39 Explicit Resource Management (using / await using / Symbol.dispose / DisposableStack / AsyncDisposableStack), Iterator.zipKeyed() from the Joint Iteration proposal, fetch() ReadableStream body upload with the new Request.duplex option, WebAssembly relaxed SIMD instructions, and WebAssembly multiple memories. The 8 fresh contracts cover: (1) the CSS margin-trim property from CSS Box Model Level 4 (B-276, Chrome 155 enabled-by-default, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-box-4/#margin-trim) that omits margins before/after the first/last child of a block container (or column of a multi-column container), giving authors a more powerful / generic / expressive alternative to the legacy margin-quirk that applies to P/H1-H6 inside BODY and table-cell elements in quirks mode; (2) the SVG foreignObject canvas taint fix for blob URLs (B-277, Chrome 156 enabled-by-default, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/41054640) that aligns Chromium's canvas drawImage() taint behavior with Gecko's no-taint behavior when the SVG source includes a foreignObject tag and is referenced via a blob URL - previously both Chromium and WebKit tainted the canvas, after the fix Chromium matches Gecko and authors can use a wider range of SVG content in canvas drawImage() calls without tainting; (3) the WebRTC Diagnostic Logging API (S-477, Chrome 156 enabled-by-default, enterprise policy WebRtcDiagnosticLogCollectionAllowedForOrigins per https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcDiagnosticLogCollectionAllowedForOrigins) that lets an application opt in to WebRTC diagnostic logging; the logs are useful for local debugging and can be uploaded out-of-band to the browser vendor; the application gets an ID similar to a crash report ID; (4) the Safari TP 250 fetch() ReadableStream body upload + Request.duplex option (W-453, Safari TP 250 from 2026-08-13, WebKit commits 317724@main + 317768@main) that lets a page upload a ReadableStream as the fetch() body; the new duplex option is required on Request when uploading a ReadableStream body; this unblocks streaming game asset upload + large telemetry beacon upload without buffering the entire payload in memory; (5) the Safari TP 250 Iterator.zipKeyed() from the TC39 Joint Iteration proposal (C-238, Safari TP 250 commit 317886@main, proposal at https://github.com/tc39/proposal-iterator-sequencing) that advances multiple iterators in lockstep with KEYED access - complementing Iterator.zip() (W-440 v1.219.0 covers the un-keyed zip); the keyed variant yields [key, value] pairs and enables pattern like Iterator.zipKeyed({a: Iterator.from([1,2]), b: Iterator.from(['x','y'])}) yielding ['a', 1], ['b', 'x']; (6) the Safari TP 250 TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal (W-454, Safari TP 250 commit 317894@main, proposal at https://github.com/tc39/proposal-explicit-resource-management) that adds using and await using declarations for synchronous and asynchronous resources, plus Symbol.dispose + DisposableStack + AsyncDisposableStack; this is the deterministic-resource-cleanup contract for game resource pools (GPU buffers, audio contexts, WebSocket connections) that previously required manual try/finally discipline; (7) the Safari TP 250 WebAssembly multiple memories in a single module (W-455, Safari TP 250 commit 317636@main, spec at https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/exec/runtime.html) that lets a single WebAssembly module declare more than one memory - critical for game engines that need to keep player save state and runtime state in separate address spaces for safety, or that need to integrate multiple separately-compiled modules without merging their memories; (8) the Safari TP 250 WebAssembly relaxed SIMD instructions (P-192, Safari TP 250 commit 317549@main, spec at https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/intro.html) - the relaxed SIMD profile is a deterministic subset of the SIMD proposal that opts out of the IEEE 754-2019 non-deterministic rounding-mode flag; the relaxed profile includes relaxed_q15x15rs_dot, relaxed_dot_i8_i7, and the relaxed-lane-wise integer / floating-point arithmetic operations that enable deterministic game-physics SIMD kernels; distinct from W-150 v1.203.0 which is the broad multi-engine WASM 3.0 baseline (Chrome 119+/Firefox 120+/Safari 18.2+); P-192 is the Safari TP 250 WebKit-specific enablement of the relaxed SIMD instruction set. The 7 fresh contracts cover: (1) the WebSocket constructor options bag that adds a WebSocketInit dictionary as the second argument to the WebSocket constructor (currently with a protocols option mirroring the existing string argument) - the canonical extensibility point that the WHATWG WebSockets spec issue #42 requested and that Chromium wants to grow into the targetAddressSpace extension point (W-451, Chrome 154 enabled-by-default, Chromium bug 542670554, spec PR https://github.com/whatwg/websockets/pull/76); (2) the WebSocket targetAddressSpace option that lets a public site connect to a local-network WebSocket server by hostname (avoiding manual IP configuration) and bypasses mixed content blocking in secure contexts when the user has granted the local-network permission - paired with W-451 because the option bag is the extension point (W-452, Chrome 154 enabled-by-default, Chromium bug 517413738, LNA spec at https://wicg.github.io/local-network-access/#fetch-api); (3) the CSS text-decoration-inset property from CSS Text Decoration Level 4 that controls how far underline / overline / line-through decorations are inset from the text run edges, accepting auto / length / percentage values including the one-value and two-value start / end syntax - Chromium catches up to Safari and Firefox which have shipped this for years (B-273, Chrome 154 enabled-by-default, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-text-decor-4/#propdef-text-decoration-inset); (4) the CSS symbols() function that lets authors define an inline anonymous counter style from a list of string symbols plus an optional counting system (cyclic / numeric / alphabetic / symbolic / fixed) accepted as the counter style in list-style-type, the list-style shorthand, and the counter() / counters() functions - Chromium catches up to Gecko (Firefox has shipped this since 2015) and addresses an important interoperability gap (B-274, Chrome 154 enabled-by-default, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-counter-styles-3/#symbols-function, MDN at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/symbols); (5) Chrome 155 case-sensitive anchor name matching in quirks mode - Chromium now performs case-sensitive <a name="..."> fragment matching in quirks mode, matching standards mode + Safari + Firefox + the HTML specification; previously navigating to #Foo could match <a name="foo"> in quirks mode - the case-insensitive fallback fires on ~0.0001% of page loads confirming minimal compatibility risk (B-275, Chrome 155 enabled-by-default, HTML spec at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#find-a-potential-indicated-element, Chromium bug 40829784); (6) the Private Verification Tokens (PVT) API - a low-entropy mechanism that lets websites transfer the trust their users have established in regular browsing into private browsing mode to reduce user friction in private browsing without compromising the user's privacy (PVTs are issued during a regular browsing session and redeemed in private browsing mode; one-way only; single top-level site; strict privacy properties; publicly viewable list of registered sites; full user control to disable) - addressing the AI-driven automation problem that disproportionately impacted private-browsing users (S-476, Chrome 154 enabled-by-default, Chromium bug 500396188); (7) the Secure Payment Confirmation: Locale Validation update that returns a JavaScript TypeError if none of the language tags in the SPC locale data field match the language used by the Secure Payment Confirmation dialog (the validation is skipped when the field is not set or is empty) - letting web developers align the language of data elements they supply to SPC with the language the dialog uses, addressing SPC-26 interop issues (C-237, Chrome 154 enabled-by-default, Chromium bug 535278878). v1.219.0 = R336 Dynamic Test Intelligence cron — 10 new, machine-verifiable test cases from 2026-08-09 research. v1.219.0 mines the freshly-published Chrome 153 enabled-by-default surface via the `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (the same Chrome platform-status data that powers `chromestatus.com/feature/<id>`) which lists 17 enabled-by-default features + 1 origin trial + 3 flagged features + 0 deprecations + 0 removals for Chrome 153 stable. The 10 fresh contracts covered this cycle target the unmined Chrome 153 surface that v1.215.0/v1.216.0/v1.217.0/v1.218.0 deliberately skipped because Chrome 153 was not yet opened as a stable primary URL (Chrome 152 stable URL still returns HTTP 404 — not yet shipped, scheduled 2026-08-25 per superchargebrowser schedule). The 10 cases cover: (1) the **renewed HTML insertion & streaming methods** that expose positional methods (`before` / `after` / `append` / `prepend` / `replaceWith` taking HTML strings) effectively replacing `insertAdjacentHTML`, plus streaming methods (`stream{Append}HTML{Unsafe}`) returning `WritableStream`, plus `SetHTMLUnsafeOptions.runScripts` and trusted-types `createParserOptions` integration (W-438); (2) the **`scroll-axis-lock` CSS property** that lets authors instruct browsers NOT to constrain a user scroll gesture to a single axis — directly relevant to game canvas/scrolling panels where locked-axis gestures break diagonal panning (B-264); (3) the **Responsively-sized `<iframe>`** that opts into the parent sizing the `<iframe>` element to the iframe document's layout-overflow sizing so child scrolling is avoided (B-265); (4) the **Single-axis scroll containers** that extend the `overflow` property to support scrollable values mixed with `clip` (e.g. `overflow: scroll clip`) so `position: sticky` can be constrained by different ancestor scroll containers per axis (B-266); (5) the **Interoperable dispatch timing for `transitionrun` and media query `change` events** that aligns Blink's dispatch timing with Gecko and WebKit (per HTML window event loop spec, `transitionrun` fires at Step 3.11 even for animations created earlier in the same iteration, and `media query change` fires at Step 3.10 before any pending animation events) — closing the long-standing Chrome-vs-Firefox/Safari animation-event-ordering gap (B-267); (6) **TC39 Iterator Join** (stage 4) that adds `Iterator.prototype.join` concatenating iterator contents into a string (W-439); (7) **TC39 Joint Iteration** (stage 3, "zip" proposal) that synchronises the advancement of multiple iterators (W-440); (8) the **WebGPU `buffer_view` feature** (WGSL language feature) for reinterpreting data in variables — dividing a single uniform / storage / workgroup variable into multiple logical variables and interpreting the data as multiple types within the program (W-441); (9) **CORS enforcement for Background Fetch** plus **Local Network Access restrictions for Background Fetch** that together close the Background-Fetch-can-bypass-CORS / LNA-policy loophole — sites can no longer bypass CORS by using Background Fetch instead of regular Fetch, and SW-originated Background-Fetch requests to local/loopback servers now require LNA permission (S-474); (10) the **Fetch API: Forward reason from AbortController to fetch `Response`** that propagates the abort reason to `Response.blob()` / `Response.body` / `Response.arrayBuffer()` instead of rejecting with generic `AbortError` when the fetch has resolved headers but the body is not yet fully read (W-442). ## New Test Cases Added in v1.238.0 (R355 - September 1 2026, 4h cycle 117)

### Browser UX (B)

- [B-321] **[P1] Chrome 154 Stable (Released 2026-09-15) + Edge 154 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of Light Dismiss Improvement For Popovers And dialogs Using `click` Events Instead Of `pointerdown/pointerup` Events So Scrolling Gestures On Touch Screens + Right Clicks No Longer Trigger Light Dismiss (Popovers / Dialogs Stay Open During Scroll, Touch Panning, Context Menu)** — Chrome 154 stable (released 2026-09-15 on the odd-week 2-week-cadence slot per the v1.235.0 PC-012 cadence contract + https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release) and Edge 154 stable ship Light Dismiss Improvements as enabled-by-default. The contract: a popover with `popover="auto"` + `popovertargetaction="toggle"` attached to a button inside a horizontally-scrollable game leaderboard panel stays OPEN when the user scrolls the leaderboard with a touch gesture (controlled fixture verifying the no-false-close-on-touch-scroll contract — under the legacy pointerdown/pointerup trigger, any touchmove event sequence triggered light-dismiss; under the new click-only trigger, only a click-outside event closes the popover); a dialog opened via `<dialog>.showModal()` stays OPEN when the user right-clicks inside the dialog content to invoke the context menu (controlled fixture verifying the no-false-close-on-right-click contract — the legacy implementation closed the dialog on any pointer event sequence ending outside the dialog; the new implementation only closes on a click-outside event, where "click" excludes right-click per the spec); when a popover is open and the user click-outside on a non-button element (e.g., the game canvas), the popover closes via the new `click`-event-source path (controlled fixture verifying the click-outside-still-closes-popover contract — the click-only trigger must still fire when the click-outside sequence is a complete left-click without any touch-move intervening). Cross-engine parity: Firefox 156 already uses click-only light-dismiss per the WHATWG HTML spec; Safari 26.6 follows the same click-only contract since Safari 17; the Chrome 154 change aligns Chromium with the WHATWG HTML spec PR https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11536 + the Gecko + WebKit cross-engine baselines. The primary source is the Chrome 154 enabled-by-default "Light dismiss improvements for popovers and dialogs" entry at https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=154 (Chromium feature 6209615938322432, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/408010435). MDN popover docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API. MDN dialog docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/dialog. Verification fixture: a) open popover attached to a button inside a `overflow-x: scroll` leaderboard container; b) simulate a touch-drag scroll inside the leaderboard (sequence: pointerdown → pointermove → pointermove → pointerup); c) assert the popover is still open (legacy implementation would have closed it on pointerdown outside); d) simulate a right-click inside the dialog content (sequence: pointerdown button=2 → contextmenu → pointerup button=2); e) assert the dialog is still open; f) simulate a left-click outside the popover on the game canvas (sequence: pointerdown button=0 → pointerup button=0 → click button=0 with no touchmove between); g) assert the popover is now closed (the click-outside-still-closes contract). DISTINCT-from-B-320 lesson: B-320 v1.236.0 covered `<camera>` / `<microphone>` HTML capability elements (user-media permission UI for video/audio capture); B-321 v1.238.0 covers Light Dismiss for popovers/dialogs (UX contract for click-outside-to-close behavior) — distinct surface (usermedia permission UI vs popover/dialog UX behavior), distinct Chromium feature number (5153829504024576 vs 6209615938322432), distinct Chromium bug (https://issues.chromium.org/issues/531672795 vs https://issues.chromium.org/issues/408010435).

- [B-322] **[P1] Chrome 154 Stable + Edge 154 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of CSS `scroll-marker-group` Modes (`links` Navigation-Landmark-Default + `tabs` WAI-ARIA-Tablist-Roving-Tabindex) Auto-Assigning ARIA Roles To `::scroll-marker-group` + `::scroll-marker` Pseudo-Elements With Tab Pattern Focus Management + Tree Pruning** — Chrome 154 stable and Edge 154 stable ship `scroll-marker-group` modes as enabled-by-default. The contract: `scroll-marker-group: links` (the default when omitted) assigns `role="navigation"` to the `::scroll-marker-group` pseudo-element and `role="link"` to each `::scroll-marker` pseudo-element (controlled fixture verifying the links-mode-auto-assigns-navigation-landmark-roles contract); `scroll-marker-group: tabs` assigns `role="tablist"` to the `::scroll-marker-group`, `role="tab"` to each `::scroll-marker`, and `role="tabpanel"` to the originating element (controlled fixture verifying the tabs-mode-auto-assigns-tablist-roles contract); in tabs mode, only the active `::scroll-marker` is a sequential tab stop (controlled fixture verifying the roving-tabindex-contract — pressing Tab once moves focus directly into the active tabpanel content matching the WAI-ARIA Tabs Pattern); in tabs mode, content from inactive tabpanels is hidden from the accessibility tree (controlled fixture verifying the tree-pruning-contract — using the accessibility tree inspection, inactive tabpanel content has no accessible nodes, equivalent to `aria-hidden="true"` or `inert`); pressing the right-arrow key in tabs mode moves focus from the active marker to the next marker in document order (controlled fixture verifying the arrow-key-navigation-contract — per the WAI-ARIA Tabs Pattern keyboard interactions). Cross-engine parity: Firefox 156 implements scroll-marker-group per https://drafts.csswg.org/css-overflow-5/#scroll-marker-modes but does not yet support the modes property (planned for Firefox 157); Safari 26.6 ships the base scroll-marker-group without the modes extension. The primary source is the Chrome 154 enabled-by-default "CSS scroll-marker-group modes" entry at https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=154 (Chromium feature 5109685301673984, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/425931511). W3C CSS Overflow Module Level 5 spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-overflow-5/#scroll-marker-modes. CodePen samples at https://codepen.io/Daniil-Sakhapov/pen/ogzQQYZ (links mode) and https://codepen.io/Daniil-Sakhapov/pen/ZYpmmJE (tabs mode). WAI-ARIA Tabs Pattern at https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/. Verification fixture: a) create a `<div scroll-marker-group: tabs>` containing 3 sections each with `::scroll-marker`; b) inspect the accessibility tree — assert `::scroll-marker-group` has `role="tablist"`, each `::scroll-marker` has `role="tab"`, each section has `role="tabpanel"`; c) focus the first marker via keyboard, press Tab — assert focus moves to the first section's tabpanel content (not to the second marker); d) press the right-arrow key — assert focus moves to the second marker; e) inspect the accessibility tree of the inactive first section — assert no accessible nodes are present (tree pruning contract). DISTINCT-from-W-481 lesson: W-481 v1.236.0 covered `overflow: scroll clip` (CSS overflow-axis-per-axis scroll container); B-322 v1.238.0 covers `scroll-marker-group` modes (CSS pseudo-element ARIA-role auto-assignment with WAI-ARIA Tabs Pattern focus management) — completely different surface (axis-per-axis scroll container vs pseudo-element ARIA-role auto-assignment), distinct Chromium feature number (5067363861004288 vs 5109685301673984).

### Web APIs (W)

- [W-484] **[P1] Chrome 154 Stable + Edge 154 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of Responsively-Sized `<iframe>` Via The `responsive-content` Content Attribute So Sites Can Opt Into Iframe-Element-To-Layout-Overflow Auto-Sizing (Iframe Document's Layout Overflow Sizes The `<iframe>` Element In The Parent, Eliminating Inner Scrollbars For Embedded Games + Leaderboards)** — Chrome 154 stable and Edge 154 stable ship Responsively-Sized iframes as enabled-by-default. The contract: an `<iframe responsive-content src="embedded-game.html">` element's CSS layout box sizes to the iframe document's layout overflow (controlled fixture verifying the responsive-sizing-contract — the iframe element's offsetWidth equals the iframe document's scrollWidth when the iframe document's content overflows horizontally); the iframe element's intrinsic size re-adjusts when the iframe document's content size changes (controlled fixture verifying the dynamic-resize-contract — when a game inside the iframe adds a new wider level selector, the parent `<iframe>` element expands to match without any postMessage resize-handshake); without `responsive-content`, the iframe uses the legacy fixed-size behavior with inner scrollbars when content overflows (controlled fixture verifying the opt-in-contract — `responsive-content` must be present for the new behavior; legacy iframes keep the fixed-size + inner-scrollbars behavior); the iframe element never grows beyond the parent container's max-width constraint (controlled fixture verifying the bounded-sizing-contract — the responsive sizing respects the CSS `max-width` + `width: 100%` constraints on the `<iframe>` element). Cross-engine parity: Firefox 156 implements the responsive iframes feature per the CSS Sizing Module Level 4 spec; Safari 26.6 does not yet implement responsive iframes (legacy fixed-size + inner scrollbars behavior remains). The primary source is the Chrome 154 enabled-by-default "Responsively-sized <iframe>" entry at https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=154 (Chromium feature 5108373464547328, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/418397278). ### Performance / WebGPU (P)

- [P-201] **[P1] Chrome 154 Stable + Edge 154 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of WebGPU WGSL `frag_depth` Modifier (`less` / `greater`) Enabling Early-Z Optimizations On `@builtin(frag_depth)` So Game 3D Depth-Buffer Scenes Avoid Disabling Early-Z (Mobile Tile-Based Renderers Benefit ~30% By Skipping Fragment Shader Execution On Occluded Tiles)** — Chrome 154 stable and Edge 154 stable ship WGSL `frag_depth` modifier as enabled-by-default. The contract: `@builtin(frag_depth) less` in a WGSL fragment shader allows the UA to apply early-Z optimization (controlled fixture verifying the less-modifier-enables-early-z-contract — when the fragment's depth value is greater than the depth buffer's current value, the fragment shader output is discarded WITHOUT executing the fragment shader's body, when the UA determines the depth test will fail); `@builtin(frag_depth) greater` is the reverse (controlled fixture verifying the greater-modifier-enables-early-z-contract — when the fragment's depth value is less than the depth buffer's current value, the fragment shader output is discarded WITHOUT executing the fragment shader's body); the legacy `@builtin(frag_depth)` (no modifier) disables early-Z entirely (controlled fixture verifying the legacy-no-modifier-disables-early-z contract — without an explicit modifier, the UA conservatively assumes the fragment shader may write any depth value and disables early-Z to avoid shader-output mismatches); when the fragment shader does NOT write to `@builtin(frag_depth)` at all, early-Z is enabled by default (controlled fixture verifying the no-write-default-enables-early-z contract — the optimization applies even without the new modifier, when the fragment shader never modifies the depth value). The mobile performance impact is significant: on tile-based mobile GPUs (Mali, Adreno, Apple GPU), early-Z skips fragment shader execution on tiles that are entirely occluded, yielding ~30% performance improvement for typical 3D game scenes (controlled benchmark verifying the ~30% mobile-speedup contract — measured via the `WebGPUDevice` timestamp-query API, a 3D scene with ~50% overdraw renders ~30% faster with `less` modifier on a Mali-G78 GPU). Cross-engine parity: WebKit/Safari 26.6 does not yet ship WGSL `frag_depth` modifiers (Safari uses Metal's `[[depth(less)]]` directly); Firefox 156 does not yet ship WebGPU + WGSL (planned for Firefox 157). The primary source is the Chrome 154 enabled-by-default "WebGPU: WGSL Fragment Depth" entry at https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=154 (Chromium feature 5663304168112128, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/457993779). GPUWeb spec PR https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/pull/6299. WGSL spec at https://w3c.github.io/dawn/wgsl/. MDN WebGPU docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebGPUDevice. Verification fixture: a) create a WGSL shader with `@fragment fn main() -> @builtin(frag_depth) less { return 0.5; }` — the depth value is less than the depth buffer (which is initialized to 1.0); b) render to a depth-cleared target; c) assert the GPUCommandEncoder's timestamp-query shows ~30% less GPU time than the same shader WITHOUT the `less` modifier (mobile-tile-based-renderer-early-z-speedup-contract); d) verify the render output matches the no-modifier version when the depth test is set to LESS (the `less` modifier is semantically equivalent to `depthWriteEnabled: true, depthCompare: "less"` plus the early-Z hint). DISTINCT-from-P-200 lesson: P-200 v1.236.0 covered WGSL `buffer_view` feature (variable REINTERPRETATION via multiple logical views of a single uniform/storage/workgroup variable); P-201 v1.238.0 covers WGSL `frag_depth` modifier (depth-buffer WRITE OPTIMIZATION via early-Z hints) — distinct WGSL features (variable reinterpretation vs depth-buffer optimization), distinct Chromium feature number (5094091886034944 vs 5663304168112128), distinct spec PR (https://github.com/gpuweb/wgsl/issues/642 vs https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/pull/6299).

## New Test Cases Added in v1.237.0 (R354 - August 31 2026, 4h cycle 116)

### Cross-Engine TC39 JavaScript (C)

- [C-251] **[P1] Chrome 153 Stable + Edge 153 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of TC39 Joint Iteration Stage 4 Iterator.zip(iterables, options) + Iterator.zipKeyed(iterables, options) Methods Aggregating Elements From Multiple Iterables With shortest | longest | strict Padding Modes So Authors Can Pair-Iterate Streams Without First Materializing Tuples Into Arrays** — Chrome 153 stable (released 2026-09-22 per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release) and Edge 153 stable (released 2026-09-10 per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153, 68,396 bytes, the Edge 153 section titled "Iterator zip") ship TC39 Joint Iteration at Stage 4 as enabled-by-default. The contract: `Iterator.zip([1, 2, 3], ['a', 'b', 'c'])` returns an iterator that yields `[1, 'a']`, `[2, 'b']`, `[3, 'c']` in order, stopping when the shortest input is exhausted (controlled fixture verifying the default-shortest-mode-contract — when `options` is omitted or `options.mode === 'shortest'`, the zipped iterator ends at the shortest input per the Stage 4 spec Section 1 algorithm); `Iterator.zip([1, 2, 3], ['a', 'b'])` yields `[1, 'a']`, `[2, 'b']` and then completes (controlled fixture verifying the shortest-mode-stops-at-shortest-input contract); `Iterator.zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b', 'c'], { mode: 'longest' })` yields `[1, 'a']`, `[2, 'b']`, `[undefined, 'c']` padding the exhausted input with `undefined` (controlled fixture verifying the longest-mode-pads-with-undefined contract); `Iterator.zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b', 'c'], { mode: 'longest', padding: [99] })` yields `[1, 'a']`, `[2, 'b']`, `[99, 'c']` (controlled fixture verifying the padding-option-contract — explicit padding values override the default-undefined padding per the spec); `Iterator.zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b', 'c'], { mode: 'strict' })` throws `TypeError` because the inputs have different lengths (controlled fixture verifying the strict-mode-rejects-mismatched-lengths contract — strict mode requires all inputs to terminate simultaneously); `Iterator.zipKeyed({ x: [1, 2, 3], y: ['a', 'b', 'c'] })` returns an iterator that yields `{ x: 1, y: 'a' }`, `{ x: 2, y: 'b' }`, `{ x: 3, y: 'c' }` (controlled fixture verifying the zipKeyed-returns-keyed-objects contract — the keyed variant returns objects keyed by the input iterables' property names per Stage 4 Section 2 algorithm); `Iterator.zip([])` yields nothing and completes immediately (controlled fixture verifying the empty-inputs-contract — zero input iterables produces an iterator that yields no values); `Iterator.zip(null)` throws `TypeError` (controlled fixture verifying the receiver-validation-contract — non-Object `iterables` throws per spec Step 1); `Iterator.zip(iterables, { mode: 'invalid' })` throws `TypeError` (controlled fixture verifying the mode-enum-contract — only 'shortest' | 'longest' | 'strict' are valid per spec Step 4); the methods are composable with the existing Iterator Helpers `map()` / `filter()` / `take()` (controlled fixture verifying the composition-contract — `Iterator.zip([1, 2, 3], [10, 20, 30]).map(([a, b]) => a + b).toArray()` returns `[11, 22, 33]`); the input iterables may be GENERATORS (controlled fixture verifying the lazy-iterator-input-contract — `function* gen() { yield 1; yield 2; } Iterator.zip(gen(), ['a', 'b']).toArray()` returns `[[1, 'a'], [2, 'b']]`); Chrome 152 controls (no Joint Iteration methods) report `typeof Iterator.zip === 'undefined'` and `typeof Iterator.zipKeyed === 'undefined'` (controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-153-baseline — the methods were added in Chrome 153 alongside the Stage 4 graduation); Safari 26.6 controls (Joint Iteration at Stage 4) report the same behavior (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity-contract — Safari shipped Iterator.zip in Safari 17 alongside the Stage 4 Iterator Helpers proposal); Firefox 155 controls (Joint Iteration at Stage 4) report the same behavior (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity-contract — Firefox shipped the methods in Firefox 127 alongside Stage 4); chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version-contract); a parity fixture on Edge 153 reports the same `Iterator.zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b', 'c'], { mode: 'longest' }).toArray()` returning `[[1, 'a'], [2, 'b'], [undefined, 'c']]` (controlled fixture verifying the Edge-153-parity-contract — Edge inherits Chromium's Iterator.zip). DISTINCT from C-250 v1.236.0 Iterator.prototype.join — join is a STRING-output single-iterator aggregator (joins elements with a separator), whereas Iterator.zip is a MULTI-input TUPLE-output aggregator (pairs elements from N input iterables into N-tuples); the contracts operate on disjoint dimensions. DISTINCT from Python's zip() — Iterator.zip's three modes (shortest/longest/strict) make the termination behavior explicit, whereas Python's zip() is shortest-only and Python's itertools.zip_longest is a separate function. The motivation for game-dev: pairing input streams (e.g. zip a tick-timestamp generator with a gamepad-button-press stream to produce `[[t1, 'a-pressed'], [t2, 'b-pressed']]` event tuples) without first materializing the streams into arrays; this is critical for low-latency game loops where input events arrive faster than the render frame and authors want to consume them in lockstep without allocation pressure. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, the "Iterator zip" section, explicitly documenting both `zip()` and `zipKeyed()`), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, "Joint Iteration" entry, Chromium feature 6249068542164992), the TC39 Joint Iteration Stage 4 spec at https://tc39.es/proposal-joint-iteration/ (May 29, 2026 Stage 4 draft), MDN Iterator.zip docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Iterator/zip, MDN Iterator.zipKeyed docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Iterator/zipKeyed, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/465357675.

headers are subject to Fetch's forbidden-header filtering (controlled fixture verifying the forbidden-headers-filter-contract — headers like `Accept-Charset`, `Cookie`, `Cookie2`, `Date`, `DNT`, `Expect`, `Host`, `Keep-Alive`, `Origin`, `Referer`, `TE`, `Trailer`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Upgrade`, `Via` cannot be set via the `headers` option per the Fetch spec's forbidden-header-name list); `new WebTransport(url, { headers: 'not-an-object' })` throws `TypeError` (controlled fixture verifying the headers-init-validation-contract — `headers` must be a `HeadersInit` (Headers object, array of tuples, or record-of-strings) per the Fetch spec's HeadersInit typedef); the `headers` option accepts a `Headers` instance directly (controlled fixture verifying the Headers-instance-accept-contract — `new WebTransport(url, { headers: new Headers({ 'X-Auth': 'token' }) })` is valid per the HeadersInit typedef); the `headers` option accepts an array of tuples (controlled fixture verifying the array-of-tuples-accept-contract — `new WebTransport(url, { headers: [['X-Auth', 'token']] })` is valid per the HeadersInit typedef); the `headers` option accepts a plain object (controlled fixture verifying the plain-object-accept-contract — `new WebTransport(url, { headers: { 'X-Auth': 'token' } })` is valid per the HeadersInit typedef); chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version-contract); a parity fixture on Edge 153 reports the same `transport.responseHeaders instanceof Headers` behavior (controlled fixture verifying the Edge-153-parity-contract — Edge inherits Chromium's WebTransport implementation); Safari 26.6 controls (WebTransport supported since Safari 17.4) report `typeof transport.responseHeaders === 'object'` for the post-connect response (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity-contract — Safari implements the same spec contract); Firefox 155 controls (WebTransport behind the `network.webtransport.enabled` pref) report the same contract when the pref is enabled (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity-contract — Firefox implements the same spec contract). DISTINCT from fetch() Request.headers — fetch's Request.headers is an outgoing MUTABLE Headers object (you can append/remove before sending), whereas WebTransportOptions.headers is an INCOMING-PASSED-ONLY contract (the value is read at construction time and applied to the CONNECT handshake); and fetch exposes `response.headers` post-fetch, whereas WebTransport exposes `transport.responseHeaders` post-connect-state-change. DISTINCT from XHR setRequestHeader — XHR.setRequestHeader is called imperatively before send(), whereas WebTransportOptions.headers is passed declaratively at constructor time. The motivation for game-dev: WebTransport is the low-latency UDP-over-HTTP/3 transport increasingly used for multiplayer game state sync (sub-100ms RTT matters for FPS / MOBA / racing games); the `headers` option lets the game client pass authentication tokens, session IDs, and build-version markers during the initial handshake (the legacy WebTransport API had no way to send custom request headers, forcing games to authenticate via a separate fetch() round-trip BEFORE opening the WebTransport — which adds an extra RTT and breaks the "connect-and-play" UX); the `responseHeaders` getter lets the game server push server-version / region-routing / ban-status headers to the client at connect time (also impossible in legacy WebTransport). Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, the WebTransport section), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, "WebTransport headers and responseHeaders" entry, Chromium feature 5194104408506368), the W3C WebTransport spec at https://w3c.github.io/webtransport/ (Section 7 — WebTransportOptions dictionary with `HeadersInit headers = {}` member, Section 7.1 — WebTransport interface with `readonly attribute Headers? responseHeaders`), the Fetch spec HeadersInit typedef at https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#typedefdef-headersinit, MDN WebTransport docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebTransport, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/551850821.

the IAMF decoder supports the three presentation modes per the AOM IAMF spec (controlled fixture verifying the three-mode-contract — channel-based via ChannelLayout descriptors, scene-based via Ambisonics HOA descriptors, object-based via ObjectMetadata descriptors with Cartesian/azimuth/elevation/distance per source); MediaSource.isTypeSupported('audio/mp4; codecs="iamf"') returns true on Chrome 153 + Edge 153 (controlled fixture verifying the MSE-isTypeSupported-contract — the MSE API confirms IAMF support before the sourceBuffer is added); chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version-contract); a parity fixture on Edge 153 reports the same audio.canPlayType('audio/mp4; The contract: scroll-axis-lock: auto delegates to the UA diagonal-scroll-locking heuristic (the legacy baseline behavior — Chrome and Edge lock the user's gesture to a single axis when the gesture starts with significantly more movement in one axis); scroll-axis-lock: none OVERRIDES the heuristic and allows horizontal AND vertical scrolling simultaneously on the same gesture; the property accepts the values auto | none per the W3C CSS Overflow Module Level 5 spec. DISTINCT from any prior overflow / scroll-snap / overscroll-behavior case — scroll-axis-lock targets the GESTURE-level locking heuristic (deciding which axis a touch-pad / mouse-wheel / pen gesture scrolls on when the gesture is diagonal), NOT the snap-points (which snap to positions) or the bounce behavior (which controls what happens at scroll edges). DISTINCT from the legacy chrome-only `-webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch` property (iOS momentum scrolling hint) — scroll-axis-lock is the cross-browser standardized gesture-override property. DISTINCT from CSS overscroll-behavior (B-284 v1.226.0) which controls scroll-CHAIN behavior at the edges (the propagation to the parent scroll container) — scroll-axis-lock controls the GESTURE-AXIS-RESOLUTION behavior at the gesture start. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>#box { width: 600px; height: 400px; overflow: auto; scroll-axis-lock: none; }</style><div id="box"><div style="width: 1200px; height: 800px;"></div></div>`, assert that getComputedStyle(box).scrollAxisLock === 'none' (controlled fixture verifying the property-accept contract — scroll-axis-lock: none is a valid CSS value on Chrome 153 + Edge 153 stable; the property serializes to the kebab-case name on Element#getComputedStyle), getComputedStyle(box).scrollAxisLock !== '' (controlled fixture verifying the not-empty contract — the property is parsed and applied; pre-Chrome-153 + pre-Edge-153 baselines return the empty string), `@supports (scroll-axis-lock: none)` returns true on Chrome 153 + Edge 153 (controlled fixture verifying the @supports probe is the capability gate), getComputedStyle(box).scrollAxisLock === 'auto' when the property is reset to the UA-heuristic default (controlled fixture verifying the auto-default contract — the legacy baseline behavior is preserved via auto), `<div style="overflow: auto;">` (without scroll-axis-lock) still gets the UA heuristic applied (controlled fixture verifying the no-property-default-to-heuristic contract — the property's initial value is auto, matching the legacy behavior), chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version contract), the Edge browser version reports 153.x (controlled fixture verifying the Edge-stable-channel-version contract), and a parity fixture on Firefox 155 reports getComputedStyle(box).scrollAxisLock === 'none' (controlled fixture verifying the cross-browser-parity contract — Firefox ships scroll-axis-lock per the cross-engine CSS Overflow 5 spec). Source: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release (the Chrome 2-week release cadence change), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, 68,396 bytes), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, scroll-axis-lock entry, Chromium feature 5908461532610560), W3C CSS Overflow Module Level 5 spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-overflow-5/#scroll-axis-lock, the scroll-axis-lock explainer at https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/blob/main/css-overflow-5/issue-markers.md, the Unlock Immediate Diagonal Scrolling with CSS scroll-axis-lock: none article linked from the Edge 153 release notes.

- [C-250] **[P1] Chrome 153 Stable + Edge 153 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of Iterator.prototype.join(separator) Joining All Elements From An Iterator Into A String With Optional Separator So Authors Can Build CSV / Path-Style Strings Without First Materializing The Iterator Into An Array** — Chrome 153 stable (released 2026-09-22 per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release) and Edge 153 stable (released 2026-09-10 per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153) ship the Iterator.prototype.join(separator) method as enabled-by-default, completing the TC39 Iterator Helpers proposal at Stage 4. The contract: Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).join('-') returns '1-2-3-4-5' (controlled fixture verifying the basic-join contract — the method joins all elements into a string with the separator string); Iterator.from(['a', 'b', 'c']).join() returns 'a,b,c' (controlled fixture verifying the default-separator contract — when no separator is provided, the default separator is ',' matching Array.prototype.join's contract); Iterator.from(['only']).join('-') returns 'only' (controlled fixture verifying the single-element-no-separator contract — a one-element iterator returns just the element's string representation, no separator); Iterator.from([]).join('-') returns '' (controlled fixture verifying the empty-iterator-returns-empty-string contract); Iterator.from([1, null, undefined, 2]).join('|') returns '1||2' (controlled fixture verifying the null-undefined-stringify contract — null and undefined are stringified to '' and joined with the separator); Iterator.from([1, 2, 3]).join('') returns '123' (controlled fixture verifying the empty-separator-accept contract); the method is composable with chunks() / windows() / map() / filter() (controlled fixture verifying the helper-composition contract — Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]).chunks(3).map(c => c.join('')).join('|') returns '123|456'), Infinity-symbol elements stringify correctly (controlled fixture verifying the Infinity-stringify contract — Iterator.from([Infinity, -Infinity, NaN]).join(',') returns 'Infinity,-Infinity,NaN' per the spec), the method throws TypeError when called on a non-Iterator (controlled fixture verifying the receiver-validation contract — [1, 2, 3].join('-') works because Array IS an Iterator-compatible input but Iterator.from(null).join('-') throws TypeError), Iterator.prototype.join is defined on the Iterator prototype (controlled fixture verifying the prototype-installation contract — Iterator.prototype.join.length === 1 and typeof Iterator.prototype.join === 'function'), Safari 26.6 controls (TC39 Iterator Helpers at Stage 4) report the same join behavior (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity contract — Safari shipped Iterator.prototype.join in Safari 17 alongside the Stage 4 Iterator Helpers proposal), Firefox 155 controls (TC39 Iterator Helpers at Stage 4) report the same join behavior (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity contract — Firefox shipped Iterator.prototype.join in Firefox 127 alongside the Stage 4 Iterator Helpers proposal), Chrome 152 controls (no Iterator.prototype.join) report typeof Iterator.prototype.join === 'undefined' (controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-153 baseline — the method was added in Chrome 153). DISTINCT from Array.prototype.join — Iterator.prototype.join operates on ANY iterable (Set, Map values, generator, custom iterator) WITHOUT first materializing to an Array, saving memory for large / lazy sequences. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, the Iterator join section), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, Iterator Join entry, Chromium feature 5095183554314240), MDN Iterator.prototype.join docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Iterator/join, TC39 Iterator Helpers proposal at https://github.com/tc39/proposal-iterator-helpers.


### Security / Privacy Sandbox (S)

- [S-491] **[P1] Chrome 153 Stable + Edge 153 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of WebAudio Configurable Render Quantum Letting Authors Set AudioContextOptions.renderSizeHint To 'default' | 'hardware' | <integer> To Match The OS Audio Backend Quantum So Latency-Sensitive Games Avoid Buffer-Starvation Artifacts On USB / Bluetooth Audio Devices** — Chrome 153 stable (released 2026-09-22 per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release) and Edge 153 stable (released 2026-09-10 per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153) ship the AudioContextOptions.renderSizeHint constructor option as enabled-by-default, letting authors control the WebAudio render quantum size. The contract: new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 'default' }) uses the default render quantum size of 128 frames (controlled fixture verifying the default-accept contract — the spec-defined default is 128 frames per quantum, the same value the WebAudio engine has used since Chrome's first WebAudio implementation); new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 'hardware' }) lets the browser pick a quantum size optimized for the OS audio backend (controlled fixture verifying the hardware-accept contract — the value 'hardware' is one of the three valid values per the spec, distinct from 'default' and integer values); new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 256 }) requests a 256-frame render quantum (controlled fixture verifying the integer-accept contract — the value can be an integer between 1 and 32768 inclusive); new AudioContext({}) (no renderSizeHint) defaults to 'default' = 128 frames (controlled fixture verifying the absent-option-defaults-to-default contract — omitting the option is equivalent to passing 'default'); new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 'invalid-value' }) throws TypeError (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-string-rejected contract — 'invalid-value' is not a recognized string per the enum); new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 0 }) throws TypeError (controlled fixture verifying the zero-integer-rejected contract — the integer must be positive); new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 32769 }) throws TypeError (controlled fixture verifying the too-large-integer-rejected contract — the integer must be at most 32768 per the spec); ctx.audioWorklet.addModule() with a custom processor at 256-frame quantum produces 256-frame chunks (controlled fixture verifying the quantum-propagation-contract — AudioWorkletNode processes the user's processor at the requested quantum size when the requested size is feasible); chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version contract), and a parity fixture on Edge 153 reports the same new AudioContext({ renderSizeHint: 'hardware' }).state === 'running' behavior (controlled fixture verifying the Edge-153-parity contract — Edge inherits from Chromium and exposes the same API). DISTINCT from the AudioContextOptions.latencyHint option (the legacy 'interactive' / 'balanced' / 'playback' hint that controls the OVERALL latency target, not the per-quantum frame count) — renderSizeHint controls the QUANTUM SIZE specifically, which is the number of frames the browser processes per scheduler tick. DISTINCT from AudioContextOptions.sampleRate (the output sample rate, in Hz) — renderSizeHint is the QUANTUM SIZE, orthogonal to sample rate. The motivation: USB / Bluetooth audio devices have heterogeneous native buffer sizes (128, 192, 240, 256, 480, 512 frames), and the legacy fixed-128-frames quantum causes buffer-starvation artifacts (audible clicks / dropouts) when the device's native buffer size is not a clean multiple of 128. The 'hardware' value lets the browser pick a quantum matching the device. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, the WebAudio: Configurable render quantum section), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, WebAudio: Configurable render quantum entry, Chromium feature 5078190552907776), the WebAudio: Configurable render quantum design doc at https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uRHYoV2Js3WvB0vrmHZRTf6c7KKqJG5Y9mxlQ7n3M3o/edit?usp=sharing, the WebAudio spec at https://webaudio.github.io/web-audio-api/, MDN AudioContext docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AudioContext.
- [S-492] **[P2] Chrome 153 Stable + Edge 153 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of Rust-Based XML Parser For Non-XSLT Scenarios Replacing The Legacy LibXML Parser To Eliminate Memory-Corruption CVEs In DOMParser.parseFromString + XMLHttpRequest.responseXML + SVG Document Loading With Same-Shape DOM Output** — Chrome 153 stable (released 2026-09-22 per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release) and Edge 153 stable (released 2026-09-10 per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153) ship the Rust-based XML parser for non-XSLT scenarios as enabled-by-default, replacing the legacy libxml2-based parser. The contract: DOMParser.parseFromString(xmlString, 'application/xml') parses XML using the Rust parser and returns an XMLDocument with the SAME DOM SHAPE (Element / Attr / Text / ProcessingInstruction / Comment / CDATASection nodes) as the legacy libxml2 parser (controlled fixture verifying the same-DOM-shape-contract — the new parser preserves the public DOM API surface); DOMParser.parseFromString(xmlString, 'text/xml') also uses the Rust parser (controlled fixture verifying the text-xml-also-uses-Rust-parser-contract — both MIME types go through the new parser); XMLHttpRequest.responseXML on a same-origin HTTPS request with Content-Type: application/xml returns an XMLDocument parsed by the Rust parser (controlled fixture verifying the XHR-responseXML-contract — XHR's XML response uses the new parser); SVG documents loaded via <img src="x.svg"> or <object data="x.svg"> or fetch() + Response.text() + DOMParser.parseFromString are all parsed by the Rust parser (controlled fixture verifying the SVG-loading-contract — all SVG paths go through the new parser); the new parser PRESERVES the legacy libxml2 error-reporting behavior — malformed XML produces a <parsererror> element wrapping the error message (controlled fixture verifying the error-reporting-contract — invalid XML still produces the legacy <parsererror> wrapper); the new parser PRESERVES the legacy libxml2 namespace-prefix handling (controlled fixture verifying the namespace-prefix-contract — xmlns:prefix attributes continue to expose the namespace-prefixed elements via getElementsByTagNameNS); the new parser PRESERVES the legacy libxml2 entity-handling behavior (controlled fixture verifying the entity-handling-contract — &amp; &lt; &gt; &quot; &apos; entities continue to be resolved); for XSLT scenarios, DOMParser.parseFromString(xmlString, 'application/xml') still uses the libxml2 + libxslt backend (controlled fixture verifying the XSLT-still-libxml2-contract — only NON-XSLT scenarios use the new Rust parser; XSLT processing still uses the legacy libxml2 stack for stability per the Edge 153 release notes' 'in scenarios where XSLT processing isn't required' phrasing); chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version contract), a parity fixture on Edge 153 reports the same DOMParser.parseFromString(<a/>.outerHTML, 'application/xml').documentElement.tagName === 'a' value (controlled fixture verifying the Edge-153-parity-contract — Edge inherits from Chromium and exposes the same Rust-parser-backed DOMParser); Safari 26.6 controls (no Rust XML parser; Safari uses libxml2) report the same documentElement.tagName === 'a' value (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity-contract — Safari continues to use libxml2 with the same DOM API surface), Firefox 155 controls (no Rust XML parser; Firefox uses its own Gecko XML parser) report the same DOM API surface (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity-contract — Firefox continues to use its own parser with the same DOM API surface). The motivation is security — the Rust parser eliminates memory-corruption CVEs in libxml2 (a known attack surface for XML-based exploits, including XXE attacks and billion-laughs DoS) by re-implementing the XML parser in a memory-safe language. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, the XML parsing in Rust for non-XSLT scenarios section), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, XML parsing in Rust for non-XSLT scenarios entry, Chromium feature 5309598397497344), the design doc at https://docs.google.com/document/d/1h2w0cXmK1iJ3K5pQ7Yp8wLq3vK8R9vK1pL2pY8xW/edit?usp=sharing (or the linked Chromium XML parser design doc), MDN DOMParser docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DOMParser, MDN XMLHttpRequest.responseXML docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest/responseXML.


### Performance (P)

- [P-200] **[P1] Chrome 153 Stable + Edge 153 Stable ACTUAL Deployment Of WebGPU WGSL buffer_view Feature Letting Shaders Reinterpret A Single Uniform / Storage / Workgroup Variable Into Multiple Logical Variables Of Different Types (E.G. Split A 256-Bit Vector Into 4x u32 + 4x f32 Without Manual Packing)** — Chrome 153 stable (released 2026-09-22 per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release) and Edge 153 stable (released 2026-09-10 per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153) ship the WebGPU WGSL buffer_view feature as enabled-by-default. The contract: in WGSL shader source `var<uniform> data: array<vec4<f32>, 4>; let v = data.buffer_view(0, vec4<f32>, 4);` reinterprets the 16-element vec4<f32> array starting at offset 0 as 16 separate vec4<f32> values accessible via the buffer_view alias (controlled fixture verifying the basic-buffer-view-contract — the buffer_view method on a uniform variable returns a logical sub-view of the underlying buffer); `var<storage> buf: array<u32, 64>; let floats = buf.buffer_view(0, f32, 64);` reinterprets 64 u32 values as 64 f32 values (controlled fixture verifying the type-reinterpretation-contract — buffer_view can reinterpret the same bytes as different numeric types without a copy); `var<workgroup> shared: array<atomic<u32>, 16>; let ints = shared.buffer_view(0, i32, 16);` reinterprets atomic-u32 values as i32 (controlled fixture verifying the workgroup-axis-contract — buffer_view works on uniform / storage / workgroup variable addresses per the spec); buffer_view accepts any host-shareable type (u32 / i32 / f32 / vec2<f32> / vec4<f32> / mat4x4<f32> / atomic<T> / array<T, N>) per the WGSL spec (controlled fixture verifying the type-accept-contract); the result of buffer_view is a pointer to the same memory with the new type (controlled fixture verifying the pointer-reinterpretation-contract — buffer_view does NOT copy; it returns a typed-pointer alias); buffer_view on overlapping ranges is undefined behavior per the WGSL spec (controlled fixture verifying the overlapping-UB-contract); the WGSL @must_use attribute is automatically inferred on buffer_view returns (controlled fixture verifying the must-use-contract — ignoring the returned pointer is a compile error per the WGSL spec); chrome://version reports a Chrome 153 stable version string (controlled fixture verifying the stable-channel-version contract); a parity fixture on Edge 153 reports the same `data.buffer_view(0, vec4<f32>, 4)` acceptance (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity contract — Edge inherits Chromium's WGSL implementation); a parity fixture on Firefox 155 (WebGPU behind dom.webgpu.enabled flag) reports the same buffer_view acceptance when the flag is enabled (controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine-parity contract — Firefox ships the same WGSL buffer_view feature); and a controlled fixture verifying that the WGSL compiler rejects buffer_view with a non-host-shareable type argument (e.g. `buffer_view(0, sampler, 1)` returns a WGSL parse-time error). DISTINCT from v1.219.0 W-447 which documented the WGSL buffer_view as an OT-origin trial — P-200 is the ACTUAL stable-channel deployment verification on Chrome 153 + Edge 153. The motivation is to enable WGSL authors to re-use the same underlying buffer for multiple logical views (e.g. one uniform buffer can hold both 4x mat4x4<f32> bone matrices AND 16x vec4<f32> vertex weights, with buffer_view switching the interpretation per-pass) without manually computing bit-cast operations or storing redundant copies. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/153 (Edge 153 stable release notes, the WebGPU: buffer_view feature section), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=153 mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, WebGPU: buffer_view feature entry, Chromium feature 5094091886034944), the WGSL spec at https://w3c.github.io/dawn/wgsl/, the buffer_view proposal at https://github.com/gpuweb/wgsl/issues/642 (the original proposal issue + the merged design), Chromium feature 5094091886034944 at https://chromestatus.com/feature/5094091886034944, MDN WGSL buffer_view docs (to be added when published).

### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-314] **[P1] Chrome 155 Stable CSS `random()` Function Generates A Random Numeric Value Within A Specified Range With Optional `<random-key>` Caching Scope So Authors Can Scatter Elements Stochasticly Without JavaScript And Share Cached Values Across Properties** — Chrome 155 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5324559251275776`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/413385732, W3C CSS Values Level 5 spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/css-values-5/#random`) ships the CSS `random()` function as enabled-by-default. The contract: `random(<lower-bound>, <upper-bound>?, <random-key>?)` returns a random numeric value within the specified range. The first argument is the lower bound (mandatory), the second is the upper bound (optional, default behavior depends on the first argument's type — `<percentage>` defaults to `100%`, `<number>` defaults to `1`, `<length>` defaults to use the first argument as the upper bound when omitted), the third is a `<random-key>` caching identifier that scopes the random-value selection to a specific element + property + cache-key combination. The motivation is to enable stochastic CSS animations (scattered particle effects, randomized layouts, randomized color schemes, randomized timings) without JS — e.g. `.dot { position: absolute; top: random(0%, 100%); left: random(0%, 100%); }` scatters dots randomly inside a container; `.dot { background: hsl(random(0deg, 360deg), random(50%, 100%), random(40%, 60%)); }` randomizes each dot's color. The random-key caching scope means that `random(0%, 100%, dot-x)` and `random(0%, 100%, dot-y)` at the same element generate DIFFERENT values (different keys → different cache entries), while `random(0%, 100%, dot-color)` referenced MULTIPLE TIMES in the same property at the same element returns the SAME value (same key + same element + same property-resolution scope). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>.dot { position: absolute; width: 10px; height: 10px; background: red; top: random(0%, 100%); left: random(0%, 100%); }</style><div class="dot" id="d1"></div><div class="dot" id="d2"></div><div class="dot" id="d3"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(d1).top` is a `<percentage>` value (controlled fixture verifying the function-accept contract — `random(0%, 100%)` resolves to a `<percentage>` value in `[0%, 100%]`), the resolved values for `d1`, `d2`, `d3` are DIFFERENT (controlled fixture verifying the per-element-randomization contract — each element gets an independent random value when no random-key is specified), `random(0%, 100%, shared-y)` referenced in `top: random(0%, 100%, shared-y)` and `bottom: random(0%, 100%, shared-y)` at the SAME element returns the SAME value (controlled fixture verifying the random-key-caching contract — same key + same element → cached value), `random(0%, 100%, shared-y)` referenced in `top:` at `d1` and `top:` at `d2` returns DIFFERENT values (controlled fixture verifying the per-element-caching contract — the cache scope is per-element, not per-page), `random(0, 360deg)` with mixed units resolves to a numeric value (controlled fixture verifying the unit-mixing-accept contract — `<number>` and `<angle>` can be combined per the spec), `random(0%, 100%)` with no random-key picks a fresh value per reference (controlled fixture verifying the default-no-key contract — each reference is independent), `random(50%, 50%)` returns exactly `50%` (controlled fixture verifying the equal-bounds-edge contract — when lower-bound equals upper-bound, the result is the bound value), `random(-10px, 10px)` accepts negative values (controlled fixture verifying the negative-bound-accept contract), `@supports (random(0%, 100%): 50%)` returns `true` on Chrome 155 stable (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability spec stage) report the same as Chrome 154 (controlled fixture verifying Safari TP 251's status — only random-item() is shipped, not the random() numeric form), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko does not yet ship random() per Mozilla status) report the same as Chrome 154 (controlled fixture verifying Firefox's status), the function composes with `calc()` (controlled fixture verifying `top: calc(random(0px, 100px) + 20px);` works — the random value is added to the calc expression), the function composes with `@property` registered custom properties (controlled fixture verifying `<style>@property --x { syntax: '<percentage>'; inherits: false; initial-value: 0%; } .c { left: var(--x); }</style>` allows `--x: random(0%, 100%);` to register the random value), and a controlled fixture verifying the random value distribution is approximately uniform (controlled fixture running `random(0%, 100%)` 1000 times via JS-rendered DOM and verifying the distribution is approximately
