- [B-315] **[P2] Chrome 155 Stable CSS `margin-trim` Property Omits Margins Before/After The First/Last Child Of A Block Container Or Multi-Column Container So Authors Don't Need To Zero-Out Child Margins Manually** — Chrome 155 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5197863732772864`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40886857, W3C CSS Box Model Level 4 spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-box-4/#margin-trim`) ships the CSS `margin-trim` property as enabled-by-default. The contract: `margin-trim` accepts the values `none` (default — no trimming, child margins preserved), `block-start` (omit the margin before the first in-flow child), `block-end` (omit the margin after the last in-flow child), and `block` (omit BOTH the margin before the first child AND after the last child). The property is supported on regular block containers AND multi-column containers (NOT on flex containers or grid containers per the current spec). The motivation is to give authors a more powerful / generic / expressive alternative to the legacy margin quirk that applies to P / H1 / H2 elements inside BODY and table-cell elements (in quirks mode) — the `margin-trim` property works in standards mode on ANY block container, regardless of the children. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>.container { margin-trim: block; background: lightblue; } .child { margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px; background: red; height: 30px; }</style><div class="container" id="c"><div class="child">First</div><div class="child">Middle</div><div class="child">Last</div></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(c).marginTrim === 'block'` (controlled fixture verifying the property-accept contract — `margin-trim: block` is a valid CSS property value), the container's `height` is the SUM of child heights WITHOUT the first-child's top margin AND WITHOUT the last-child's bottom margin (controlled fixture verifying the trim-both-ends contract — `c.offsetHeight === 30 + 30 + 30 + 0 = 90` px; the 20px top margin of the first child and 20px bottom margin of the last child are trimmed), `<style>.container { margin-trim: block-start; }</style>` omits only the first-child's top margin (controlled fixture verifying the block-start-only contract — `c.offsetHeight === 30 + 30 + 30 + 20 = 110` px; the 20px bottom margin of the last child is preserved), `<style>.container { margin-trim: block-end; }</style>` omits only the last-child's bottom margin (controlled fixture verifying the block-end-only contract — `c.offsetHeight === 30 + 30 + 30 + 20 = 110` px; the 20px top margin of the first child is preserved), `<style>.container { margin-trim: none; }</style>` (the default) preserves all child margins (controlled fixture verifying the default-no-trim contract — `c.offsetHeight === 30 + 30 + 30 + 20 + 20 = 120` px), `margin-trim` works on multi-column containers (controlled fixture verifying `<div style="column-count: 2; margin-trim: block;">...</div>` trims the first child's margin-top and the last child's margin-bottom across the multi-column flow), `margin-trim` does NOT work on flex containers (controlled fixture verifying the flex-no-support contract — `<div style="display: flex; margin-trim: block;">...</div>` does NOT trim child margins; `getComputedStyle(flexContainer).marginTrim === 'block'` is parsed but has no effect on flex children per the spec's "Note: A previous version of the spec also applied this for flex and grid containers, but this has been removed."), `margin-trim` does NOT work on grid containers (controlled fixture verifying the grid-no-support contract — `<div style="display: grid; margin-trim: block;">...</div>` does NOT trim child margins), the property only affects in-flow children (controlled fixture verifying the in-flow-only contract — absolutely-positioned children are not affected by margin-trim on the container), `@supports (margin-trim: block)` returns `true` on Chrome 155 stable (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate), `Chrome 154` controls (no `margin-trim` property) report `margin-trim: block` as a CSS parser warning and the property is ignored (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 154 baseline lacks the property — `getComputedStyle(c).marginTrim === ''`), `Safari TP 250` controls (Safari TP 250 ships `margin-trim` per WebKit status) report the same as Chrome 155 (controlled fixture verifying Safari's spec-compliance — the property is shipped in Safari TP 250+), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko ships `margin-trim` per Mozilla status) report the same as Chrome 155 (controlled fixture verifying Firefox's spec-compliance), and a controlled fixture verifying the interaction with `gap` and `padding` (controlled fixture `margin-trim: block; padding: 20px; gap: 10px;` — the gap is preserved between siblings, the padding is preserved inside the container, and only the first-child's top margin + last-child's bottom margin are trimmed per the spec). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror (Chrome 155 enabled-by-default, `Margin-trim` entry), Chromium feature `5197863732772864`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40886857, W3C CSS Box Model Level 4 spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-box-4/#margin-trim`.

- [B-316] **[P2] Chrome 155 Stable `<install>` HTML Element `manifestId` Attribute Pins The Install To A Specific Manifest Identity So App Stores Can Disambiguate Multiple PWAs From The Same Origin And Prevent Cross-Manifest Install Hijacking** — Chrome 155 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5152834368700416`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/454827186, docs at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rGvLhD4SR8Y9M1wVmqgyesPNkbZGU7HOqlttjEFJ5Vo/edit?tab=t.tmx19oox759l#heading=h.j3tt49hqiuck`, sample at `https://microsoftedge.github.io/Demos/pwa-install-element`) ships the `<install>` HTML element `manifestId` attribute as enabled-by-default. The `manifestId` attribute lets authors pin the install to a SPECIFIC manifest identity (as declared by the manifest's `id` field) so the browser doesn't accidentally match against a different manifest variant on the same origin. The motivation is to enable app stores that host MULTIPLE PWAs from the same origin (e.g. an aggregator that hosts a puzzle PWA and a casual PWA both from `https://store.example/`) to install a SPECIFIC one rather than letting the browser pick the "best" manifest match. The attribute works alongside the existing `src` attribute (B-272 v1.221.0) — `src` selects the manifest URL, `manifestId` selects the manifest ID. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page is on `https://store.example/` and contains `<install id="inst" src="/puzzles/manifest.webmanifest" manifestId="/puzzles/">Install Puzzle</install>` and the manifest at `/puzzles/manifest.webmanifest` has `"id": "/puzzles/"`, assert that `inst.manifestId === '/puzzles/'` (controlled fixture verifying the IDL-reflection contract — the `manifestId` IDL attribute reflects the `manifestId` HTML attribute), the install flow resolves to the manifest at `/puzzles/manifest.webmanifest` AND matches against the `id` field `/puzzles/` (controlled fixture verifying the manifestId-matching contract — the browser uses BOTH the src URL and the manifestId to select the manifest; mismatches cause the install to fail with a meaningful error), `<install id="inst2" src="/puzzles/manifest.webmanifest" manifestId="/wrong-id/">` with a wrong manifestId throws `NotFoundError` when activated (controlled fixture verifying the mismatched-manifestId-rejection contract — the browser rejects the install if the manifest's id field doesn't match), `<install id="inst3" src="/puzzles/manifest.webmanifest">` (no manifestId) allows the browser to match against any manifest at the src URL (controlled fixture verifying the no-manifestId-default contract — the browser uses the src URL only and matches the first / best manifest), `<install id="inst4" manifestId="/puzzles/">` (no src, with manifestId) installs the current page's manifest filtered by the manifestId (controlled fixture verifying the no-src-with-manifestId contract — the manifestId is used to filter among manifests on the current origin), `manifestId` accepts relative paths and absolute URLs (controlled fixture verifying `manifestId="/puzzles/"` and `manifestId="https://other-origin.example/puzzles/"` are both valid), `Chrome 154` controls (no `manifestId` attribute; only the basic `<install>` element from B-272 v1.221.0) report `inst.manifestId === ''` and the attribute is silently ignored (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 154 baseline lacks the attribute), `Chrome 153` controls (no `<install>` element) report `document.createElement('install') instanceof HTMLUnknownElement === true` and the `manifestId` attribute is irrelevant (controlled fixture verifying the pre-install-element baseline), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `<install>` element) parse `<install>` as `HTMLUnknownElement` and the `manifestId` attribute is silently dropped (controlled fixture verifying Safari's status), `Firefox 155` controls (no `<install>` element) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying Firefox's status), the `manifestId` attribute composes with `referrerpolicy` (controlled fixture verifying `<install src="/m.webmanifest" manifestId="/x/" referrerpolicy="no-referrer">` — the `manifestId` doesn't affect the referrer policy, which still controls the manifest fetch's Referer header), and a controlled fixture verifying the IDL attribute accepts setting programmatically (controlled fixture `inst.manifestId = '/other/';` updates the IDL property — the new value is sent to the browser when the install is triggered). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror (Chrome 155 enabled-by-default, `Web app HTML install element` entry — the description explicitly mentions "given a manifest URL and optional manifest ID" — and Chrome 155 is the first milestone where the `manifestId` attribute is exposed as a separate attribute per the docs URL), Chromium feature `5152834368700416`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/454827186, Element docs at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rGvLhD4SR8Y9M1wVmqgyesPNkbZGU7HOqlttjEFJ5Vo/edit?tab=t.tmx19oox759l#heading=h.j3tt49hqiuck`, sample at `https://microsoftedge.github.io/Demos/pwa-install-element`.

### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-477] **[P1] Chrome 155 Stable TC39 `import ... with { type: "text" }` Text Modules Let Authors Inline Plain-Text Resources (Changelogs, License Texts, Build Info, Game Levels) Into JavaScript Modules As A String Default Export Without JS Fetch Round-Trips** — Chrome 155 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5191512456560640`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/494350643, TC39 Import Text proposal at `https://tc39.es/proposal-import-text/`) ships the TC39 Import Text (Text Modules) proposal as enabled-by-default. The contract: JavaScript modules can use `import text from "./asset.txt" with { type: "text" };` to import a plain-text file as a string default export. The imported string is the raw bytes of the text file decoded as UTF-8 — the text is treated as INERT data (no JS execution, no HTML parsing, no eval). The motivation is to enable static inclusion of plain-text resources (changelogs, license texts, build info, level definitions, SVG-as-string for inline injection, CSV data, JSON-as-string for runtime parse, i18n message catalogs) without requiring JS `fetch()` round-trips. DISTINCT from v1.227.0 W-464 which covers the CSS-side `@import "url" text;` Chrome 154 contract — W-464 is CSS-side (inlining text INTO a stylesheet), W-477 is TC39 module-side (inlining text INTO a JS module). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a file `/changelog.txt` with content `"Version 1.0.0\nReleased 2026-08-28"` (served with `Content-Type: text/plain`) and a module `/app.js` containing `import changelog from "./changelog.txt" with { type: "text" }; export default changelog;`, assert that the imported `changelog` is exactly the string `"Version 1.0.0\nReleased 2026-08-28"` (controlled fixture verifying the text-content-round-trip contract — the imported string equals the file content verbatim, including newlines), the import is a STATIC module graph entry (controlled fixture verifying the static-import contract — the import is resolved at module-load time; no fetch round-trip is required at runtime), `import text from "./asset.txt" with { type: "text" };` throws a `TypeError` when the file returns a non-text MIME type like `text/javascript` (controlled fixture verifying the no-js-execution-via-text-contract — the text import path is NOT a JS execution path; attempting to use it for JS files throws), `import text from "./empty.txt" with { type: "text" };` for an empty file resolves to the empty string `""` (controlled fixture verifying the empty-file-edge contract), `import text from "./utf8.txt" with { type: "text" };` for a UTF-8 file containing non-ASCII characters resolves to the properly-decoded UTF-8 string (controlled fixture verifying the UTF-8-decode contract — multi-byte sequences are correctly decoded), the import does NOT trigger the no-`fetch`-observable side effect (controlled fixture verifying the no-fetch-round-trip contract — the import is resolved via the module loader, NOT via `fetch()`; this means cross-origin imports use the module-graph CORS rules, not the `fetch()` CORS rules), a failed import (file returns 404) throws a `TypeError` at module-load time (controlled fixture verifying the network-failure-fallback contract — module loading fails loudly), the import attribute accepts only `type: "text"` (controlled fixture verifying the type-validation contract — `import text from "./asset.txt" with { type: "json" };` throws a `TypeError` per the spec's enum-restriction; the import attribute is an enum: `text` / `bytes` / etc.), the import is cached per URL by the module loader (controlled fixture verifying the cache contract — repeat imports are served from the module graph cache; the file is fetched once), `Chrome 154` controls (no TC39 Import Text feature) report `import ... with { type: "text" }` throws a `SyntaxError` (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 154 baseline lacks the feature — the import attributes syntax is rejected by the parser), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari TP 251 does not yet ship Import Text per WebKit status; the proposal is Chrome 155 first) report the same as Chrome 154 (controlled fixture verifying Safari's status), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox 153 ships Text Module imports behind a flag per Mozilla status; Firefox 155 may or may not have the flag on) report partial support (controlled fixture verifying Firefox's status — Firefox may report `undefined` for the import or may support it depending on the flag state), the import composes with dynamic `import()` expressions (controlled fixture verifying `const { default: text } = await import("./asset.txt", { with: { type: "text" } });` — the dynamic form also supports the import attributes), and a controlled fixture verifying the import's content is NOT executed as a module even if the file's MIME type is `application/javascript` (controlled fixture serving `./looks-like-js.txt` with `Content-Type: application/javascript` containing `globalThis.__executed = true;` and asserting `globalThis.__executed !== true` after the import — the text is treated as inert data, not executed as JS, regardless of the MIME type). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror (Chrome 155 enabled-by-default, `Import Text (Text Modules)` entry), Chromium feature `5191512456560640`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/494350643, TC39 Import Text proposal at `https://tc39.es/proposal-import-text/` (the import attributes syntax + the CreateTextModule Synthetic Module Record contract), W3C Manifest PR #1175 (the manifestId contract mentioned in W-477 — wait, this is a different PR; for W-477 the relevant PR is the TC39 proposal itself, not the manifest PR).

- [W-478] **[P2] Chrome 155 Stable Permissions-Policy `web-app-installation` Directive Allows Or Disallows Use Of The Web Install API + `<install>` Element On Origins The Enterprise Controls (Internal Sites, Iframes) Independent Of The Global `WebAppInstallByUserEnabled` Enterprise Policy** — Chrome 155 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5183481574850560`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/333795265, docs at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/12nSXJLm8mW0gWZ_yjlXfrV8r9gwJliVt4WVa-209-KA/edit?tab=t.0`, sample at `https://microsoftedge.github.io/Demos/pwa-install-api`) ships the `web-app-installation` Permissions-Policy directive as enabled-by-default. ### Compatibility / Cross-Browser (C)

- [C-247] **[P1] Chrome 155 Stable Enterprise Policy `WebAppInstallByUserEnabled` Broadly Disables User Web-App Installs Initiated Via `navigator.install()` Or `<install>` Element (Without Affecting The Legacy `beforeinstallprompt` Event) So Enterprises Can Block The New Declarative Install Paths Without Breaking Existing Apps** — Chrome 155 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5183481574850560`, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/333795265, docs at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/12nSXJLm8mW0gWZ_yjlXfrV8r9gwJliVt4WVa-209-KA/edit?tab=t.0`, Edge policy docs at `https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-policies/webappinstallbyuserenabled`) ships the `WebAppInstallByUserEnabled` enterprise policy as enabled-by-default. The policy accepts the values `1` (default — user web-app installs enabled for `navigator.install()` AND `<install>` element) and `0` (user web-app installs disabled — the API rejects with `NotAllowedError`, the `<install>` element's click is silently aborted). The policy applies to BOTH the Web Install API and the `<install>` element (Chrome 155's two declarative install paths). The policy does NOT affect the legacy `beforeinstallprompt` event-based install flow — apps that rely on the legacy event continue to work because the legacy flow is governed by the browser's own install-availability heuristics, not by the `WebAppInstallByUserEnabled` policy. The motivation is to let enterprises disable the new declarative install paths without affecting existing apps that use the legacy event flow. - [B-318] **[P1] Chrome 152 Stable (Released 2026-08-25) ACTUAL Deployment Of window-drag CSS Property Standardizing + Renaming The Legacy app-region Property To window-drag With Explicit move / none Inheritance Behavior So Installed Desktop PWA Window Drag Regions Work Cross-Browser With The Same Author Code** — Chrome 152 stable (released 2026-08-25 per https://developer.chrome.com/release-notes/152 stable release-notes URL, 145 KB) ships the window-drag CSS property as enabled-by-default. ### Process / Pipeline (PC)

- [PC-012] **[P0] Chrome Release Cadence Changed From 4-Week To 2-Week Cycle Starting With Chrome 153 Stable On 2026-09-08 Doubling The Surface Area The Test Library Must Track Per Cycle From This Point Forward (Every Cycle Now Must Verify Both Even-Week + Odd-Week Chrome Stable Releases)** — Google announces on 2026-03-03 (per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release + https://9to5google.com/2026/03/03/chrome-two-week-updates + https://betanews.com/article/google-is-speeding-up-chromes-development-and-release-schedule) that starting with Chrome 153 stable on 2026-09-08, Chrome moves from a 4-week release cycle (the cadence that has been in place since 2021) to a 2-week release cycle. The new cadence: a NEW Chrome STABLE ships every 2 weeks (Tue-Sep-08 153, Tue-Sep-22 154, Tue-Oct-06 155, Tue-Oct-20 156, ...). Beta cuts happen on Mondays, stable cuts on Tuesdays, early stable releases on Wednesdays, full stable releases 2 weeks after the prior stable. The release schedule table for 153 + 154 in the announcement: M153 (old) Branch Mon-Aug-24 / Beta Promotion Wed-Aug-26 / Stable Cut Tue-Sep-08 / Early Stable Release Wed-Sep-09 / Stable Release Tue-Sep-22; M153 (new) Branch Mon-Aug-17 / Beta Promotion Wed-Aug-19 / Stable Cut Tue-Aug-25 / Early Stable Release Wed-Aug-26 / Stable Release Tue-Sep-08; M154 (old) Branch Mon-Sep-21 / Beta Promotion Wed-Sep-23 / Stable Cut Tue-Oct-06 / Early Stable Release Wed-Oct-07 / Stable Release Tue-Oct-20; M154 (new) Branch Mon-Aug-31 / Beta Promotion Wed-Sep-02 / Stable Cut Tue-Sep-08 / Early Stable Release Wed-Sep-09 / Stable Release Tue-Sep-22. The Cadence-Change contract that the test library must honor from this point forward: each 4h Dynamic Test Intelligence cycle must NOW check BOTH the upcoming EVEN-week stable release (e.g. M154 on Sep-22) AND the upcoming ODD-week stable release (e.g. M153 on Sep-08, M155 on Oct-06, M156 on Oct-20, ...) - the prior 4-week cadence assumption let the test library cover one Chrome stable every ~28 days; the new 2-week cadence cuts that in half, doubling the surface area per cycle. The test-library meta-contract: each 4h cycle that ships new test cases MUST cite the chromium superchargebrowser release calendar URL (https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule or https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=N mirror for the upcoming milestone N stable) AND must verify that the chromestatuslite mirror for the upcoming milestone exists (HTTP 200) AND must verify the upcoming milestone stable release-notes URL exists (HTTP 200 for developer.chrome.com/release-notes/N) by the time the cycle that covers it completes. DISTINCT from every prior CAT-NNN case body - PC-012 is the META-contract that governs HOW the test library itself evolves, not a web-platform contract that the test library verifies. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a test-harness page that reads await fetch("https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=154") and await fetch("https://developer.chrome.com/release-notes/154"), assert that the chromestatuslite mirror for the upcoming milestone returns HTTP 200 by the cycle that covers it (controlled fixture verifying the chromestatuslite-mirror-available contract - the single-source primary URL pattern from v1.218.0-v1.234.0 must continue to work for the 2-week cadence milestones; if chromestatuslite falls behind, the library must use developer.chrome.com/release-notes/N as the primary URL), developer.chrome.com/release-notes/154 returns HTTP 200 by the cycle that covers Chrome 154 stable (controlled fixture verifying the stable-release-notes-URL-available contract), the Chromium release calendar at https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule reports the new 2-week cadence for milestones 153+ (controlled fixture verifying the release-calendar-reflects-new-cadence contract), Math.floor((Date.now() - Date.parse("2026-09-08")) / (14 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)) returns the milestone index since the cadence change (controlled fixture verifying the milestone-since-cadence-change-arithmetic contract - a deterministic way to compute which milestone the current cycle should cover), the 4h cron (R352) covers milestone N BETA surface on the Monday after the milestone cuts (controlled fixture verifying the 4h-cron-betabet-cadence contract - the library cycles at 4h intervals which divides evenly into the 2-week cadence; every 2 weeks the library will have ~84 cycles of BETA coverage before the stable ships, up from ~42 cycles under the 4-week cadence), and the 4h cron covers milestone N STABLE surface on the Wednesday after the milestone cuts (controlled fixture verifying the 4h-cron-stable-cadence contract - the library cycles at 4h intervals which divides evenly into the 2-week cadence; every 2 weeks the library will have ~83 cycles of STABLE coverage before the NEXT milestone ships). Source: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release (Chrome 2-week release cycle announcement blog post, dated 2026-03-03, 14 KB), https://9to5google.com/2026/03/03/chrome-two-week-updates (9to5google coverage of the same announcement with the M153/M154 schedule table), https://betanews.com/article/google-is-speeding-up-chromes-development-and-release-schedule (BetaNews coverage), https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule (the Chromium release calendar, the authoritative source for the new cadence), https://chromestatuslite.com/?version=N mirrors (the single-source primary URL pattern from v1.218.0-v1.234.0 that must continue to scale with the 2-week cadence).

### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-309] **[P1] Safari TP 251 CSS `corner-shape` Longhand Property Sets Per-Corner Curve Shape To `round` | `squircle` | `bevel` | `scoop` | `notch` For Non-Circular Organic UI Corner Geometry Independent Of `border-radius`** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26 for macOS Golden Gate and macOS Tahoe, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 319205@main, bug 184950973, spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-borders-4/#corner-shaping`) ships the CSS `corner-shape` longhand property as enabled-by-default. The contract introduces a separate property that controls the SHAPE of the corner curve independently from the radius set via `border-radius`. The property accepts the values `round` (default — circular-arc interpolation, matches the pre-existing `border-radius` baseline), `squircle` (superellipse interpolation that creates a more gradual curve near the corner and a sharper transition away from it), `bevel` (straight cut-off from the radius point inward to the corner — creates a chamfered corner), `scoop` (concave inward curve — opposite of round), and `notch` (concave inward cut — opposite of bevel). The motivation is to let pages create organic UI shapes (e.g. iOS-style squircle icons, asymmetric corner shapes) without manually composing SVG paths. The `corner-shape` property is set per-corner via the longhand and is also implicitly set when the Chrome 155 corner shorthand properties (`corner-top-left` etc. from B-304) declare a shape keyword alongside the radius. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>#d { width: 200px; height: 100px; background: cyan; border-radius: 24px; corner-shape: squircle; }</style><div id="d"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(d).cornerShape === 'squircle'` (controlled fixture verifying the per-element-property-accept contract — the longhand `corner-shape` property is a separate computed-value from `border-radius`), `getComputedStyle(d).borderRadius === '24px'` (controlled fixture verifying the orthogonal-radius contract — `border-radius` still reports the radius length and `corner-shape` reports the shape interpolation independently), the rendered `<div>` shows a 200x100 box with squircle corners (visual rendering with a superellipse curve rather than a circular arc; controlled fixture verifying the visual-shape contract — the corner curve uses the superellipse interpolation per the CSS Borders Level 4 spec), `corner-shape: bevel` renders a chamfered-corner box where the corner is cut straight from the radius point (controlled fixture verifying the bevel-shape contract — the bevel shape replaces the corner radius with a straight chamfer), `corner-shape: scoop` renders a concave inward curve at the corner (controlled fixture verifying the scoop-shape contract — the scoop shape is the inverse of round, curving inward toward the box interior), `corner-shape: notch` renders a concave inward cut (controlled fixture verifying the notch-shape contract — the notch shape is the inverse of bevel, creating an inward-angled corner), `corner-shape: round` (the default) renders a circular-arc corner equivalent to the pre-existing `border-radius` behavior (controlled fixture verifying the round-default contract — the default shape matches the legacy baseline), the property is inheritable (controlled fixture verifying the inheritance contract — children inherit `corner-shape` from the parent unless they explicitly reset it), individual corners can be set via `corner-top-left-shape` etc. (controlled fixture verifying the per-corner-longhand contract — `corner-top-left-shape: bevel; corner-bottom-right-shape: squircle;` creates an asymmetric box), `@supports (corner-shape: squircle)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `corner-shape` longhand support; the property is behind a flag in Safari 26.6) report `getComputedStyle(d).cornerShape === ''` (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline lacks the longhand — only the `border-radius` baseline is present), `Chrome 155` controls (Chrome 155 ships the corner shorthand properties from B-304 that SET `corner-shape` as a side-effect, but does not yet expose `corner-shape` as a standalone longhand on every element) report `getComputedStyle(d).cornerShape === 'round'` because Chrome 155 treats `corner-shape` as a per-corner-shorthand-only side-effect — the standalone longhand is not yet first-class on Chrome 155 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 155 surface ships the SHORTHAND but not the standalone LONGHAND — distinct from the Safari TP 251 standalone longhand), `Firefox 155` controls (no `corner-shape` longhand) report `getComputedStyle(d).cornerShape === ''` (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline lacks the property entirely), the property is animatable via CSS Transitions / Animations (controlled fixture verifying `transition: corner-shape 0.5s` transitions between values like `round` and `squircle` smoothly per the spec), the `corner-shape` value is preserved in `clip-path` rendering when an element has `border-radius: 24px; corner-shape: squircle; clip-path: view-box` (controlled fixture verifying the clip-path-composition contract — the squircle corner shape propagates to the clip-path output), and a controlled fixture verifying the `corner-shape` property combines correctly with the `border-radius: <length> <length>` two-value syntax for elliptical corners (e.g. `border-radius: 24px 16px; corner-shape: squircle;` creates a squircle ellipse corner rather than a circle). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 319205@main, bug 184950973), W3C CSS Borders Module Level 4 Editor's Draft at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-borders-4/#corner-shaping` (the `corner-shape` property grammar + the `round | squircle | bevel | scoop | notch` value list). The acceptance gate verifies the standalone longhand + the per-corner-shorthand override + the visual-shape contract + the multi-value enumeration + the cross-engine parity in a single Playwright session on Safari TP 251 + Chrome 155 + Firefox 155 for the cross-engine parity live-fire part.

- [B-310] **[P1] Safari TP 251 CSS `object-view-box` Property Overrides The `<svg>` `<view>` Element For Embedded `image/svg+xml` Rendering With `view-box / view-box-clip / none` Values So Authors Can Specify The Initial Viewport Without Modifying The SVG Asset Itself** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 318981@main, bug 132624217, spec at `https://svgwg.org/svg2-draft/coords.html#ObjectViewBoxProperty`) ships the CSS `object-view-box` property as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the SVG `<view>` element semantics to a CSS property that lets authors specify the initial viewport for an SVG asset embedded via `<img src="/asset.svg">` or `background-image: url("/asset.svg")`. The property accepts the values: `view-box` (the default for SVG-typed images — uses the `<svg>` root element's `viewBox` attribute as the initial viewport), `view-box-clip` (uses the `viewBox` and additionally clips the rendered SVG to the viewBox bounds, hiding any element that extends beyond the viewBox), or `none` (no viewBox-based rendering — uses the SVG's natural size). The motivation is to let pages reuse the same SVG asset at different viewports WITHOUT modifying the asset itself. Without this property, the only way to control the SVG rendering viewport was to either (a) edit the SVG file to add a `<view>` element, (b) use SVG fragment URLs like `<img src="/asset.svg#view-id">` which requires the SVG to define the view, or (c) wrap the SVG in a `<svg viewBox="...">` parent in HTML which defeats the purpose of using `<img>`. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing an SVG asset `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100"><circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red"/></svg>` and a host page with `<img id="i" src="/asset.svg" style="width: 200px; height: 200px; object-view-box: view-box;">`, assert that `getComputedStyle(i).objectViewBox === 'view-box'` (controlled fixture verifying the property-accept contract — `object-view-box: view-box` is a valid CSS property value per the SVG 2 spec), the rendered `<img>` shows the SVG fitted into the 200x200 box using the SVG's natural `viewBox` aspect ratio (controlled fixture verifying the natural-viewBox-rendering contract — the `<img>` element respects the SVG's `viewBox` attribute and renders the SVG into the 200x200 box preserving the SVG's coordinate system), the SVG renders the `<circle>` at the SVG coordinate position (50, 50) (controlled fixture verifying the coordinate-preservation contract — the SVG's internal coordinates are preserved; the `<circle>` is at SVG-coord (50, 50) which renders at the center of the 200x200 box), `<img src="/asset.svg" style="object-view-box: view-box-clip;">` clips the rendered SVG to the viewBox bounds (controlled fixture verifying the clip-contract — any SVG content that extends beyond the viewBox is clipped to the viewBox), `<img src="/asset.svg" style="object-view-box: none;">` uses the SVG's natural size WITHOUT honoring the viewBox (controlled fixture verifying the no-viewBox-fallback contract — the SVG renders at its natural `width`/`height` attributes regardless of the `viewBox` content; the SVG's coordinate system is NOT scaled to the viewBox bounds), `@supports (object-view-box: view-box)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate), the property works on `background-image: url("/asset.svg")` (controlled fixture verifying the background-image-accept contract — the property applies to SVG backgrounds just as it applies to `<img>` elements per the CSS Backgrounds Level 3 + SVG 2 specs), the property composes with `object-fit: cover` and `object-fit: contain` (controlled fixture verifying the object-fit-composition contract — `object-view-box: view-box; object-fit: cover;` uses the viewBox as the rendered coordinate system AND fits the rendering to the element box using the cover or contain strategy), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `object-view-box` support; the property is behind a flag) report `getComputedStyle(i).objectViewBox === ''` (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline lacks the property — the SVG renders using the legacy `viewBox` semantics), `Chrome 155` controls (no `object-view-box` support; the property is not yet shipped in Chromium per the spec) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no `object-view-box` support; the property is not yet shipped in Gecko per the spec) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), the property is animatable via CSS Transitions / Animations (controlled fixture verifying `transition: object-view-box 0.5s` transitions between values like `view-box` and `view-box-clip` smoothly per the spec), the property works on `<svg>` elements rendered inline (controlled fixture verifying the inline-svg-accept contract — `<svg style="object-view-box: view-box;">...</svg>` applies the property to the inline SVG element; the rendering uses the SVG's viewBox as the initial viewport), and a controlled fixture verifying that the property interacts correctly with `preserveAspectRatio` (when both `object-view-box: view-box` and an SVG element's `preserveAspectRatio` are set, the `preserveAspectRatio` value takes precedence for the aspect-ratio-fit semantics — controlled fixture verifying the interaction contract). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 318981@main, bug 132624217), W3C SVG 2 Editor's Draft at `https://svgwg.org/svg2-draft/coords.html#ObjectViewBoxProperty` (the `object-view-box` property grammar + the `view-box / view-box-clip / none` values).

- [B-311] **[P2] Safari TP 251 CSS `random-item()` Function Picks A Random Item From A Comma-Separated List With Property-Scoped Caching Key So `random-item(--key, a, b, c)` Returns The Same Value Across Multiple References In The Same Property At The Same Element** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 319180@main, bug 181816677, spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-5/#random-item`) ships the CSS `random-item()` function as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing CSS `random()` function with a new `random-item(<custom-ident>?, <value>#)` signature where the optional `<custom-ident>` is the CACHING KEY that scopes the random-item selection to a specific element + property + cache-key combination. When the same `random-item(--my-key, a, b, c)` is referenced MULTIPLE TIMES in the same property at the same element, ALL references return the SAME value (the cached selection); when the cache-key differs (e.g. `random-item(--other-key, a, b, c)`), a NEW random value is picked. The motivation is to enable stochastic CSS animations (e.g. randomize a card layout across multiple `transform`, `background-color`, `width`, `height` properties for the same element) where each property needs a CONSISTENT random value across multiple references. Without the caching key, every reference would pick independently — which is the desired behavior for INDEPENDENT randomization but breaks CONSISTENT randomized layouts. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>.card { --theme: random-item(theme, dark, light, colorful); background: var(--theme); border-color: var(--theme); box-shadow: 0 0 8px var(--theme); }</style><div class="card" id="c"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(c).backgroundColor === getComputedStyle(c).borderColor === getComputedStyle(c).boxShadow` color (controlled fixture verifying the caching-key-consistency contract — the same `random-item(theme, dark, light, colorful)` reference across three property accesses returns the SAME value because they share the same cache-key `theme` + the same element + the same property-resolution scope), `<style>.a { color: random-item(theme, red, green, blue); } .b { color: random-item(theme, red, green, blue); }</style><div class="a"><span class="b"></span></div>` reports `getComputedStyle(div).color` and `getComputedStyle(span).color` may differ (controlled fixture verifying the per-element-caching contract — the cache key is per-element, not per-page; the cache key + the element identity is the caching scope), `random-item(seed, x, y, z)` with a numeric cache-key picks a random item (controlled fixture verifying the arbitrary-cache-key-accept contract — the cache-key is a `<custom-ident>` per the spec; numeric strings like `seed` are valid custom-idents), `random-item(key, 1px, 2px, 4px)` accepts length values (controlled fixture verifying the length-value-accept contract — the function accepts any `<value>` per the CSS Values spec), `random-item(key, 10%, 20%, 30%)` accepts percentage values (controlled fixture verifying the percentage-accept contract), `random-item(key, red, blue)` with TWO values picks one of two (controlled fixture verifying the two-value-edge contract — the function accepts one-or-more values), `random-item(key, red)` with ONE value returns that value (controlled fixture verifying the single-value-edge contract), `@supports (random-item(key, a, b): foo)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate — pre-Safari-TP-251 controls report `false`), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `random-item()` support; the function is Safari TP 251 first) report `random-item(...)` is a parse error and the property falls back to the initial value (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline), `Chrome 155` controls (no `random-item()` support; the function is Safari TP 251 first) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no `random-item()` support) report the same (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), the function composes with `var(--var)` references (controlled fixture verifying `random-item(key, var(--option-a), var(--option-b))` works — the function accepts `var()` as a value argument), the function is evaluable in `@property` registered custom properties (controlled fixture verifying the registered-property-accept contract — `<style>@property --random-bg { syntax: '<color>'; inherits: false; initial-value: red; } .c { --random-bg: random-item(key, red, green, blue); background: var(--random-bg); }</style>` registers a color-typed random property), and a controlled fixture verifying the caching scope is reset across DIFFERENT property declarations at the same element (controlled fixture `random-item(key, a, b)` in `background-color` is cached independently from `random-item(key, a, b)` in `border-color` per the spec's property-scoped caching contract). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 319180@main, bug 181816677), CSS Values Level 5 Editor's Draft at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-5/#random-item` (the `random-item()` function grammar with the caching-key contract).

- [B-312] **[P1] Safari TP 251 `@supports at-rule(...)` Tests If A CSS At-Rule Is Supported In The Current Engine So Authors Can Branch CSS On At-Rule Support (e.g. `@supports at-rule(@scope)` vs `@supports at-rule(@container)`) Independent Of Property / Selector Support** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 318482@main, bug 87884897, spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-conditional-4/#at-rule-supports`) ships the `@supports at-rule(...)` conditional rule as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing `@supports` at-rule with a new `at-rule(<at-rule>)` syntax that tests whether the user agent RECOGNIZES the named at-rule, independent of whether the at-rule is implemented or whether the at-rule's contents are valid. The motivation is to let authors branch CSS on at-rule support (e.g. `@scope`, `@layer`, `@container`, `@view-transition`) without requiring the at-rule's full machinery to be available. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>@supports at-rule(@scope) { .a { color: red; } }</style><div id="a" class="a"></div>`, assert that the `@supports at-rule(@scope)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the at-rule-recognition contract — Safari TP 251 recognizes `@scope` and `@supports at-rule(@scope)` returns `true`; the contained rule `color: red` is applied to `.a`), `@supports at-rule(@layer)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the layer-at-rule-accept contract — Safari TP 251 also supports `@layer`), `@supports at-rule(@container)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the container-at-rule-accept contract — Safari TP 251 supports `@container`), `@supports at-rule(@view-transition)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the view-transition-at-rule-accept contract — Safari TP 251 supports `@view-transition`), `@supports at-rule(@unknown-rule)` returns `false` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the unknown-at-rule-rejection contract — Safari TP 251 does NOT recognize `@unknown-rule`; the contained rules are not applied), `@supports not at-rule(@scope)` returns `false` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the not-at-rule-inverse contract — the inverse negation returns the boolean inverse; the contained rules are not applied because the negation is `false`), the `@supports at-rule(...)` syntax can be combined with property / selector tests via `and` / `or` (controlled fixture verifying the boolean-composition contract — `@supports at-rule(@scope) and (display: flex)` returns `true` if both `@scope` is recognized AND `display: flex` is supported), the `@supports at-rule(...)` syntax is composable inside `@import` conditions (controlled fixture verifying the import-condition-accept contract — `@import url("theme.css") supports(at-rule(@scope));` imports the theme CSS only if the engine recognizes `@scope`), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `@supports at-rule(...)` support; the syntax is Safari TP 251 first) report `CSS.supports('at-rule(@scope)') === false` (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline), `Chrome 155` controls (no `@supports at-rule(...)` support; the syntax is Safari TP 251 first) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no `@supports at-rule(...)` support; the syntax is Safari TP 251 first) report the same (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), `@supports at-rule(@scope)` is composable with `@scope` (controlled fixture verifying the recursive-accept contract — the at-rule test returns `true` AND the contained `@scope` rule applies within the conditional block), `@supports at-rule(@property)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the property-at-rule-accept contract — Safari TP 251 supports `@property`), `@supports at-rule(@font-face)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the font-face-at-rule-accept contract — the legacy `@font-face` at-rule is recognized), and a controlled fixture verifying the JS-side `CSS.supports('at-rule(@scope)')` round-trip (controlled fixture verifying the JS-CSSOM API round-trip — the JS-side `CSS.supports()` static method returns the same boolean as the CSS-conditional block). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 318482@main, bug 87884897), W3C CSS Conditional Rules Module Level 4 Editor's Draft at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-conditional-4/#at-rule-supports` (the `at-rule()` supports function + the boolean composition contract).

- [B-313] **[P2] Safari TP 251 CSS `ident()` Function Resolves A `<custom-ident>` From A Whitelist And `inherit()` Function References The Computed Value Of A Custom Property At A Specific Position So Authors Can Build Composable CSS Helper Functions** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 319049@main for `ident()` (bug 184732904) and commit 319062@main for `inherit()` (bug 184738624), spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-5/#ident` and `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-variables-2/#inherit-fn`) ships the CSS `ident()` and `inherit()` functions as enabled-by-default. The contract: (a) `ident(<ident>...)` accepts one or more `<custom-ident>` values and resolves to the computed value of the FIRST matching custom-ident that the user agent recognizes as a known CSS keyword (e.g. `ident(auto, none, inherit)` returns `auto` because `auto` is recognized); (b) `inherit()` returns the computed value of a custom property at the current element, similar to `var()` but WITHOUT requiring the property to be defined at the current element — `inherit()` references the inherited value (the cascade-computed value that the element WOULD inherit if the property were unset). The motivation is to let authors build composable CSS helper functions that work across the cascade without explicit `@property` registration. For `ident()`, a typical use is `<style>:root { --display-mode: ident(modal, dialog, none); } .dialog { display: var(--display-mode); }</style>` where `--display-mode` resolves to `modal` because `modal` is recognized as a `display` value; without `ident()`, authors would need to write `--display-mode: modal` directly. For `inherit()`, a typical use is to read the cascade-computed value of a custom property in a `@property` registered syntax. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>:root { --font-color: ident(red, blue, green); } #a { color: var(--font-color); }</style><div id="a"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(a).color === 'rgb(255, 0, 0)'` (controlled fixture verifying the ident-resolution contract — `ident(red, blue, green)` resolves to `red` because `red` is the first recognized `<color>` value in the list; the resolved value is computed as a `<color>` and assigned to the property), `<style>:root { --bg-color: ident(unknown1, unknown2, blue); } #b { background-color: var(--bg-color); }</style><div id="b"></div>` reports `getComputedStyle(b).backgroundColor === 'rgb(0, 0, 255)'` (controlled fixture verifying the fallback-to-last-valid contract — when the first values are unrecognized, `ident()` falls back to the next recognized value; the spec requires at least one recognized value per the values-5 spec), `<style>:root { --shadow: inherit(); } #c { box-shadow: 0 0 8px var(--shadow); }</style><div id="c" style="--shadow: red;"></div>` reports `getComputedStyle(c).boxShadow === 'rgb(255, 0, 0) 0px 0px 8px 0px'` (controlled fixture verifying the inherit-function-contract — `inherit()` resolves to the cascade-inherited value of the property at the current element, which is `red` from the inline style), `@supports (ident(red, green): red)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the ident-accept contract), `@supports (inherit(): red)` returns `true` on Safari TP 251 (controlled fixture verifying the inherit-accept contract), `ident()` is composable with `var()` (controlled fixture verifying `var(--my-color, ident(red, blue))` works — the fallback chain composes `var()` and `ident()`), `inherit()` is composable with `@property` registered custom properties (controlled fixture verifying the registered-property-accept contract — `@property --shadow-color { syntax: '<color>'; inherits: true; initial-value: red; } #d { box-shadow: 0 0 8px inherit(); }` resolves `inherit()` to the cascade-inherited value of `--shadow-color`), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `ident()` / `inherit()` support; the functions are Safari TP 251 first) report `ident(...)` and `inherit(...)` as parse errors (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline), `Chrome 155` controls (no `ident()` / `inherit()` support) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no `ident()` / `inherit()` support) report the same (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), `ident()` accepts an arbitrary number of arguments (controlled fixture verifying `ident(a, b, c, d, e)` returns the first recognized value among the five), `inherit()` defaults to the cascade-computed value (controlled fixture verifying the cascade-computed-value contract — `inherit()` resolves to the cascade-computed value, NOT the registered-property initial-value), `inherit()` is composable inside `calc()` (controlled fixture verifying `calc(inherit() + 8px)` works — `inherit()` resolves inside calc expressions), and a controlled fixture verifying `ident()` is not equivalent to `var(--registered-ident)` (controlled fixture noting `ident()` is a static keyword-match; `var()` is a dynamic custom-property lookup; the two functions have different semantics per the spec). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commits 319049@main + 319062@main, bugs 184732904 + 184738624), CSS Values Level 5 Editor's Draft at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-5/#ident` (the `ident()` function grammar) and CSS Custom Properties Level 2 Editor's Draft at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-variables-2/#inherit-fn` (the `inherit()` function spec).


### Cross-Engine TC39 JavaScript (C)

- [C-246] **[P2] Safari TP 251 `Iterator.prototype.chunks()` And `Iterator.prototype.windows()` Slice Iterators Into Sub-Iterators Of A Specified Size With `Iterator.prototype.chunks(n)` Yielding `[n]`-Sized Arrays And `Iterator.prototype.windows(n)` Yielding `[n]`-Sized Sliding Windows** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 318479@main, bug 183892687, proposal at `https://github.com/tc39/proposal-iterator-chunking`) ships the TC39 Iterator Chunking proposal's two methods `Iterator.prototype.chunks(n)` and `Iterator.prototype.windows(n)` as enabled-by-default. The contract: (a) `Iterator.prototype.chunks(n)` partitions the underlying iterator into sub-iterators of size `n` (the LAST sub-iterator may have fewer than `n` items if the input is not evenly divisible) and yields each sub-iterator as an array; (b) `Iterator.prototype.windows(n)` produces sliding windows of size `n` over the underlying iterator — each window is an array of `n` consecutive items, the iterator yields `inputLength - n + 1` windows (if the input has fewer than `n` items, no windows are yielded), and the windows overlap (the last item of one window is the first item of the next). The motivation is to enable streaming processing patterns (chunked batch processing, sliding-window aggregations) without manually managing an index buffer. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page is on `https://game.example/` and `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])` is the input, assert that `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]).chunks(3)` yields `[1, 2, 3]`, `[4, 5, 6]`, `[7]` on subsequent `.next()` calls (controlled fixture verifying the chunk-size-of-3 contract — the input is partitioned into sub-iterators of size 3; the LAST chunk has 1 item because 7 is not evenly divisible by 3), `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]).chunks(3).toArray()` returns `[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7]]` (controlled fixture verifying the toArray-composition contract — the chunks are composable with the existing `Iterator.prototype.toArray()` method), `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]).windows(3)` yields `[1, 2, 3]`, `[2, 3, 4]`, `[3, 4, 5]`, `[4, 5, 6]`, `[5, 6, 7]` on subsequent `.next()` calls (controlled fixture verifying the window-size-of-3 contract — the input produces 5 overlapping windows of size 3; windows slide by 1 item each step), `Iterator.from([1, 2]).windows(3)` yields nothing (controlled fixture verifying the window-too-small-fallback contract — when the input has fewer items than the window size, no windows are produced), `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3]).chunks(1)` yields `[1]`, `[2]`, `[3]` (controlled fixture verifying the chunk-size-of-1 edge — the chunk size can be 1), `Iterator.from([]).chunks(5)` yields nothing (controlled fixture verifying the empty-input-fallback contract — an empty input produces no chunks), `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).chunks(5)` yields `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` (controlled fixture verifying the chunk-size-equals-input-length contract — when the chunk size equals the input length, exactly one chunk is yielded), the methods compose with other iterator helpers (controlled fixture verifying `Iterator.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]).chunks(2).map(chunk => chunk.length)` returns `[2, 2, 2]` — the chunks are composable with `.map()`), the methods return `Iterator` instances (controlled fixture verifying `chunks(3) instanceof Iterator === true` and `windows(3) instanceof Iterator === true` per the standard `Iterator` contract), the methods handle non-array iterables (controlled fixture verifying `new Set([1, 2, 3, 4]).chunks(2)` works because the methods internally call `Iterator.from()` on the input), an invalid chunk size (e.g. `chunks(0)` or `chunks(-1)`) throws `RangeError` (controlled fixture verifying the input-validation contract — chunk size must be a positive integer per the spec), `Safari TP 250` controls (no chunking methods; the proposal is TP 251 first) report `typeof Iterator.prototype.chunks === 'undefined'` and `typeof Iterator.prototype.windows === 'undefined'` (controlled fixture verifying the TP 250 baseline lacks the methods), `Chrome 155` controls (no chunking methods; the proposal is Safari TP 251 first) report the same as TP 250 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no chunking methods; the proposal is Safari TP 251 first) report the same (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), and a controlled fixture verifying the methods handle iterators from `Iterator.from(generator())` where the underlying generator is infinite (controlled fixture verifying `Iterator.from(infiniteGenerator()).chunks(3)` yields successive sub-arrays lazily as the consumer requests them — the chunks do NOT eagerly collect the infinite sequence into memory; the method is a lazy sub-iterator that pulls from the underlying iterator on demand). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 318479@main, bug 183892687), TC39 Iterator Chunking proposal at `https://github.com/tc39/proposal-iterator-chunking` (the `Iterator.prototype.chunks()` and `Iterator.prototype.windows()` spec with the chunk-size + window-size semantics).


### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-476] **[P1] Safari TP 251 `HTMLMediaElement.removeTextTrack()` Removes A Previously-Added Text Track From The Media Element So Dynamic Captions / Subtitles Can Be Unmounted Without Replacing The Whole Media Source** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 318250@main, bug 183365541, spec at `https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/media.html#dom-mediacontroller-removetexttrack`) ships the `HTMLMediaElement.removeTextTrack()` method as enabled-by-default. The contract: `HTMLMediaElement.removeTextTrack(textTrack)` removes a previously-added `TextTrack` object from the media element's `textTracks` TextTrackList. The method is the INVERSE of `HTMLMediaElement.addTextTrack()` (which has been supported since HTML5) — together they let pages DYNAMICALLY add and remove text tracks (e.g. user-selected caption language, dynamically-switched subtitle tracks) without replacing the whole media source. The motivation is to enable multi-language caption switching where the page maintains a pool of `TextTrack` objects and adds / removes them based on user preference, rather than having to re-load the entire media element. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page is on `https://game.example/` and contains `<video id="v" src="/game-trailer.mp4" controls></video>`, assert that `v.textTracks.length === 0` (controlled fixture verifying the initial-state contract — the media element starts with no text tracks), `const track1 = v.addTextTrack('captions', 'English', 'en');` adds a text track (controlled fixture verifying the addTextTrack-accept contract — `v.textTracks.length === 1` after the add; `v.textTracks[0] === track1`), `const track2 = v.addTextTrack('subtitles', 'Spanish', 'es');` adds a second text track (controlled fixture verifying the multi-track-accept contract — `v.textTracks.length === 2` after the second add; both tracks are in the list), `v.removeTextTrack(track1);` removes the first track (controlled fixture verifying the removeTextTrack-contract — `v.textTracks.length === 1` after the remove; `v.textTracks[0] === track2`; the removed track is no longer accessible via `textTracks`), `v.removeTextTrack(track2);` removes the remaining track (controlled fixture verifying the remove-all-tracks-contract — `v.textTracks.length === 0` after the remove; the media element has no text tracks), `v.removeTextTrack(null);` or `v.removeTextTrack(undefined);` throws `TypeError` (controlled fixture verifying the null-input-validation contract — the input must be a `TextTrack` object per the spec; null and undefined throw), `v.removeTextTrack(track1);` AFTER `track1` was already removed throws `NotFoundError` (controlled fixture verifying the already-removed-validation contract — the track must be in the list; removing an already-removed track throws per the spec), the `cuechange` event listeners on the removed track do NOT fire after the track is removed (controlled fixture verifying the listener-cleanup-contract — adding a `cuechange` listener to a track and then removing the track causes the listener to stop firing; the removed track is detached from the media element's text-tracks pipeline), `track.mode` is preserved on the removed track object (controlled fixture verifying the detached-track-state-contract — the `TextTrack` object's `.mode` property is unchanged after `removeTextTrack()`; the page can re-add the track later with `addTextTrack()` and the mode is preserved), the `track.cues` list is preserved on the removed track (controlled fixture verifying the detached-track-cues-contract — `track.cues.length === 0` after addTextTrack (which creates an empty cues list); removing the track does NOT clear the cues; a re-add restores the track with its cues intact), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `removeTextTrack()` method; the method is Safari TP 251 first) report `typeof v.removeTextTrack === 'undefined'` (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline lacks the method — pages that need to remove text tracks must replace the entire media source), `Chrome 155` controls (no `removeTextTrack()` method; the method is Safari TP 251 first) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no `removeTextTrack()` method; the method is Safari TP 251 first) report the same (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), the method is composable with `track.mode = 'hidden' | 'showing' | 'disabled'` (controlled fixture verifying the mode-composition contract — `addTextTrack()` + `track.mode = 'showing'` + `removeTextTrack()` works for hiding + showing captions dynamically), and a controlled fixture verifying the method is reflected in the media element's `texttracks` change event (controlled fixture verifying the change-event-contract — adding a text track fires a `change` event on `textTracks`; removing a text track fires another `change` event with the track's `track` property set to the removed track per the HTML spec). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 318250@main, bug 183365541), WHATWG HTML Living Standard at `https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/media.html#dom-mediacontroller-removetexttrack` (the `removeTextTrack()` method spec + the validation contract + the `NotFoundError` exception).



### Security / Privacy (S)

- [S-488] **[P2] Safari TP 251 RegExp Buffer Boundaries Proposal Adds `\A` (String Start), `\z` (Absolute String End), `\Z` (Final Terminator End) Anchors And `\b` / `\B` Improvements For Multi-Line Buffer Matching** — Safari Technology Preview 251 (released 2026-08-26, via `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/`, WebKit commit 318415@main, bug 178287060, proposal at `https://github.com/tc39/proposal-regexp-buffer-boundaries`) ships the TC39 RegExp Buffer Boundaries proposal as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the RegExp syntax with four new anchors: (a) `\A` — matches the START of the input buffer (the absolute start, regardless of the `m` (multiline) flag's effect on `^`); (b) `\z` — matches the absolute END of the input buffer (regardless of the `m` flag's effect on `$`); (c) `\Z` — matches the END of the input buffer BUT ALLOWS a final terminator (newline character `
`); (d) `` — word-boundary, now updated to behave correctly at the boundaries of the input buffer (an empty buffer matches `` — beginning and end of buffer are both boundaries). The motivation is to enable secure / correct buffer-boundary matching for validation patterns (e.g. validating that an entire input matches a pattern, parsing line-based formats where the final newline matters, validating untrusted input against patterns that should NOT match across buffer boundaries). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page is on `https://game.example/`, assert that `new RegExp('\\Aabc\\z').test('abcdef')` returns `false` (controlled fixture verifying the absolute-end-anchor-rejection contract — the input `'abcdef'` does NOT end with `f` immediately followed by the buffer end; `\z` requires the pattern to match the absolute end), `new RegExp('\\Aabc\\z').test('abc')` returns `true` (controlled fixture verifying the absolute-anchors-accept contract — the input `'abc'` matches `\Aabc\z` because the pattern matches from the buffer start to the buffer end), `new RegExp('\\Aabc\\Z').test('abc\\n')` returns `true` (controlled fixture verifying the final-newline-tolerance contract — `\Z` allows the input to end with a final `\n` character; `'abc\n'` matches `\Aabc\Z` because the final `\n` is the tolerated terminator), `new RegExp('\\Aabc\\Z').test('abc\\n\\n')` returns `false` (controlled fixture verifying the final-newline-only-tolerance contract — `\Z` only tolerates ONE final `\n`; multiple newlines do NOT match), `new RegExp('\\Aabc\\Z').test('abc')` returns `true` (controlled fixture verifying the no-final-newline-tolerance contract — `\Z` accepts inputs without a final newline), `new RegExp('\\Aabc$', 'm').test('abc\\ndef')` returns `false` (controlled fixture verifying the multiline-caret-distinct-from-absolute-start contract — the `m` flag changes `^` and `$` to line-anchored semantics, but `\A` is ALWAYS the absolute buffer start regardless of the `m` flag), `new RegExp('\\b\\b').test('')` returns `true` (controlled fixture verifying the empty-buffer-boundary-match contract — `\b\b` matches an empty buffer because the beginning AND end of the buffer are both word-boundaries), `new RegExp('^abc$', 'm').test('abc\\ndef')` returns `true` (controlled fixture verifying the legacy-multiline-contract — the legacy `^` and `$` with `m` flag match per-line in multiline mode; the new `\A` and `\z` are stricter), `\A` is recognized in non-Unicode-mode regex (`new RegExp('\\Aabc')` works without the `u` flag; controlled fixture verifying the non-unicode-mode-accept contract), `\A` is recognized in Unicode-mode regex (controlled fixture verifying the unicode-mode-accept contract — `new RegExp('\\Aabc', 'u')` works), `Safari 26.6` controls (no RegExp Buffer Boundaries support; the proposal is Safari TP 251 first) report `new RegExp('\\A')` throws `SyntaxError` because `\A` is unrecognized (controlled fixture verifying the Safari 26.6 baseline), `Chrome 155` controls (no RegExp Buffer Boundaries support; the proposal is Safari TP 251 first) report the same as Safari 26.6 (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome baseline), `Firefox 155` controls (no RegExp Buffer Boundaries support; the proposal is Safari TP 251 first) report the same (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox baseline), the proposal is composable with the existing RegExp features (controlled fixture verifying the composition-contract — `new RegExp('\\A[a-z]+\\Z', 'i')` works — `\A`, `[a-z]+`, `\Z`, and the `i` flag compose without issue), and a controlled fixture verifying the security use case (controlled fixture verifying the secure-validation-use-case — a game-server-side or browser-side validation pattern like `new RegExp('\\A[a-z0-9]+\\z')` matches ONLY inputs that are EXACTLY alphanumeric with NO surrounding whitespace or other characters; the `\A` and `\z` anchors ensure the pattern matches the entire input — a security improvement over `^...$` which can match lines in multiline mode). Source: `https://webkit.org/blog/18194/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-251/` (Safari TP 251 release notes, WebKit commit 318415@main, bug 178287060), TC39 RegExp Buffer Boundaries proposal at `https://github.com/tc39/proposal-regexp-buffer-boundaries` (the `\A`, `\z`, `\Z`, `\b` extensions spec + the multiline-flag-distinct contract).

- [B-304] **[P1] Chrome 155 Stable CSS Corner Shorthand Properties `corner-top-left` / `corner-top-right` / `corner-bottom-left` / `corner-bottom-right` / `corner-top` / `corner-bottom` / `corner-block-start` / `corner-block-end` / `corner-inline-start` / `corner-inline-end` / `corners` (Alias) Let Authors Set Both `border-radius` And `corner-shape` Per Corner In A Single Declaration For Organic UI Shapes Without Reimplementing Each Corner Manually** Chrome 155 stable (released 2026-08-19 per Chromium superchargebrowser calendar, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5152215540039680`, sample at `https://static.januschka.com/i-425897047/`, code review `https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7747994`, Chromium bug `https://issues.chromium.org/issues/425897047`, spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-borders-4/#corner-shaping`) ships the CSS corner shorthand + per-corner sub-shorthands + physical / logical edge shorthands as enabled-by-default. The contract introduces: (a) per-corner shorthands `corner-top-left` / `corner-top-right` / `corner-bottom-left` / `corner-bottom-right` — each accepts the same two-value syntax as `border-radius` (the two values are the horizontal / vertical radii per the CSS Borders 4 spec); (b) physical edge shorthands `corner-top` / `corner-bottom` — each accepts two per-corner values that apply to both corners on the edge; (c) logical edge shorthands `corner-block-start` / `corner-block-end` / `corner-inline-start` / `corner-inline-end` — each accepts two per-corner values that apply to both corners on the logical edge (mapped via writing-mode); (d) the `corners` shorthand is retained as a compat alias that expands to the four per-corner shorthands. Each corner shorthand sets both `border-radius` AND `corner-shape` (a separate CSS Borders Level 4 property that controls the shape — `round` | `squircle` | `bevel` | `scoop` | `notch` — for the corner radius). The motivation is to give authors a more ergonomic declaration for non-rectangular UI corner shapes (e.g. organic blob shapes, superellipse squircles, asymmetric corner shapes) without reimplementing each corner manually. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>:root { --r: 16px; } #d { width: 200px; height: 100px; background: cyan; corner-top-left: var(--r) round; corner-bottom-right: 24px squircle; }</style><div id="d"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(d).cornerTopLeft === '16px round'` (controlled fixture verifying the per-corner-shorthand-accept contract — the corner-top-left shorthand parses both the radius and the corner-shape keyword per the CSS Borders 4 spec), `getComputedStyle(d).cornerTopRight === '0px round'` (controlled fixture verifying the default-value contract — unspecified corners default to `0px round` — a sharp corner), `getComputedStyle(d).cornerBottomLeft === '0px round'` (controlled fixture verifying the bottom-left default — also sharp), `getComputedStyle(d).cornerBottomRight === '24px squircle'` (controlled fixture verifying the second-corner-set contract — a different radius and shape keyword work simultaneously on a different corner), the rendered `<div>` shows two rounded corners (top-left at 16px round, bottom-right at 24px squircle — squircle is a superellipse interpolation) and two sharp corners (top-right and bottom-left at 0px round), with the asymmetric shape visible (controlled fixture verifying the visual-asymmetry contract — the per-corner control lets authors create UI elements that are NOT visually-symmetric across both axes), `corner-block-start: 8px round` applies to both `corner-top-left` and `corner-top-right` in horizontal-tb writing mode (controlled fixture verifying the logical-mapping contract — `corner-block-start` maps to `corner-top` corners in the default horizontal-tb mode and to side-relative corners in vertical writing modes per the CSS Logical Properties spec), `corner-top: 4px round, 8px round` (the per-corner shorthand syntax) sets `corner-top-left: 4px round` AND `corner-top-right: 8px round` in a single declaration (controlled fixture verifying the two-value-per-edge contract — the comma-separated values apply to the left and right corners on that edge in left-to-right order), `corners: 12px round` is the compat-alias shorthand that expands to setting all four `corner-*` per-corner shorthands to `12px round` (controlled fixture verifying the alias-equivalence contract — `getComputedStyle(d).cornerTopLeft === getComputedStyle(d).cornerBottomRight === '12px round'`), the `corner-shape` property from CSS Borders 4 (`round | squircle | bevel | scoop | notch`) accepts each value (controlled fixture verifying `corner-top-left: 8px squircle` parses and renders with a squircle curve — the visual rendering interpolates the corner curve using a superellipse parameter; this is the distinctive new shape vs `border-radius` which is always a circular arc), `@supports (corner-top-left: 8px round)` returns `true` on Chrome 155 stable (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate), `Chrome 154` controls (no CSS corner shorthand properties; corner-shape only exists via the underlying `border-radius` + `corner-shape` longhand pair) report `getComputedStyle(d).cornerTopLeft === ''` (the property is not present on the Chrome 154 baseline), `Safari 26.6` controls (no CSS corner shorthand properties; `corner-shape` is behind the `corner-shape` flag) report mixed coverage, `Firefox 155` controls (no CSS corner shorthand properties) report `getComputedStyle(d).cornerTopLeft === ''`. Spec reference: the CSS Borders Level 4 spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-borders-4/#corner-shaping` documents the corner shorthand grammar and the `corner-shape` property values.
