- [B-305] **[P1] Chrome 155 Stable JPEG XL (image/jxl) Decoding Support In Blink Using jxl-rs Adds Progressive Decoding For Improved Perceived Loading Performance + Wide Color Gamut / HDR / High Bit Depth / Animation Support For Game Asset Pipelines** Chrome 155 stable (released 2026-08-19 per Chromium superchargebrowser calendar, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5114042131808256`, Chromium bug `https://crbug.com/411805066`, decoder source `https://github.com/libjxl/jxl-rs`, spec at `https://www.iso.org/standard/85066.html` for ISO/IEC 18181) ships JPEG XL decoding support in Blink as enabled-by-default. The motivation is to add a modern image format to the Blink image pipeline that offers: (a) progressive decoding for improved perceived loading performance — the image renders a coarse preview that refines as more data arrives, so users see SOMETHING within ~50ms regardless of network speed; (b) wide color gamut support — full 16-bit per channel color depth for accurate color reproduction on P3 / Rec.2020 displays; (c) HDR support — preserves high-dynamic-range metadata via the PQ or HLG transfer functions for HDR-capable displays; (d) high bit depth — full 8 / 10 / 12 / 16-bit-per-channel decode; (e) animation support — animated JPEG XL (similar to animated WebP / animated PNG / animated GIF) for game UI sprites / loading indicators / avatar frames. The decoder is `jxl-rs`, a memory-safe pure-Rust implementation that mitigates the security risk of C/C++ decoders. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where `/test.jxl` is a 256x256 JPEG XL image, assert that `<img id="img" src="/test.jxl" alt="test">` loads and decodes the image (controlled fixture verifying the MIME-accept contract — `<img>.complete === true` after the network fetch + decode completes, and the rendered image is visible at the natural dimensions), `HTMLImageElement.src` accepts the `image/jxl` MIME type (controlled fixture verifying `img.naturalWidth === 256` and `img.naturalHeight === 256` after the decode completes), the `<source type="image/jxl">` element inside a `<picture>` works (controlled fixture verifying the source-selection contract — `<picture><source type="image/jxl" srcset="/test.jxl"><img src="/fallback.png"></picture>` selects the JPEG XL source when the browser supports it, falling back to the `<img>` for non-supporting browsers), the `Accept` request header includes `image/jxl` (controlled fixture verifying the content-negotiation contract — the browser automatically adds `image/jxl` to the `Accept` header after the JPEG XL decoder registers, so servers can serve `image/jxl` based on the request header without changing the `<img src>` URL), animated JPEG XL frames decode and play (controlled fixture verifying the animation contract — `<img src="/animated.jxl">` with 8 looping frames plays the animation in a `<img>` element), progressive decoding renders a coarse preview before the final decode completes (controlled fixture verifying the progressive-decoding contract — the `loading="lazy" decode="async"` attribute on the `<img>` element renders a coarse preview within ~50ms of network fetch start, then refines to the final image as more data arrives; the progressive preview has a fuzzy / under-detailed appearance that matches the JPEG XL progressive stream's first layer), HDR metadata via PQ transfer function is preserved (controlled fixture verifying the HDR contract — a JPEG XL image with PQ transfer function metadata renders with the PQ curve on an HDR-capable display; on a non-HDR display the image falls back to the sRGB-relative colorimetric mapping per the ISO/IEC 18181 spec), `Chrome 154` controls (no JPEG XL decoder in Blink) report `<img>.complete === false` for `<img src="/test.jxl">` (the browser downloads the file but cannot decode it, so `complete` remains `false` and no image renders; a Network panel trace shows the response with `Content-Type: image/jxl` and `200 OK` but the rendered area is blank), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari has shipped JPEG XL support since Safari 17 — `macOS Sonoma 14` and `iOS 17` and later) report `<img>.complete === true` and the image renders, `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox has JPEG XL support behind the `image.jxl.enabled` preference, default off) report mixed coverage depending on the preference. Spec reference: ISO/IEC 18181 (JPEG XL) at `https://www.iso.org/standard/85066.html` documents the container + codec spec; the jxl-rs decoder at `https://github.com/libjxl/jxl-rs` is the open-source Rust implementation that Chrome 155 uses. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the MIME-accept + decode-complete + progressive-rendering + animation play + HDR metadata + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 155 stable for the live-fire part.


- [B-306] **[P2] Chrome 155 Stable `closest-corner` And `farthest-corner` Radius Keywords For `circle()` And `ellipse()` Basic Shapes Match The Long-Standing `radial-gradient()` Behavior So The Same Shape Syntax Accepted By Gradients Now Works For `clip-path` / `shape-outside` / `offset-path`** Chrome 155 stable (released 2026-08-19 per Chromium superchargebrowser calendar, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=155` mirror, Chromium feature `5100672946143232`, code review `https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7767079`, Chromium bug `https://crbug.com/361617757`, spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes-1/#basic-shape-functions`) ships the `closest-corner` and `farthest-corner` radius keywords for the `circle()` and `ellipse()` basic-shape functions as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing `circle(<shape-radius>?)` and `ellipse(<shape-radius>{2}?)` basic-shape function syntax to accept the two new radius keywords in addition to the existing `closest-side` and `farthest-side` keywords. The semantic is: (a) `closest-side` — radius equals the distance from the shape's center to the nearest side of the reference box (existing, pre-Chrome-155); (b) `farthest-side` — radius equals the distance to the farthest side of the reference box (existing, pre-Chrome-155); (c) `closest-corner` (new) — radius equals the Euclidean distance from the shape's center to the nearest CORNER of the reference box; (d) `farthest-corner` (new) — radius equals the Euclidean distance from the shape's center to the farthest CORNER of the reference box. The new keywords MATCH the long-standing behavior of `radial-gradient(circle, ...)` / `radial-gradient(ellipse, ...)`, which has accepted `closest-corner` (the DEFAULT for both circle and ellipse gradient shapes) and `farthest-corner` since CSS Images Level 3. The motivation is to give authors ONE shape syntax across `clip-path` / `shape-outside` / `offset-path` that matches what they already use in `radial-gradient`. Without the new keywords, authors have to compute the corner distance manually and pass an explicit `<length-percentage>` to the `circle()` / `ellipse()` basic-shape functions. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>#d { width: 200px; height: 100px; background: cyan; clip-path: circle(closest-corner at 50% 50%); }</style><div id="d"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(d).clipPath === 'circle(at 50% 50%)'` (the canonical computed-value form, with the corner radius inferred from the reference box; controlled fixture verifying the keyword-accept contract — `closest-corner` is a valid `<shape-radius>` value per the CSS Shapes Level 1 spec), the `circle(closest-corner at 50% 50%)` shape has a radius of approximately `50px` for a `200px × 100px` reference box (controlled fixture verifying the closest-corner-radius contract — for a `200 × 100` box centered at `50% 50%`, the nearest corner is `sqrt((100-50)^2 + (50-50)^2) = 50px` to the top-left OR top-right corner; the radius is `50px`; the clipped shape is a circle of radius 50 centered at (100, 50)), `circle(farthest-corner at 50% 50%)` shape has a radius of approximately `111.8px` for the same `200 × 100` box (controlled fixture verifying the farthest-corner-radius contract — the farthest corner from center (100, 50) is the bottom-left corner at (0, 100), at distance `sqrt(100^2 + 50^2) ≈ 111.8px`), `ellipse(closest-corner closest-side at 50% 50%)` shape has horizontal / vertical radii that match the closest-corner / closest-side distances (controlled fixture verifying the ellipse-keyword-pair contract — `ellipse` accepts one or two radius keywords, each independently), `circle(closest-corner)` is the DEFAULT for `radial-gradient(circle, ...)` gradient shapes — both now use the same radius keyword (controlled fixture verifying the parity-with-radial-gradient contract), `circle()` without a radius argument uses `closest-corner` per CSS Shapes L1 spec (controlled fixture verifying the default-radius-contract — `circle() === circle(closest-corner)` per the spec's default-value rule), `shape-outside: circle(closest-corner at 50% 50%)` works the same way as `clip-path` (controlled fixture verifying the second-property-accept contract — the new radius keywords are recognized in `shape-outside` per the CSS Shapes Level 2 spec), `offset-path: circle(closest-corner at 50% 50%)` works the same way (controlled fixture verifying the third-property-accept contract — the new radius keywords are recognized in `offset-path` per the CSS Motion Path Level 1 spec), `@supports (clip-path: circle(closest-corner))` returns `true` on Chrome 155 stable (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate — pre-Chrome-155 controls return `false`), `Chrome 154` controls (no `closest-corner` / `farthest-corner` radius keywords for the `circle()` / `ellipse()` basic-shape functions) either drop the keyword (silent fallback) OR treat it as an unrecognized value per the spec (controlled fixture verifying that `getComputedStyle(d).clipPath` falls back to `border-box` or `none` instead of the desired circle; the legacy control only accepts `closest-side` / `farthest-side` / explicit `<length-percentage>`), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari has shipped `closest-corner` / `farthest-corner` for basic-shape functions since Safari 16 — `2022`) report `getComputedStyle(d).clipPath` returns the expected circle, `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox has shipped the new keywords behind `layout.css.basic-shape-circle-closest-corner.enabled` preference in Firefox 143+) report mixed coverage. Spec reference: the CSS Shapes Level 1 spec at `https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes-1/#basic-shape-functions` documents the `<shape-radius>` grammar that includes the four keywords. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the keyword-accept contract + the radius computation contract + the multi-property-parity contract + the `@supports` probe + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 155 stable for the live-fire part.


- [B-307] **[P1] Chrome 156 Stable Optional Descriptors For `CSS.registerProperty()` / `@property` Rule Lets Authors Omit `syntax` / `inherits` / `initial-value` Descriptors With Sensible Defaults So CSS Custom-Property Registration Is Less Verbose** Chrome 156 stable (released 2026-09-02 per Chromium superchargebrowser calendar post-cadence-shift, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=156` mirror, Chromium feature `5168674259468288`, Chromium bug `https://issues.chromium.org/issues/491802759`, spec at `https://drafts.css-houdini.org/css-properties-values-api-1/#at-property-rule`) ships optional descriptors for registered CSS custom properties as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing `CSS.registerProperty()` JS API and the `@property` CSS at-rule to allow authors to OMIT any of the three descriptors (`syntax` / `inherits` / `initial-value`), with sensible defaults: (a) omitted `syntax` defaults to the universal syntax `*` (any value is valid); (b) omitted `inherits` defaults to `false` (the property does NOT inherit by default — matching the unregistered custom-property default); (c) omitted `initial-value` defaults to the guaranteed-invalid initial value (the property's `getPropertyValue()` returns `""` per the CSS Custom Properties Level 1 spec when accessed in a context where no other value has been set). Invalid descriptors use the normal CSS fallback behavior (the rule is ignored, the property remains unregistered, the custom property behaves as an unregistered custom property). The motivation is to reduce the boilerplate for CSS custom-property registration — pre-Chrome-156, an author had to write `{syntax: "<color>", inherits: true, initialValue: "red"}` for EVERY property registration; with Chrome 156, the author can write `CSS.registerProperty({name: "--my-color"})` and let the defaults take over. Critical for game CSS frameworks that register dozens of custom properties for theming. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<script>CSS.registerProperty({name: "--my-default-color"}); CSS.registerProperty({name: "--my-inheriting-color", inherits: true});</script>`, assert that the `CSS.registerProperty({name: "--my-default-color"})` call with NO other descriptors succeeds without throwing (controlled fixture verifying the minimal-registration contract — the API accepts the bare-minimum descriptor set per the CSS Properties and Values API spec), the registered `--my-default-color` accepts any value (controlled fixture verifying the universal-syntax-default contract — an element with `<style>:root { --my-default-color: red; } .c { color: var(--my-default-color); }</style><div class="c" id="d">` has `getComputedStyle(d).color === 'rgb(255, 0, 0)'` AND `<style>:root { --my-default-color: 16px; }</style>` works because `syntax: "*"` allows the value), the registered `--my-inheriting-color` inherits by default (controlled fixture verifying the inherits-default contract — an element with `style="--my-inheriting-color: rgb(0, 255, 0)"` passes the value to descendants; `getComputedStyle(d).getPropertyValue('--my-inheriting-color') === 'rgb(0, 255, 0)'` for a `<div id="d">` descendant of the inheriting element), an invalid `syntax` value in `CSS.registerProperty({name: "--bad-color", syntax: "potato"})` causes the registration to fail and the property remains unregistered (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-syntax-fallback contract — the descriptor's invalid value per the spec means the whole registration is ignored; an attempt to read `--bad-color` via `getPropertyValue` returns `""` because the property was never registered), the `@property` CSS at-rule syntax mirrors the JS API contract (controlled fixture verifying the CSS-rule-parity contract — `<style>@property --my-css-default {} @property --my-css-inheriting { inherits: true; }</style>` creates the same two registered properties; the empty `@property --my-css-default {}` rule registers with all three descriptors defaulting — `syntax: "*"`, `inherits: false`, `initial-value: guaranteed-invalid`), the registered custom property's serialized `PropertyRule` IDL attribute exposes the defaults (controlled fixture verifying the IDL-roundtrip contract — `CSS.registerProperty.get('--my-default-color').syntax === '*'`, `.inherits === false`, `.initialValue === undefined` per the spec's guaranteed-invalid mapping), `@supports CSS.registerProperty(...)` returns `true` on Chrome 156 stable (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate), the registered property participates in CSS animations (controlled fixture verifying the animation-enablement contract — `@keyframes fade { from { --my-color: red; } to { --my-color: blue; } }` interpolates the registered property only if it has a registered `syntax` of `<color>`; the new `syntax: "*"` default does NOT enable animation interpolation, matching the unregistered custom-property behavior), `Chrome 155` controls (no optional-descriptors contract; the CSS Properties and Values API requires ALL three descriptors — `syntax`, `inherits`, `initial-value` — to be specified; omitting any of them throws `TypeError: Failed to execute 'registerProperty' on 'CSS'`) report `CSS.registerProperty({name: "--my-default-color"})` throws `TypeError` (controlled fixture verifying the throw contract — the pre-Chrome-156 API requires all three descriptors; bare-minimum registration fails synchronously), `Safari 26.6` controls (no CSS Houdini `registerProperty` support; the Properties and Values API was an origin trial that did not graduate to stable Safari) report `typeof CSS.registerProperty === 'undefined'` (the API is not present in Safari), `Firefox 155` controls (CSS Houdini `registerProperty` shipped in Firefox 128 — `2024`) report `CSS.registerProperty` works but with the strict all-three-descriptors contract matching the pre-Chrome-156 behavior (controlled fixture verifying which descriptors Firefox supports by default). Spec reference: the CSS Properties and Values API Level 1 spec at `https://drafts.css-houdini.org/css-properties-values-api-1/#at-property-rule` documents the optional-descriptor semantics with the universal-syntax / guaranteed-invalid defaults. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the minimal-registration accept + the universal-syntax-default + the inherits-default + the invalid-syntax fallback + the CSS-at-rule parity + the IDL round-trip + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 156 stable for the live-fire part.


- [B-308] **[P1] Mobile Touch-Action `none` And WCAG 2.2 § 2.5.7 / § 2.5.8 Target-Size-Minimum Contract — Touch Targets ≥ 24×24 CSS Pixel Hit Area With No Native Gesture Hijacking For Game Playability On Mobile Without "Iframe Load Is Not Playability" Pitfall** (Web-platform primitive + WCAG 2.2 contract. Not Chrome-specific — controlled fixture verifies the contract on Chrome 155+ AND Safari 26.6 AND Firefox 155+.) Per the W3C WCAG 2.2 Recommendation at `https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/` (specifically § 2.5.7 `Target Size (Minimum)` Level AA — at least 24×24 CSS pixels of hit area; § 2.5.8 `Target Size (Enhanced)` Level AAA — at least 44×44 CSS pixels), per the W3C CSS Touch Action spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/touch-action-1/`, per the GameZipper 2026 mobile-game UX audit findings ("iframe load is not playability", "iframe load does not prove that the game accepted the input", "the play button is covered by another layer; cross-origin focus prevents keyboard input; touch input may fail on mobile"), the following contract MUST hold for any browser-game UI on mobile: (a) all interactive targets (buttons / tap-zones / canvas hot-spots) must have a hit area of at least 24×24 CSS pixels per WCAG 2.2 AA / or 44×44 CSS pixels per WCAG 2.2 AAA — measured via `elementFromPoint(centerX, centerY)` returning the expected element over a 24×24 grid around the target center; (b) the canvas / interactive region must NOT have any CSS `touch-action` declaration other than `none` (which DISABLES all default browser gestures — pinch-zoom, pan, double-tap-zoom — for the duration of the touch) when the game wants exclusive touch input handling; (c) `touch-action: none` MUST be applied to the canvas element itself (not a parent container) so the gesture-hijacking only applies within the canvas bounds. This case is the machine-verifiable version of the playability audit pitfalls. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<canvas id="c" width="800" height="600" style="touch-action: none;"></canvas><div id="tap-zone" style="position: absolute; top: 10px; left: 10px; width: 60px; height: 60px; background: cyan;"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(canvas).touchAction === 'none'` (controlled fixture verifying the touch-action-accept contract — the canvas element accepts the `touch-action: none` CSS value per the CSS Touch Action spec; the canvas is now in exclusive-touch mode), the canvas has a 24×24 hit area at center (controlled fixture verifying the WCAG 2.2 AA target-size contract — `document.elementFromPoint(canvasCenterX, canvasCenterY) === canvas` for a 24×24 grid of test points centered on the canvas center), any tap-target with `width: 60px; height: 60px` has a hit area of at least 24×24 CSS pixels (controlled fixture verifying the 24×24-pixel-target contract — `document.elementFromPoint(zoneCenterX, zoneCenterY) === zone` for a 24×24 grid around the zone center), the tap-target with `width: 44px; height: 44px` satisfies the 44×44 target-size AAA contract (controlled fixture verifying the 44×44-pixel-AAA-target contract), the tap-target with `width: 20px; height: 20px` (the small-target case) FAILS the WCAG 2.2 AA target-size minimum (controlled fixture verifying the negative-test contract — the controlled fixture verifies that 20px is correctly identified as a WCAG 2.2 violation for the purposes of the test harness' calibration), `window.getComputedStyle(canvas).touchAction !== 'manipulation'` (controlled fixture verifying the exclusive-touch contract — the canvas does NOT use the `manipulation` value which would allow user panning + double-tap-zoom; `none` is required for exclusive touch), the canvas `pointerdown` event fires on synthetic tap (controlled fixture verifying the synthetic-tap-accept contract — Playwright dispatches a `page.touchscreen.tap(canvasCenterX, canvasCenterY)` call; the canvas's `pointerdown` event handler fires within 100ms; this is the controlled-fixture's definitive proof that the canvas accepts input AFTER the launch screen), `document.elementFromPoint` does NOT return an `<iframe>` ancestor (controlled fixture verifying the iframe-load-is-not-playability pitfall — even if the canvas is rendered inside an iframe, the `elementFromPoint` returns the canvas (NOT the iframe, NOT the iframe's parent) at every test point; the iframe-load event firing does NOT prove the canvas is reachable via pointer events — `elementFromPoint` is the authoritative proof), `document.elementFromPoint` does NOT return an overlay element (controlled fixture verifying the play-button-covered pitfall — the controlled fixture places a sibling overlay `<div style="position: absolute; ...">` over the canvas and verifies that `elementFromPoint(canvasCenterX, canvasCenterY) === overlay` (NOT canvas) when the overlay is at full opacity; the test harness verifies that the overlay does NOT cover the canvas in the production game, by removing the overlay and re-running `elementFromPoint`), the canvas has `tabindex="0"` (controlled fixture verifying the keyboard-focus contract — the canvas is focusable via keyboard so that keyboard-only users can interact; WCAG 2.1 § 2.1.1 `Keyboard` requires that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface), Safari 26.6 controls on iOS Safari (the hardest mobile-WebKit target) report the same `touch-action: none` + 24×24-pixel-target behavior (controlled fixture verifying cross-engine parity via the Playwright `webkit` browser driver), Firefox 155 controls on Android Firefox report `touch-action: none` works identically (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox mobile-WebKit contract), the iframe-load metric (`<iframe>.contentDocument.readyState === 'complete'`) is recorded but is NOT a substitute for the canvas-acceptance metric (controlled fixture explicitly noting the iframe-load metric in a `@comment` is NOT sufficient — the test fails unless `elementFromPoint` + `pointerdown` event-fire ALSO pass). Spec reference: the W3C WCAG 2.2 Recommendation at `https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/` documents § 2.5.7 / § 2.5.8 target-size minima; the CSS Touch Action Level 1 spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/touch-action-1/` documents the `touch-action: none` value; the GameZipper 2026 mobile-game UX audit findings at `https://dev.to/linsheng4g/what-i-learned-auditing-a-129-page-html5-catalog-iframe-load-is-not-playability-2li2` documents the iframe-load pitfall + the controlled-fixture acceptance pattern. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the WCAG 2.2 AA target-size + WCAG 2.2 AAA target-size + touch-action-none + canvas-pointerdown accept + iframe-load-is-not-playability counterexample + cross-engine parity in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 155+ AND a touchscreen-enabled Safari iOS simulator AND Firefox Android for the cross-engine parity live-fire part.



### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-474] **[P1] Cross-Browser Web Audio `setValueCurveAtTime` Re-Trigger Safety — `linearRampToValueAtTime` Is Spec-Compliant For Re-Triggered Drums / Arpeggiators Whereas `setValueCurveAtTime` Throws `DOMException: Can't add events during a curve event` On Firefox With Strict Spec Compliance So Drum-Hit / Hi-Hat Patterns With Look-Ahead Scheduling Must Use Linear Ramps Across All Browsers** (Cross-browser Web Audio contract, NOT Chrome-specific. Primary source: the CHIPTRACKER Firefox audio crash postmortem at `https://xyntaro-arcade.itch.io/chiptracker/devlog/1559053/patch-v20266-firefox-audio-crash-fix` from `20 June 2026`. Per the W3C Web Audio API spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#dom-audioparam-setvaluecurveattime` and `https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#dom-audioparam-linearramptovalueattime`.) Firefox strictly enforces the Web Audio spec rule that `setValueCurveAtTime()` schedules a "curve event" on an `AudioParam` and that NO other event may be scheduled on the same `AudioParam` while the curve is active (between its start and end time). Chrome / Chromium silently allows the additional events. This means a game that schedules re-triggering drum hits (e.g. `setValueCurveAtTime(kickCurve, kickTime, 0.05)` every beat) with a 200ms look-ahead scheduler will silently work in Chrome but THROW `Uncaught DOMException: AudioParam.setValueAtTime: Can't add events during a curve event` on Firefox within a few beats at higher BPMs (because the next hi-hat envelope starts before the previous curve's end time). The postmortem-documented fix is to use `linearRampToValueAtTime` instead — linear ramps interpolate the same way `setValueCurveAtTime` does (straight-line segments between curve points) but DO NOT create a "curve event" — they are free to be cancelled and re-scheduled at any time. The case is the machine-verifiable version of this Firefox-vs-Chrome divergence for any browser-game audio engine with a tempo-driven scheduler. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where `AudioContext` is constructed and a drum-hit pattern of 4 hit events per second is scheduled with a 200ms look-ahead, assert that constructing the `AudioContext` succeeds on all three browser engines (controlled fixture verifying the AudioContext-construct contract — `new AudioContext()` succeeds on Chrome 155+ stable, Safari 26.6, and Firefox 155), the `OscillatorNode` + `GainNode` graph wires up correctly (controlled fixture verifying the audio-graph-construct contract — `oscillator.connect(gain).connect(audioContext.destination)` succeeds; the gain node reaches `audioContext.destination`), `setValueCurveAtTime` schedules a curve on the gain param (controlled fixture verifying the curve-schedule contract — `gain.gain.setValueCurveAtTime(envelope, t+0.1, 0.05)` schedules a curve event on the gain param from time `t+0.1` for 50ms), on Chrome 155+ stable, re-triggering `setValueCurveAtTime` BEFORE the previous curve ends succeeds silently (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome-permissive contract — `gain.gain.setValueCurveAtTime(envelope, t+0.14, 0.05)` does NOT throw even though `t+0.14` is BEFORE `t+0.15` (the previous curve ends at `t+0.15`)), on Firefox 155, re-triggering `setValueCurveAtTime` BEFORE the previous curve ends THROWS `DOMException` (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox-strict contract — `gain.gain.setValueCurveAtTime(envelope, t+0.14, 0.05)` throws `DOMException: AudioParam.setValueAtTime: Can't add events during a curve event`; the catch-block fires), on Safari 26.6, the behavior matches Chrome's permissive model (controlled fixture verifying the Safari-permissive parity — Safari allows the re-trigger without throwing, matching Chrome's behavior), `linearRampToValueAtTime` does NOT throw on Firefox when re-triggering within the previous curve's active window (controlled fixture verifying the spec-compliant-fix contract — `gain.gain.linearRampToValueAtTime(0, t+0.14)` does NOT throw on Firefox 155 OR Chrome 155+ OR Safari 26.6; the linear ramp does NOT create a "curve event" per the Web Audio API spec), `cancelScheduledValues(t)` cancels both `setValueCurveAtTime` curves AND `linearRampToValueAtTime` ramps (controlled fixture verifying the cancel-both contract — `gain.gain.cancelScheduledValues(t)` clears all scheduled values from time `t` onward, regardless of whether they were scheduled via `setValueCurveAtTime` or `linearRampToValueAtTime`), the helper function `applyCurve(param, curve, startTime, duration) { param.setValueAtTime(curve[0], startTime); for (let i = 1; i < curve.length; i++) param.linearRampToValueAtTime(curve[i], startTime + (duration * i) / (curve.length - 1)); }` (the postmortem-documented fix) works on all three browser engines (controlled fixture verifying the helper-function contract — the helper produces an identical audio output on Chrome / Safari / Firefox; the cross-engine audio-eventual-identity test confirms the gain value at `startTime + duration/2` is the curve-midpoint value within ±1e-6 float precision), the 100-tempo drum pattern (16 hits in 1 second at 100 BPM with 50ms envelopes) does NOT throw on any browser (controlled fixture verifying the full-pattern-parity contract — the postmortem-tested pattern of 16 re-triggered drums at 100 BPM does NOT throw on Chrome / Safari / Firefox when using `linearRampToValueAtTime`; the equivalent test with `setValueCurveAtTime` ONLY works on Chrome / Safari and FAILS on Firefox), `window.AudioContext` is available on all three engines (controlled fixture verifying the AudioContext-availability contract — the controlled fixture is constructed on `new (window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext)()` to handle the Safari prefix), the audio eventually reaches the destination on all three engines (controlled fixture verifying the audio-reach-destination contract — `gain.gain.value` reads the current gain value after the scheduler has run; the value matches the curve's last point within ±1e-6 float precision). Spec reference: the W3C Web Audio API spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#dom-audioparam-setvaluecurveattime` documents the curve-event semantics that restrict concurrent event scheduling; the Web Audio API spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/#dom-audioparam-linearramptovalueattime` documents the ramp behavior that has no such restriction; the CHIPTRACKER postmortem at `https://xyntaro-arcade.itch.io/chiptracker/devlog/1559053/patch-v20266-firefox-audio-crash-fix` documents the production-grade fix pattern. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the AudioContext-construct + the chart-curve-schedule + the cross-browser divergence (Chrome permissive, Firefox strict, Safari permissive) + the linear-ramp-fix working on all three engines + the cancelScheduledValues-on-both + the full-pattern-parity in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 155+ stable AND Firefox 155 stable for the cross-engine parity live-fire part.


- [W-475] **[P2] WASM Input-Event Detection On Cross-Origin Embeds — Host Page Must Receive `keydown` / `keyup` Events After WASM Game Loses Focus On Clicking Outside The Iframe On Poki-Style Aggregator Pages** (Cross-browser / cross-embed WASM game input contract, NOT Chrome-specific. Primary source: the YoYoGames GameMaker-Bugs `#8549` issue at `https://github.com/YoYoGames/GameMaker-Bugs/issues/8549` from `2024-11-28` last updated `2025-06-04`.) Per the W3C HTML Living Standard at `https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#focusable-area` (which determines whether a clicked element receives / retains focus) and per the W3C WebAssembly JavaScript Interface spec at `https://webassembly.github.io/spec/js-api/` (which defines the WASM JS bindings that game engines like GameMaker / Unity WebGL / PlayCanvas use to register `keydown` / `keyup` handlers), the following contract MUST hold for any WASM game embedded in an iframe on a Poki-style aggregator page: (a) when the user clicks INSIDE the iframe (i.e. inside the game canvas), the iframe receives focus; (b) the WASM game's JS-side `keydown` / `keyup` event listeners registered via `document.addEventListener` (or `window.addEventListener`) receive subsequent keyboard events; (c) when the user clicks OUTSIDE the iframe (back to the aggregator page), the iframe LOSES focus and the WASM game's keyboard listeners stop receiving events (this is the expected `focus` semantics); (d) when the user clicks BACK INSIDE the iframe (re-focusing the iframe), the iframe re-receives focus AND the WASM game's keyboard listeners re-receive events. The known pitfall (per the GameMaker Bugs issue) is that on some embed configurations (WASM games exported as `.zip` to itch.io / Newgrounds / Poki-style aggregator pages), the iframe does NOT receive focus on initial click because the outer page (aggregator) has a higher-level focus target that absorbs the click. The user's workaround in the GameMaker issue is to register the listener at `window` instead of `document` (the listener fires regardless of where focus is, but only when the iframe is the active browsing context). This case is the machine-verifiable version of the iframe-focus contract for any WASM-game embed. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing an iframe `<iframe id="game" src="/wasm-game.html"></iframe>` where `/wasm-game.html` is a stub page that registers `<script>document.addEventListener('keydown', e => { parent.postMessage({type: 'keydown', key: e.key}, '*'); }); document.addEventListener('keyup', e => { parent.postMessage({type: 'keyup', key: e.key}, '*'); });</script>` and the parent page has `<div id="outside-zone" style="position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; width: 100px; height: 100px; background: pink;"></div>`, assert that clicking INSIDE the iframe focuses it (controlled fixture verifying the iframe-focusable contract — `iframe.contentWindow.document.activeElement` reflects the iframe's currently-focused element OR `iframe.contentWindow === document.activeElement` after the click; the WASM game's stub page receives focus), sending `keydown` to the iframe via synthetic-keyboard (Playwright `page.keyboard.press('ArrowUp')` after `page.frame('game').focus()`) is received by the WASM game's `keydown` listener (controlled fixture verifying the iframe-keydown-delivery contract — the parent page receives a `postMessage({type: 'keydown', key: 'ArrowUp'})` message via the WASM game's `keydown` listener; the message round-trip via `parent.postMessage` is the controlled-fixture's definitive proof that the iframe received AND processed the keyboard event), clicking OUTSIDE the iframe (the `outside-zone`) blurs the iframe (controlled fixture verifying the iframe-blur contract — after `await outside-zone.click()`, `iframe.contentWindow.document.activeElement === iframe.contentWindow.document.body` (or null) — the iframe has lost focus to the aggregator page's `outside-zone`), sending `keydown` while the iframe is NOT focused does NOT deliver to the WASM game's `keydown` listener (controlled fixture verifying the no-delivery-when-not-focused contract — `page.keyboard.press('ArrowUp')` (the parent-page-focused event) does NOT propagate to the iframe's WASM-game `keydown` listener; the parent page's `message` event handler does NOT receive a `postMessage`), clicking BACK INSIDE the iframe re-focuses it (controlled fixture verifying the iframe-refocus contract — after `await iframe.click()`, the iframe re-receives focus; `iframe.contentWindow.document.activeElement === iframe.contentWindow.document.body` is acceptable as the iframe has at least one focusable element OR the iframe itself is the active element), `keydown` events ARE delivered after the re-focus (controlled fixture verifying the redelivery contract — `page.keyboard.press('ArrowUp')` after the re-focus delivers to the iframe's WASM-game `keydown` listener; the parent page's `message` event handler receives a `postMessage({type: 'keydown', key: 'ArrowUp'})`), the WASM-game page can register listeners via `window.addEventListener` as an alternative (controlled fixture verifying the window-listener contract — when the listener is registered on `window` instead of `document`, the same delivery semantics apply; this is the GameMaker-Bugs-issue work-around pattern), on Poki-style aggregator pages (controlled fixture using `https://poki.com` as the parent) the iframe-focus behavior is the same as a local parent page (controlled fixture verifying the cross-origin-embed parity contract — the parent page is on a different origin than the WASM-game iframe; the iframe-focus behavior is NOT origin-bound), the GameMaker / PlayCanvas / Unity WebGL engine stubs all bind keyboard listeners via `window.addEventListener` (controlled fixture verifying the engine-listener-binding contract — `window.addEventListener('keydown', cb)` registered in the WASM-game's JS-side glue receives the events; the test harness simulates each engine's listener-binding pattern via inline stubs), the stub registers `addEventListener('blur', () => ...)` and `addEventListener('focus', () => ...)` on the iframe's `contentWindow` to log focus transitions (controlled fixture verifying the focus-transition-traceability contract — the parent page receives `postMessage({type: 'blur'})` when the iframe loses focus and `postMessage({type: 'focus'})` when it re-receives focus; the focus-transition log is the controlled-fixture's definitive proof of when the iframe is focused). Spec reference: the W3C HTML Living Standard at `https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#focusable-area` documents the focus / blur semantics that govern iframe focus on click; the W3C WebAssembly JS Interface spec at `https://webassembly.github.io/spec/js-api/` documents the JS bindings that game engines use to register input listeners; the GameMaker Bugs issue `#8549` at `https://github.com/YoYoGames/GameMaker-Bugs/issues/8549` documents the production failure mode. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the iframe-focusable contract + the iframe-keydown-delivery contract + the iframe-blur contract + the iframe-refocus contract + the cross-origin-embed parity + the window-listener alternative in a single Playwright session with two browser contexts (parent + iframe on different origins) running on Chrome 155+ AND Firefox 155 for the cross-engine parity live-fire part.



### Security / Privacy Sandbox (S)

- [S-487] **[P0] Third-Party iframe Content With `permission-policy` Sandbox Headers Can Silently Hijack Click Events Even After The Same-Origin Policy Is Honored — Cross-Origin Clickjacking Detection Requires CSP `frame-ancestors` + X-Frame-Options Whitelisting + `Permissions-Policy` Restrictive Policies For Game Embeds On Poki-Style Aggregator Pages** (Cross-origin security contract for iframe-based game embeds, NOT Chrome-specific. Primary source: the OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet at `https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Clickjacking_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html` and the W3C CSP3 `frame-ancestors` directive spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#frame-ancestors-and-frame-src`.) Per the OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet, any game embedded via `<iframe>` on a Poki-style aggregator page is VULNERABLE to clickjacking if the game page does NOT have: (a) an `X-Frame-Options` header set to `DENY` / `SAMEORIGIN` / `ALLOW-FROM https://allowed-origin.example` to restrict which origins can embed the page in a frame; (b) a CSP `frame-ancestors` directive (which supersedes `X-Frame-Options` in modern browsers) set to `'self'` (only same-origin embeds) or `'none'` (no embeds) or a specific origin list; (c) a `Permissions-Policy` header with restrictive features (e.g. `payment=()`, `camera=()`, `microphone=()`, `geolocation=()`) to prevent the game page from being embedded inside a malicious parent that could capture these features; (d) the `allowtransparency` / `sandbox` attributes on the iframe in the parent (sandboxing the iframe restricts the iframe's permissions including allow-scripts / allow-same-origin / allow-popups). The known pitfall (per the OWASP cheat sheet and various CVE reports from `2022-2026`) is that a game page WITHOUT these headers can be embedded in a malicious parent that overlays invisible UI on top of the iframe, hijacking clicks the user thinks go to the game (e.g. clicking an in-game "shoot" button actually clicks a "transfer funds" button in the parent). The case is the machine-verifiable version of the clickjacking-defense contract for any browser-game embed. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the game page is served with `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-ancestors 'none'">` (the strictest setting — refuse ALL embeds), assert that `<iframe src="/game.html">` from a different origin FAILS to load (controlled fixture verifying the frame-ancestors-none contract — the iframe refuses to load and the browser shows a `Refused to display in a frame because an ancestor violates the configured Content-Security-Policy` console message in the parent page), the game page's X-Frame-Options header is `DENY` (controlled fixture verifying the X-Frame-Options-DENY contract — `curl -I /game.html` returns `X-Frame-Options: DENY`; any iframe embed fails), the game page's X-Frame-Options header is `SAMEORIGIN` (controlled fixture verifying the X-Frame-Options-SAMEORIGIN contract — `curl -I /game.html` returns `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`; only same-origin embeds succeed; cross-origin embeds fail), the game page's `frame-ancestors 'self'` allows same-origin embeds but blocks cross-origin embeds (controlled fixture verifying the frame-ancestors-self contract — `<iframe src="/game.html">` from the SAME origin succeeds; `<iframe src="/game.html">` from a different origin fails), the game page's `Permissions-Policy` blocks `payment` / `camera` / `microphone` / `geolocation` features (controlled fixture verifying the permissions-policy-restrictive contract — `curl -I /game.html` returns `Permissions-Policy: payment=(), camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`; an attempt to use these features from within the iframe (via JS) fails: `typeof window.PaymentRequest === 'undefined'` (or calling `new PaymentRequest()` throws `NotAllowedError`), the parent page embedding the iframe uses `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms"` on the iframe (controlled fixture verifying the sandbox-attribute contract — the iframe element restricts the iframe's permissions; without `allow-scripts`, the game page's scripts cannot run; without `allow-same-origin`, the game page cannot access its own origin's storage from inside the iframe), the parent page's CSP `frame-src` directive whitelists game origins (controlled fixture verifying the CSP-frame-src-whitelist contract — `Content-Security-Policy: frame-src https://allowed-game-origin.example` on the parent page restricts which origin can be embedded in an iframe; cross-origin embeds fail with a CSP violation), the parent page's CSP `child-src` / `worker-src` directives are restrictive (controlled fixture verifying the related-CSP-directives contract — `child-src 'self' https://allowed-game-origin.example` and `worker-src 'self'` block unauthorized sub-resources from being loaded), the game page is fully isolated from cross-origin clickjacking attacks (controlled fixture verifying the full-isolation contract — the malicious-parent scenario described in the OWASP cheat sheet is BLOCKED: an attacker page `attacker.example` cannot embed `game.example` in an iframe because the game page has `frame-ancestors 'none'`; even if the attacker embeds the game in a partial-overlay, the user's click on the iframe ALWAYS reaches the game page (NOT the attacker's overlay) because the browser enforces the framing policy), Chrome 155+ controls (Chrome enforces CSP3 `frame-ancestors` per the spec) report the correct refusal (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome-CSP3-enforcement contract — the iframe refuses to load when `frame-ancestors 'none'` is set), Safari 26.6 controls (Safari enforces CSP3 `frame-ancestors` per the spec) report the same refusal (controlled fixture verifying the Safari-CSP3-enforcement parity), Firefox 155 controls (Firefox enforces CSP3 `frame-ancestors` per the spec) report the same refusal (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox-CSP3-enforcement parity), the older `X-Frame-Options: DENY` header is honored on all three engines (controlled fixture verifying the legacy-X-Frame-Options contract — `X-Frame-Options: DENY` blocks all embeds on Chrome / Safari / Firefox), `frame-ancestors 'self'` AND `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` allow same-origin but block cross-origin embeds (controlled fixture verifying the combined-directives contract — both directives together provide defense-in-depth). Spec reference: the W3C CSP3 spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#frame-ancestors-and-frame-src` documents the `frame-ancestors` directive semantics that supersede `X-Frame-Options`; the OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet at `https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Clickjacking_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html` documents the production-grade defense-in-depth pattern; the Permissions-Policy spec at `https://www.w3.org/TR/permissions-policy-1/` documents the `Permissions-Policy` header semantics. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'` + `X-Frame-Options: DENY` + `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` + `frame-ancestors 'self'` + `Permissions-Policy` restrictive + `sandbox` attribute + CSP `frame-src` whitelist + the cross-engine parity in a single Playwright session with three browser contexts (legitimate parent / malicious parent / game-page) running on Chrome 155+ stable AND Safari 26.6 stable AND Firefox 155 stable for the cross-engine parity live-fire part.

### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-300] **[P2] Chrome 150 Stable AccentColor And AccentColorText System Colors Lets Authors Access The User's OS Accent Color In CSS For Installed-PWA OS-Theme-Integration So Game UI Matches Native Theming Without Hardcoded Values — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 5068127364186112, spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-4/#css-system-colors per the CSS Color Module Level 4 Recommendation) ships the AccentColor and AccentColorText system colors as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing CSS system colors (defined in CSS Color 4 § 6.1) with two new keywords: AccentColor (the user's OS-configured accent color, e.g. macOS accent / Windows accent / ChromeOS accent / iOS tint color) and AccentColorText (the contrasting text color that should be readable on top of AccentColor per WCAG contrast requirements). The motivation is to let installed web applications match the user's OS theme without hardcoded accent values. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page is installed as a PWA and rendered on the initial profile (the prerequisite per the spec for AccentColor to be populated by the host OS), assert that `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('background-color').match(/rgb\(/ || 'accentcolor'` (controlled fixture verifying the system-color-accept contract - the CSS keyword `accentcolor` is a valid <color> value per the CSS Color 4 spec, and within an installed-PWA context the computed background-color resolves to the OS accent color in `rgb(R, G, B)` form), a CSS rule like `:root { --user-accent: AccentColor; }` sets the custom property to the OS accent color (controlled fixture verifying the custom-property-roundtrip contract - the CSS custom property accepts system-color values per the CSS Variables Level 1 spec), `getComputedStyle(d).color` for a sibling element with `color: AccentColorText` returns the high-contrast counterpart color (e.g. `rgb(255, 255, 255)` when the OS accent is dark, `rgb(0, 0, 0)` when the OS accent is light; controlled fixture verifying the contrast-pair contract - AccentColorText is the WCAG-compliant contrasting color per OS heuristics), the system-color keywords are NOT populated when the page is NOT installed as a PWA or NOT on the initial profile (controlled fixture verifying the context-restriction contract - per the spec the system color is only set in the installed-PWA-initial-profile context, NOT in the regular browser-tab context, where AccentColor falls back to the UA default of `CanvasText` per the CSS Color 4 fallback table), `AccentColor` and `AccentColorText` are recognized as keywords in the `color`, `background-color`, `border-color`, `outline-color`, `text-decoration-color`, `fill`, and `stroke` properties (controlled fixture verifying the multi-property-accept contract - the new system colors work across all <color> properties, not just text/background), the keywords are NOT recognized in `image()` function input position (controlled fixture verifying the image-restriction contract - `background-image: image(AccentColor)` is invalid because `image()` requires a URL or <image> argument, not a system-color keyword; per the spec `image(<color>)` accepts solid-color images but not the AccentColor system-color keyword), `Chrome 149` controls (no AccentColor / AccentColorText system colors - the prior Chrome stable) report the computed background-color as the empty string OR the initial CanvasText color when the system-color keyword is set (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 149 baseline lacks the AccentColor system colors), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not yet ship AccentColor / AccentColorText; the WebKit Bugzilla bug 241866 is still open as of the chromestatuslite retrieval 2026-08-25) report the same as Chrome 149 - the keywords are not recognized, falling back to the initial value (controlled fixture verifying the Safari gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox ships AccentColor / AccentColorText per the Firefox standards-position issue marked "Shipped/Shipping") report the correct OS accent color in installed-PWA contexts (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox pre-existing parity), and a controlled fixture verifying that the system colors automatically track OS theme changes without page reload (the user changes their OS accent color in macOS System Settings, and the page's computed `background-color: AccentColor` reflects the new color without requiring a refresh - controlled fixture verifying the live-tracking contract per the CSS Color 4 spec). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror (36,930 bytes - 26 enabled + 2 OT + 6 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 150 stable; the case body comes from the 'Enabled by default in 150' section entry 'AccentColor and AccentColorText system colors' linked to feature 5068127364186112). Primary evidence: W3C CSS Color Module Level 4 Recommendation at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-4/#css-system-colors (the AccentColor / AccentColorText system-color keywords + the installed-PWA context restriction); Chromium tracking bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40229450 (the Blink-side implementation); WebKit standards-position issue https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=241866 (Safari not yet shipping); the 25+ upvotes on the Chromium tracking bug (developer interest signal).

- [B-301] **[P2] Chrome 150 Stable Optional Rounding Parameter For polygon() Basic Shape Lets Authors Specify Corner-Rounding Length Without Manually Computing Bezier Curves So Game UI Polygon Borders Round Without Custom Code — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 6636392944893952, CSSWG issue https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/9843, interactive demo at https://codepen.io/yisi/pen/NPRLEQN) ships the optional rounding parameter for the polygon() basic-shape function as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing polygon() shape syntax from `polygon([<length-percentage> ]#)` to `polygon([<length-percentage> ]# [round <'border-radius'>]?)` where the optional `round <border-radius>` suffix specifies a uniform corner-rounding radius applied to all polygon vertices. The motivation is to let pages round polygon corners (a common need for organic / rounded UI shapes) without manually composing SVG path data with quadratic Bezier curves at each vertex. The motivation aligns with the existing SVG 2 polygon-rounding techniques but provides a CSS-native, declarative solution. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<div id="d" style="clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100% round 16px); width: 200px; height: 100px; background: red;"></div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(d).clipPath === 'polygon(0px 0px, 200px 0px, 200px 100px, 0px 100px round 16px)'` (controlled fixture verifying the syntax-accept contract - the `round <length>` suffix is parsed and the computed-value reflects the canonicalized length with the round modifier preserved), the rendered polygon shows a 200x100 rectangle with 16px rounded corners instead of sharp corners (controlled fixture verifying the rendering contract - the corner-rounding is applied to all four vertices uniformly per the `<border-radius>` value; the visual rendering matches a 16px-corner-radius rectangle), `polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100% round 50%)` accepts percentage values for the corner radius (controlled fixture verifying the percentage-accept contract - per the spec the round radius accepts the same `<length-percentage>` as border-radius), `polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100% round 0px)` with a 0 radius renders the original sharp-cornered polygon (controlled fixture verifying the no-rounding-fallback contract - the legacy syntax still works and renders identical to the pre-Chrome-150 behavior), `polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100% round -16px)` with a negative radius is rejected and falls back to no `clip-path` (controlled fixture verifying the negative-value-rejection contract - negative radii are invalid per the spec; the declaration is ignored and the element renders without clip-path), the round radius value is bounded by the polygon's inscribed-circle radius (controlled fixture verifying the geometric-bounds contract - a round radius larger than half the polygon's smallest dimension is clamped to that bound; per the spec the rounding is bounded by the available geometry), `shape-outside: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100% round 8px)` accepts the round parameter in shape-outside as well (controlled fixture verifying the shape-outside-accept contract - the round suffix works in both `clip-path` and `shape-outside` per the spec), `Chrome 149` controls (no polygon() round parameter - the prior Chrome stable) report `getComputedStyle(d).clipPath === 'polygon(...)'` WITHOUT the `round` suffix when the declaration includes `round 16px` (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 149 baseline lacks the round parameter; the suffix is treated as invalid and the declaration is silently dropped to the pre-Chrome-150 polygon syntax), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not yet ship the polygon() round parameter; the CSSWG issue 9843 is still open on the WebKit side as of the chromestatuslite retrieval 2026-08-25) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Safari gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox does not yet ship the polygon() round parameter; the CSSWG issue 9843 has "No signal" on the Mozilla side) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox gap), the round radius is composable with `clip-path` reference syntax (`clip-path: polygon(...) round 8px;` on a `<div>` whose sibling has `clip-path: url(#my-shape);` works independently; controlled fixture verifying the compositional-contract - the round suffix is per-shape and does not affect URL-referenced clip-paths), and a controlled fixture verifying the `round` parameter does not affect SVG `<polygon>` element rendering (the CSS `polygon()` basic-shape function is distinct from the SVG `<polygon>` element; the SVG `<polygon>` always renders sharp corners unless a `stroke-linejoin: round` is set; controlled fixture verifying the CSS-vs-SVG-distinction contract). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror (36,930 bytes - 26 enabled + 2 OT + 6 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 150 stable; the case body comes from the 'Enabled by default in 150' section entry 'Allow optional rounding parameter for polygon()' linked to feature 6636392944893952). Primary evidence: CSSWG issue https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/9843 (the spec PR adding the round parameter); interactive demo at https://codepen.io/yisi/pen/NPRLEQN (the working Chromium implementation that was the basis for the Chrome 150 shipping); the CSS Shapes Module Level 1 spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-shapes-1/#funcdef-polygon (the polygon() basic-shape function grammar with the round suffix extension).

- [B-302] **[P2] Chrome 150 Stable Animatable zoom CSS Property Lets Pages Transition And Animate The CSS zoom Property So Game Cameras And Pinch-To-Zoom Transitions Smoothly Scale Layouts Without transform: scale() — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 5183671737909248) ships the animatable zoom contract as enabled-by-default. The contract changes the existing CSS `zoom` property (a long-supported non-standard property that scales the entire element's box and contents, similar to `transform: scale()` but participating in layout — i.e. adjacent elements reflow) from a non-animatable discrete value to an animatable interpolated value. The contract: `zoom: 1` can transition smoothly to `zoom: 2` via CSS `@keyframes` or `transition: zoom 1s linear`, with intermediate values computed per the CSS Easing specification; the animation interpolates zoom as a `<number>` (e.g. `zoom: 1.5` is the midpoint between `zoom: 1` and `zoom: 2`). The motivation is to complement the existing `transform: scale()` animations (which do NOT affect layout — adjacent elements do NOT reflow) with `zoom` animations (which DO affect layout — adjacent elements reflow as the zoomed element grows). This is critical for game camera zoom and browser-style page-zoom UIs where the surrounding UI should reflow. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<div id="d" style="zoom: 1; transition: zoom 0.5s linear;"></div>` and a JS handler that sets `d.style.zoom = '2'`, assert that the element's computed `zoom` value transitions from `1` to `2` over 0.5 seconds (controlled fixture verifying the transition-accept contract - the zoom property is animatable via the CSS transition property, unlike the pre-Chrome-150 behavior where zoom was non-animatable), the intermediate `getComputedStyle(d).zoom` value at `t=250ms` is approximately `1.5` (controlled fixture verifying the linear-interpolation contract - at the midpoint of a linear transition the zoom value is the linear interpolation midpoint between start and end values, per the CSS Easing Level 1 spec), the element's bounding box (`d.getBoundingClientRect()`) grows from `100x100` to `200x200` over the transition duration (controlled fixture verifying the layout-affecting contract - zoom affects layout, so adjacent siblings reflow as the element grows; this is the key difference from `transform: scale()`), `@keyframes zoom-pulse { from { zoom: 1; } to { zoom: 1.2; } }` animation iterates the zoom value smoothly (controlled fixture verifying the keyframes-accept contract - the zoom property is animatable inside CSS keyframes), `transform: scale()` and `zoom` can be used simultaneously and compose multiplicatively (controlled fixture verifying the composition contract - `transform: scale(2); zoom: 1.5;` yields a visual scale of 3x because the two transforms compose multiplicatively; `getComputedStyle(d).zoom === '1.5'` AND `getComputedStyle(d).transform !== 'none'` per the CSS spec), `Chrome 149` controls (no animatable zoom - the prior Chrome stable) report `getComputedStyle(d).zoom === '2'` immediately after setting the new value (no transition fires; the legacy zoom property was non-animatable in Chrome 149), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit may support animatable zoom per the CSS Zoom spec implementation; the property has been animatable in Safari since Safari 13.1+) report the same transition behavior as Chrome 150 (controlled fixture verifying the Safari pre-existing parity), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox supports the zoom property; animatable zoom is also shipped in Firefox per the CSS Zoom spec implementation status) report the same transition behavior as Chrome 150 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox pre-existing parity), the animation preserves the document layout flow (adjacent siblings are pushed down/right as the zoomed element grows; controlled fixture verifying the layout-flow-contract - zoom triggers re-layout whereas transform does not), and a controlled fixture verifying that `zoom` is exposed in the CSSOM `CSSStyleDeclaration` API (`document.getElementById('d').style.zoom === '2'`; the property is readable and writable on the inline-style declaration per the CSS Object Model spec). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror (36,930 bytes - 26 enabled + 2 OT + 6 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 150 stable; the case body comes from the 'Enabled by default in 150' section entry 'Animatable zoom' linked to feature 5183671737909248). Primary evidence: CSS Viewport / CSS Zoom spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-viewport/ (the zoom property spec) + the CSS Easing specification at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-easing/ (the transition interpolation contract).

- [B-303] **[P2] Chrome 150 Stable CSS text-fit Property Scales Font Size Of Text Nodes To Perfectly Fit Container Width Without JS Workarounds So Game UI Dynamic Content Always Fills Available Space — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 5104141688635392, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-text-5/#text-fit-property, explainer at https://github.com/explainers-by-googlers/css-fit-text/blob/main/README.md) ships the CSS `text-fit` property as enabled-by-default. The contract: the `text-fit` property accepts the values `size` (default — no scaling) or `fill` (the new value — scales the font-size of text nodes so the text perfectly fills the container width, with all text visible without overflow). The motivation is to let pages achieve the common UX pattern of "fit this headline / dynamic content to fill the available horizontal space" without JS-based font-size calculations or trial-and-error. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<div id="d" style="width: 200px; height: 50px; text-fit: fill; font-size: 16px;">A long headline that needs to fit the container width</div>`, assert that `getComputedStyle(d).textFit === 'fill'` (controlled fixture verifying the computed-value contract - the text-fit IDL reflects the parsed keyword), the rendered text size is LARGER than the initial 16px font-size (because the text needs to fill 200px width; controlled fixture verifying the font-size-scaling contract - the browser computes the optimal font-size to fill the container width without overflow), the rendered text DOES NOT overflow the container width (controlled fixture verifying the no-overflow contract - the text-fit: fill value ensures the text fits the container width, even at the cost of font-size scaling), `text-fit: size` (the default) leaves the font-size unchanged (controlled fixture verifying the no-scaling-fallback contract - the legacy text-rendering behavior is preserved when text-fit: size), `<div style="width: 200px; ### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-472] **[P1] Chrome 150 Stable CSS URL Request Modifiers (cross-origin() / integrity() / referrer-policy()) Lets CSS url() Functions Control CORS / SRI / Referrer-Policy For Fetched Resources Without HTML Markup Changes — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 5111997147512832) ships the CSS url() request modifiers as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing CSS `url()` function syntax from `url("<url>")` to `url("<url>" [cross-origin(<cors-mode>)] [integrity("<integrity-string>")] [referrer-policy(<referrer-policy>)])` where the optional modifiers control the fetch behavior of the referenced resource directly from CSS. The three modifiers are: (a) `cross-origin(<cors-mode>)` — accepts the values `anonymous` or `use-credentials`, mirroring the HTML `<img crossorigin>` attribute and the Fetch API's `mode` option; (b) `integrity("<integrity-string>")` — accepts an SRI integrity hash string, mirroring the HTML `<img integrity>` attribute; (c) `referrer-policy(<referrer-policy>)` — accepts a referrer-policy value, mirroring the HTML `<a referrerpolicy>` attribute. The motivation is to give authors fine-grained control over cross-origin access, subresource integrity, and referrer policy for CSS-loaded resources (background images, fonts, SVG references, imported stylesheets, list-style-images, border-image-sources) without requiring HTML markup or JavaScript changes. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where `crossorigin-cors.example.com/image.png` is served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, assert that `<div style="background-image: url('https://crossorigin-cors.example.com/image.png' cross-origin(anonymous)); width: 100px; height: 100px;"></div>` loads the image successfully (controlled fixture verifying the cross-origin modifier accept contract - the `cross-origin(anonymous)` modifier causes the fetch to use CORS anonymous mode per the CSS URL spec), `<img style="background-image: url('https://cdn.example.com/image.png' integrity('sha384-XXXX'))">` with an integrity hash that does NOT match the response triggers a console error AND the resource is NOT loaded (controlled fixture verifying the integrity modifier accept contract - the integrity hash is verified per the SRI spec; mismatches are reported and the resource is blocked), `<link style="background-image: url('https://cdn.example.com/image.png' referrer-policy('no-referrer'));">` with the referrer-policy modifier omits the Referer header from the request (controlled fixture verifying the referrer-policy modifier accept contract - the Referer header is omitted per the Referrer Policy spec when no-referrer is specified), `url('image.png')` without modifiers loads with default fetch behavior (controlled fixture verifying the no-modifier-fallback contract - the legacy url() syntax still works per the pre-Chrome-150 behavior), `url('image.png' invalid-modifier(foo))` with an invalid modifier falls back to the no-modifier default behavior and the invalid modifier is ignored (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-modifier-fallback contract - per the CSS URL spec invalid modifiers are silently ignored, NOT rejected), the modifiers apply to CSS-loaded fonts (`@font-face { src: url('https://cdn.example.com/font.woff2' cross-origin(anonymous)) format('woff2'); }`; controlled fixture verifying the font-accept contract - the modifiers apply to @font-face src URLs per the CSS Fonts spec), the modifiers apply to CSS-imported stylesheets (`@import url('https://cdn.example.com/styles.css' referrer-policy('strict-origin')) screen and (max-width: 600px);`; controlled fixture verifying the import-accept contract - the modifiers apply to @import URLs), `Chrome 149` controls (no URL request modifiers - the prior Chrome stable) report `getComputedStyle(d).backgroundImage` as `none` or as a syntax error when modifiers are present (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 149 baseline lacks the modifier parsing; the url() function rejects the syntax entirely), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not yet ship URL request modifiers; the CSSWG issue is still open on the WebKit side) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Safari gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox does not yet ship URL request modifiers; the CSSWG issue has "No signal" on the Mozilla side) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox gap), and a controlled fixture verifying that combining all three modifiers (`url('https://cdn.example.com/image.png' cross-origin(anonymous) integrity('sha384-XXXX') referrer-policy('no-referrer'))`) is a valid syntax and applies all three fetch behaviors simultaneously (controlled fixture verifying the modifier-composition contract - the three modifiers are independent and compose per the CSS URL spec). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror (36,930 bytes - 26 enabled + 2 OT + 6 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 150 stable; the case body comes from the 'Enabled by default in 150' section entry 'CSS URL request modifiers' linked to feature 5111997147512832). Primary evidence: CSS Values Module Level 4 Editor's Draft at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-4/#url-type (the url() type grammar with the optional modifiers); Subresource Integrity spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/SRI/ (the integrity hash verification contract); HTML Referrer Policy spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/referrer-policy/ (the referrer-policy values).

- [W-473] **[P2] Chrome 150 Stable CSS background-clip: border-area Clips Background To The Area Painted By Border Strokes So Game UI Gradient Borders Render Without border-image Workarounds — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 6234471210811392, spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-backgrounds-4/) ships the `background-clip: border-area` value as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing `background-clip` property (which accepts `border-box | padding-box | content-box | text`) with a new `border-area` value that clips an element's background to the area painted by its border strokes, taking border-width and border-style into account while ignoring transparency from border-color. the CSSWG issue has limited Mozilla engagement) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox gap), the new value is composable with `background-origin` (controlled fixture verifying the origin-clip-composition contract - `background-origin: border-box; background-clip: border-area;` defines the origin AND clip region independently), and a controlled fixture verifying that `background-clip: border-area` does NOT affect the element's `border-image` rendering (the legacy border-image syntax continues to work;
