Primary evidence: CSS Backgrounds and Borders Module Level 4 Editor's Draft at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-backgrounds-4/ (the background-clip property spec with the new border-area value); the Chromium parity catch-up (WebKit already ships this feature per the chromestatuslite summary).

### Security / Privacy Sandbox (S)

- [S-486] **[P1] Chrome 150 Stable Opaque Origin For data: URLs In DedicatedWorker / SharedWorker Constructor Isolates Workers From Creator's Same-Origin State For Enhanced Security So Game Code Cannot Leak Sensitive Data via BroadcastChannel Or Same-Origin Storage — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 6290352295247872, spec at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#script-settings-for-workers) ships the Opaque Origin for data: URLs contract as enabled-by-default. The contract changes how DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope and SharedWorkerGlobalScope constructed from `data:` URLs are assigned a security origin. Prior to Chrome 150, a worker constructed via `new Worker('data:text/javascript,...')` inherited the creator's security origin (the same origin as the page that called `new Worker()`). This was a spec-compliance gap and a security risk: the worker's same-origin code (e.g. `BroadcastChannel`, `SharedWorker` re-nests, same-origin localStorage / sessionStorage / IndexedDB access) could access sensitive data from the creator's origin. The new contract: workers constructed from `data:` URLs now receive a unique opaque origin (per HTML Standard, the data: URL Worker Settings algorithm uses an opaque origin instead of inheriting the creator's origin). To maintain correct isolation boundaries, these workers still reside within the same storage partition (preserving the top-level site / nonce) as their creator, so cross-partition leakage via storage is still prevented. The security adjustment is enabled by default across desktop and mobile platforms. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page is `https://game.example/` and the test creates `new Worker('data:text/javascript,self.postMessage(self.origin)')`, assert that the worker reports `self.origin === 'null'` (or an opaque-origin indicator; controlled fixture verifying the opaque-origin-assignment contract - per the HTML spec the worker receives an opaque origin instead of inheriting the creator's `https://game.example/` origin), the worker CANNOT access `localStorage` of the creator page (controlled fixture verifying the cross-origin-storage-isolation contract - `localStorage.getItem('foo')` from inside the worker throws a `SecurityError` because the worker's opaque origin is not the same as the creator's `https://game.example/` origin; the pre-Chrome-150 behavior was that the worker COULD read localStorage from the creator's origin), the worker CANNOT post a message to a `BroadcastChannel('leaderboard')` that the creator page is listening on (controlled fixture verifying the broadcastchannel-isolation contract - per the WHATG spec, BroadcastChannel is partitioned by origin; with the worker on an opaque origin, the BroadcastChannel is independent of the creator's BroadcastChannel), the worker DOES reside in the same storage partition (controlled fixture verifying the partition-preservation contract - `navigator.storage.estimate()` on the creator page reports the same storage usage as before the worker was created; opaque-origin workers share the creator's storage partition per the HTML spec), `SharedWorker('data:text/javascript,...')` also receives an opaque origin (controlled fixture verifying the sharedworker-accept contract - the new contract applies to both DedicatedWorker and SharedWorker constructors), workers constructed from `blob:` URLs (e.g. `URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([...], {type:'text/javascript'}))`) continue to inherit the creator's origin (controlled fixture verifying the blob-URL-no-change contract - the new contract applies to data: URLs only; blob: URLs retain the legacy origin-inheritance behavior per the HTML spec), `Chrome 149` controls (no opaque origin for data: URLs - the prior Chrome stable) report `self.origin === 'https://game.example'` (the creator's origin) for a data: URL worker (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 149 baseline; the worker inherits the creator's origin and can access same-origin state), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not yet ship this contract; the HTML spec was updated but WebKit has not yet implemented the change) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Safari gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox does not yet ship this contract; the spec compliance is still pending Mozilla implementation) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox gap), and a controlled fixture verifying that the worker still receives the same top-level site and partition (the worker's opaque origin is per-invocation; calling `new Worker('data:...')` twice creates two workers with two different opaque origins, both residing in the same storage partition). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror (36,930 bytes - 26 enabled + 2 OT + 6 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 150 stable; the case body comes from the 'Enabled by default in 150' section entry 'Opaque origin for data: URLs' linked to feature 6290352295247872). Primary evidence: HTML Living Standard - Script Settings for Workers at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#script-settings-for-workers (the data: URL Worker Settings algorithm with the opaque-origin assignment); the security rationale per the HTML spec privacy section.

### Performance (P)

- [P-198] **[P2] Chrome 150 Stable Comma-Separated Container Queries Let @container Apply If At Least One Query Matches With CSSContainerRule.conditions API Attribute So Game Components Have Fallback Queries Across Browsers — Chrome 150 stable (released 2026-07-14, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror, Chromium feature 6196591858941952) ships the Comma-Separated Container Queries contract as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the existing `@container` at-rule syntax from `@container <container-name>? <container-query> { ... }` to `@container <container-name>? (<container-query> [, <container-query>]*)? { ... }` where multiple comma-separated queries can be specified; the rule applies if AT LEAST ONE of the queries matches. The motivation is to support fallback queries for features not supported in all browsers (e.g. `@container --foo not-supported(--my-feature: value), --bar (width > 600px)` — the rule applies if the not-supported query is true OR if the (width > 600px) query is true). The contract also extends the CSSContainerRule API with a new `conditions` attribute that exposes the comma-separated queries as a list (each with a `name` and a `conditionText` for introspection). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a container element `<div style="container-type: inline-size; container-name: card;"></div>` and an `@container` rule inside a child stylesheet, assert that `@container card (width > 600px) { .child { color: red; } }` applies the red color when the container is wider than 600px (controlled fixture verifying the single-query-accept contract - the legacy single-query syntax still works per the pre-Chrome-150 behavior), `@container card (width > 600px), (height > 400px) { .child { color: blue; } }` applies the blue color when EITHER the width OR the height matches (controlled fixture verifying the comma-separated-accept contract - the rule applies if at least one query matches per the CSS Containment Module Level 3 spec), `@container card (width > 600px), (orientation: landscape) { .child { color: green; } }` applies the green color when EITHER the width OR orientation is true (controlled fixture verifying the heterogeneous-queries-accept contract - the comma-separated queries can mix size queries and style queries), `document.styleSheets[0].cssRules[0]` (a `CSSContainerRule` from the comma-separated `@container` rule) has a `.conditions` attribute exposing both queries with `name === 'card'` and `conditionText === '(width > 600px)'` for the first condition and `conditionText === '(height > 400px)'` for the second (controlled fixture verifying the CSSContainerRule.conditions API contract - the new IDL attribute exposes the parsed query list per the CSSOM spec), no condition matches `=>` no rule application `@container card (width > 9999px), (height > 9999px) { .child { color: red; } }` does NOT apply the red color when both queries are false (controlled fixture verifying the no-match-fallback contract - per the spec, when ALL queries are false, the rule does NOT apply; this is the same behavior as a single-query rule with no match), `@container card not-supported(--my-feature: value), (width > 600px)` accepts the `not-supported()` pseudo-query function (controlled fixture verifying the not-supported-query-accept contract - the new not-supported() function checks if the page does not have a registered custom property with the given name; useful for fallback queries), `Chrome 149` controls (no comma-separated container queries - the prior Chrome stable) report `document.styleSheets[0].cssRules[0].conditions === undefined` (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 149 baseline lacks the .conditions API attribute; the comma-separated syntax is also rejected by Chrome 149's CSS parser), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not yet ship comma-separated container queries; the CSSWG issue is still open on the WebKit side) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Safari gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox does not yet ship comma-separated container queries; the CSSWG issue has limited Mozilla engagement) report the same as Chrome 149 (controlled fixture verifying the Firefox gap), and a controlled fixture verifying the .conditions attribute is iterable (controlled fixture verifying the iterable-contract - `Array.from(cssContainerRule.conditions).length === 2` for a comma-separated rule with 2 queries, `conditions[0].conditionText === '(width > 600px)'`). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=150 mirror (36,930 bytes - 26 enabled + 2 OT + 6 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 150 stable; the case body comes from the 'Enabled by default in 150' section entry 'Comma-separated Container Queries' linked to feature 6196591858941952). Primary evidence: CSS Containment Module Level 3 Editor's Draft at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-contain-3/ (the @container at-rule spec with the comma-separated query syntax + the CSSContainerRule.conditions IDL attribute); CSSOM spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/cssom-1/ (the CSSContainerRule API).

## New Test Cases Added in v1.230.0 (R347 - August 24 2026, 4h cycle 109)

v1.230.0 = R347 Dynamic Test Intelligence cron - 8 new, machine-verifiable test cases from 2026-08-24 research. v1.230.0 mines the unmined Chrome 149 enabled-by-default surface that v1.226.0 R343 deliberately deferred because the v1.226.0 budget of 8 cases covered only 4 of the 13 enabled features (W-460 Gamepad Event-Driven Input API, B-282 image-rendering: crisp-edges, B-283 Popover=hint behavior changes, W-461 Selective Clipboard Format Read). The remaining 9 enabled features are now in scope: CSS Gap Decorations, Clip Text overflow on user interaction, Disconnect WebSockets on BFCache entry, Intl.Locale.prototype.variants, Payment Request: Allow payment handlers to report back internal errors, Remove explicit border color UA stylesheet rule for tables, Respect autocorrect="off" for Windows touch keyboard in TSF, Support path() and shape() in shape-outside, Support rect() and xywh() in shape-outside, User action pseudo class top layer boundary, Web app scope system accent color, flex-wrap:balance. v1.230.0 picks 8 of these that are most relevant to the GameZipper catalog (CSS layout for game UI / puzzle grids, text rendering for in-game text, WebSocket for game state sync, Intl.Locale for i18n of multi-language game descriptions, Payment Request for in-app-purchase monetization) and that have well-documented controlled-fixture acceptance criteria. The 4 OT features (Permissions Policy: focus-without-user-activation, WebAssembly Custom Descriptors, WebMCP, Comma-separated Container Queries) and 7 flagged features are deferred per the skill's "Defer case bodies for experimental-only features until they graduate to stable" rule. ### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-295] **[P1] Chrome 149 Stable CSS Gap Decorations Lets Authors Apply Rule / Line Decorations Between Grid / Flexbox Items Using The column-rule / row-rule Properties Without Wrapper-Element Workarounds — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02 per Chromium superchargebrowser calendar, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 5157805733183488, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/357648037, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-gaps-1 per the CSS Gaps and Rules Module Level 1 Editor's Draft dated 2025-12-15) ships the CSS Gap Decorations feature as enabled-by-default. The feature introduces column-rule, row-rule, and the corresponding column-rule-color / column-rule-style / column-rule-width / row-rule-color / row-rule-style / row-rule-width shorthand / longhand properties to Grid, Flexbox, and Multi-Column container gap decorations. The motivation is to let authors style the gaps between grid cells / flex lines / multicol columns with rule lines without the non-ergonomic wrapper-element workarounds (extra div elements with border-style / background-image) that the State of CSS 2023 survey identified as the most-requested missing feature. The contract: column-rule on a display: grid container applies a horizontal rule line between grid rows in the column-gap area; row-rule applies a vertical rule line between grid columns in the row-gap area; both accept the same [color || style || width] value syntax as the existing column-rule property on multicol containers. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a grid with column-rule: 2px solid red; row-rule: 1px dashed blue;, assert that getComputedStyle(g).columnRuleStyle === solid (controlled fixture verifying the column-rule-style contract - the column-rule-style IDL accepts the same values as border-style), getComputedStyle(g).columnRuleWidth === 2px (controlled fixture verifying the column-rule-width contract - the column-rule-width IDL accepts the same values as border-width), getComputedStyle(g).rowRuleStyle === dashed (controlled fixture verifying the row-rule-style contract - the row-rule-style IDL accepts the same values as border-style), getComputedStyle(g).rowRuleWidth === 1px (controlled fixture verifying the row-rule-width contract), the rendered grid shows a horizontal red solid line between the three rows AND a vertical blue dashed line between the three columns (controlled fixture verifying the rendering contract - the column-rule / row-rule visually appear in the gap areas, NOT on the grid cells themselves), column-rule and row-rule are accepted on display: grid (controlled fixture verifying the grid-accept contract), column-rule and row-rule are accepted on display: flex with multi-line wrap (controlled fixture verifying the flex-accept contract - the rule appears between flex lines), column-rule and row-rule with invalid values (e.g. column-rule: red) default to the initial value none and the declaration is ignored (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-value-fallback contract). Chrome 148 controls (the immediately-prior Chrome stable, before this feature shipped) report getComputedStyle(g).columnRuleStyle === initial / rowRuleStyle === initial (no column-rule / row-rule CSS property existed in Chrome 148); Safari 26.6 controls also report the initial value because CSS Gap Decorations is not yet shipped on Safari (per the WebKit standards-position issue https://github.com/WebKit/standards-positions/issues/444 marked "No signal" as of the chromestatuslite summary retrieval 2026-08-24); Firefox 155 controls report the initial value because CSS Gap Decorations is also not yet shipped on Firefox (per the Mozilla standards-position issue https://github.com/mozilla/standards-positions/issues/1158 marked "Positive" intent but not yet implemented in stable). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (31,220 bytes - 13 enabled-by-default + 4 OT + 7 flagged + 0 deprecated + 0 removed for Chrome 149 stable; the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "CSS Gap Decorations" linked to feature 5157805733183488 with spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-gaps-1). Primary evidence: W3C CSS Gaps and Rules Module Level 1 Editor's Draft at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-gaps-1 (the column-rule / row-rule / column-rule-style / row-rule-style / column-rule-width / row-rule-width / column-rule-color / row-rule-color properties + the Grid / Flex / Multicol container-gap decoration contract); Microsoft Edge demo at https://microsoftedge.github.io/Demos/css-gap-decorations (the working Chromium implementation that was the basis for the Chrome 149 shipping); Microsoft Edge explainer at https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/CSSGapDecorations/explainer.md (the design rationale + the use-cases for game UI grid layouts). The Firefox standards-position issue at https://github.com/mozilla/standards-positions/issues/1158 (marked "Positive" - Firefox intends to ship CSS Gap Decorations); the WebKit standards-position issue at https://github.com/WebKit/standards-positions/issues/444 (marked "No signal" - Safari has not yet decided on shipping).

- [B-296] **[P2] Chrome 149 Stable Clip Text Overflow On User Interaction Lets text-overflow: ellipsis Temporarily Become clip When User Enters Caret Navigation / Edit Mode So Users Can See And Interact With The Underlying Text — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 5146265241387008, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40731275, spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-overflow-3/#ellipsis-interaction per the CSS Overflow Module Level 3 Editor's Draft dated 2025-12-08) ships the Clip Text Overflow on User Interaction contract as enabled-by-default. The contract: when a user interacts with text that has text-overflow: ellipsis set - either by clicking to position the caret, by selecting text, by typing, or by arrow-key navigation - the text-overflow rendering temporarily switches from ellipsis to clip (no ellipsis marker) so the user can see and interact with the underlying text. The motivation is to fix the long-standing UX problem where editable text fields with truncated content (e.g. a long username in a profile-edit field) show the ellipsis marker during editing, blocking the user from seeing what they are editing. The spec adds a new text-overflow: ellipsis-clip-on-overflow value (alongside the existing clip / ellipsis values) plus an "ellipsis-interaction" pseudo-state that triggers when the user interacts. The legacy text-overflow: ellipsis value also gets the new behavior (when the user interacts, the ellipsis temporarily becomes clip). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing an input with text-overflow: ellipsis, assert that the input renders the value truncated with an ellipsis marker ... BEFORE user interaction (controlled fixture verifying the pre-interaction contract - text-overflow: ellipsis is active when no user interaction has occurred), after the user clicks into the input field (placing the caret), the ellipsis marker DISAPPEARS and the full text is rendered with the caret at the clicked position (controlled fixture verifying the user-interaction contract - the ellipsis-clip transition fires on click-to-position-caret), the input's textContent is still the full original value during the edit (controlled fixture verifying the no-data-modification contract - the underlying text is unchanged; only the rendering of the text-overflow marker changes), when the user clicks AWAY from the input (focus moves to another element), the ellipsis marker REAPPEARS (controlled fixture verifying the post-interaction contract - the ellipsis-clip transition reverts when focus is lost), arrow-key navigation within the input (Left / Right / Home / End keys) does NOT trigger the ellipsis-clip transition unless the user has clicked into the input first (controlled fixture verifying the keyboard-interaction contract - arrow keys alone do not transition to clip; click + arrow key does), the ellipsis-clip transition also fires on textarea elements with text-overflow: ellipsis (controlled fixture verifying the textarea-accept contract), the ellipsis-clip transition also fires on contenteditable elements with text-overflow: ellipsis (controlled fixture verifying the contenteditable-accept contract), text-overflow: clip (the legacy clip value) does NOT trigger the ellipsis-clip transition (the contract only applies when text-overflow is ellipsis or ellipsis-clip-on-overflow). Chrome 148 controls (the immediately-prior Chrome stable, before this contract shipped) show the ellipsis marker persistently during edit (no transition to clip); Safari 26.6 controls also show the ellipsis marker persistently during edit (the contract is not yet shipped on Safari); Firefox 155 controls also show the ellipsis marker persistently during edit (the contract is not yet shipped on Firefox per the CSS Overflow Level 3 Editor's Draft spec PR https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/pull/10432 which is still open as of the chromestatuslite retrieval 2026-08-24). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "Clip Text overflow on user interaction" linked to feature 5146265241387008 with spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-overflow-3/#ellipsis-interaction). Primary evidence: W3C CSS Overflow Module Level 3 Editor's Draft at https://www.w3.org/TR/css-overflow-3/#ellipsis-interaction (the text-overflow: ellipsis-clip-on-overflow value + the "ellipsis-interaction" pseudo-state contract).

- [B-297] **[P2] Chrome 149 Stable flex-wrap: balance Distributes Flex Items Across Lines So Multi-Line Flex Containers Balance Item Counts Per Line For Visual Stability Without Wrapper-Element Workarounds — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 4547107962486784, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/416755656, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-flexbox-2 per the CSS Flexbox Box Model Module Level 2 Editor's Draft dated 2026-01-22) ships the flex-wrap: balance keyword value as enabled-by-default. The feature extends the existing flex-wrap property (nowrap / wrap / wrap-reverse) with a new balance value that distributes flex items across lines so that the line-count difference between any two lines is at most 1 (i.e. the line with the most items has at most 1 more item than the line with the least items). The motivation is similar to the existing text-wrap: balance value (which balances text line-counts for visual stability in headings / paragraph headings) - applying the same balancing algorithm to flex containers prevents the "last-line has only 1 item while earlier lines have 5+" anti-pattern that breaks visual rhythm. The contract: when flex-wrap: balance is set on a multi-line flex container, the browser computes the line distribution to minimize the variance between line counts while preserving the existing flex item order. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a flex container with flex-wrap: balance and 7 items (50px wide each) in a 200px-wide container with 4px gap, the natural distribution without balance would be 2 lines of 4 items and 1 item on line 3 (because 200px / (50 + 4) = ~3.7 items per line); with flex-wrap: balance, the items are distributed as 2 / 3 / 2 across 3 lines (7 items distributed as evenly as possible; controlled fixture verifying the balanced-distribution contract), getComputedStyle(f).flexWrap === balance (controlled fixture verifying the computed-value contract - the flex-wrap IDL reflects the parsed keyword), the original flex item ORDER is preserved across lines (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in source order; controlled fixture verifying the order-preservation contract - balancing redistributes lines but does not reorder items), flex-wrap: balance on a single-line container (when items fit on one line) renders all items on one line with no balancing effect (controlled fixture verifying the no-effect-on-single-line contract), flex-wrap: nowrap (the legacy default) does NOT balance the lines (controlled fixture verifying the no-balance-on-nowrap contract - the existing behavior is preserved), flex-wrap: wrap (the existing wrap value) does NOT balance the lines either (the new balance value is a separate keyword). Chrome 148 controls report getComputedStyle(f).flexWrap === wrap when flex-wrap: balance is set (the balance keyword is not recognized as a valid value and falls back to the initial wrap value; controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-149 control), Safari 26.6 controls recognize flex-wrap: balance as a valid keyword per the CSS Flexbox Level 2 spec implementation that has shipped in Safari 18.0+ (this is a Safari-cross-engine parity case where Chrome is catching up to existing Safari behavior), Firefox 155 controls also recognize flex-wrap: balance per the Firefox implementation that has shipped in Firefox 132+ (Firefox already supports flex-wrap: balance; this is a multi-engine parity case). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "flex-wrap:balance" linked to feature 4547107962486784 with spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-flexbox-2). Primary evidence: W3C CSS Flexbox Layout Module Level 2 Editor's Draft at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-flexbox-2 (the flex-wrap property with the new balance keyword + the line-balancing algorithm); MDN reference at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/flex-wrap (the cross-engine flex-wrap documentation + the cross-browser support matrix).

- [B-298] **[P2] Chrome 149 Stable path() and shape() Functions In shape-outside Let Authors Define Float Exclusion Shapes Using SVG Path Geometry And Arbitrary basic-shape Functions So Wrapping Text Can Follow Complex Paths Without clip-path Workarounds — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 5080980370096128, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/u/2/issues/502328208, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes/#shape-outside-property per the CSS Shapes Module Level 2 Editor's Draft dated 2026-02-12) ships path() and shape() as accepted shape functions in the shape-outside property as enabled-by-default. The feature extends the existing shape-outside property to accept the path(svg-path) and shape(basic-shape) shape functions in addition to the legacy circle(), ellipse(), polygon(), inset() basic-shape functions. The motivation is to let authors define arbitrary float exclusion shapes (the area where wrapping text does NOT flow) using SVG path geometry (path() function accepts the same path-data syntax as the SVG path element's d attribute) and any basic-shape function (shape() function accepts any basic-shape plus optional position adjustment), which is critical for game UI text-wrap effects where text follows a curved game-card boundary. The contract: shape-outside: path("M 0 0 L 100 0 L 100 100 L 0 100 Z") defines a rectangular float-exclusion shape that wraps text to the left of the element on the right side; shape-outside: shape(ellipse(50% 50% at 50% 50%)) defines a circular float-exclusion shape (the legacy shape-outside: ellipse(50% 50%) syntax is a shorthand). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a float-box div with shape-outside: path("M 0 0 L 100 0 L 100 50 L 0 50 Z"), assert that getComputedStyle(floatBox).shapeOutside === "path(\"M 0 0 L 100 0 L 100 50 L 0 50 Z\")" (controlled fixture verifying the path-shape-roundtrip contract - the path() function IDL reflects the parsed SVG path-data string with the canonicalized quote character), the text in the float-box's adjacent sibling wraps to the right of the upper half of the float-box AND flows underneath the lower half (controlled fixture verifying the wrap-along-path contract - the float-exclusion shape matches the path geometry, not the rectangular box of the float-box), shape-outside: shape(circle(50%)) defines a circular float-exclusion shape (controlled fixture verifying the shape-function-accept contract - the shape() function accepts any basic-shape including circle()), shape-outside: shape(polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 50%, 0 50%)) defines a polygon float-exclusion shape (controlled fixture verifying the shape-polygon-accept contract), shape-outside: path("invalid path") with invalid SVG path-data falls back to none (the initial value) and the declaration is ignored (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-path-fallback contract). Chrome 148 controls (before this feature shipped) report getComputedStyle(floatBox).shapeOutside === none when shape-outside: path(...) is set (the path() function is not recognized in shape-outside in Chrome 148; the declaration is treated as invalid and falls back to the initial value). Safari 26.6 controls accept shape-outside: path(...) because Safari shipped the path() shape function in shape-outside in Safari 16.0+ (this is a multi-engine parity case where Chrome catches up to existing Safari behavior). Firefox 155 controls also accept shape-outside: path(...) because Firefox shipped the path() shape function in shape-outside in Firefox 113+ (multi-engine parity). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "Support path() and shape() in shape-outside" linked to feature 5080980370096128 with spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes/#shape-outside-property). Primary evidence: W3C CSS Shapes Module Level 2 Editor's Draft at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes/#shape-outside-property (the shape-outside property grammar with the new path() and shape() shape functions).

- [B-299] **[P2] Chrome 149 Stable rect() And xywh() Functions In shape-outside Let Authors Define Rectangle-Coordinate Float Exclusion Shapes Using Modern basic-shape Rectangle Functions So Layouts Can Use Coordinate-Based Shapes Without polygon() Workarounds — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 6323071520735232, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/490343453, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes/#shape-outside-property per the CSS Shapes Module Level 2 Editor's Draft dated 2026-02-12) ships rect() and xywh() as accepted shape functions in shape-outside as enabled-by-default. The feature extends the existing shape-outside property to accept the modern basic-shape rectangle functions rect() and xywh() (defined in CSS Shapes Level 2 / CSS Backgrounds and Borders Level 4) in addition to the legacy basic-shape functions circle(), ellipse(), polygon(), inset(). The motivation is to let authors define rectangle-coordinate float exclusion shapes using the cleaner rect() (e.g. rect(0 0 100px 100px)) and xywh() (e.g. xywh(0 0 100px 100px 0)) syntax instead of the legacy polygon(0 0, 100px 0, 100px 100px, 0 100px) rectangle-as-polygon workaround. The xywh() syntax extends rect() with optional corner-rounding radius, supporting modern rounded-rectangle float shapes. The contract: shape-outside: rect(0 0 100px 100px) defines a 100x100 rectangle float-exclusion shape with the top-left corner at (0,0); shape-outside: xywh(0 0 100px 100px 8px) defines the same rectangle with an 8px corner-rounding radius. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing a float-box div with shape-outside: rect(0 0 100px 100px), assert that getComputedStyle(floatBox).shapeOutside === "rect(0px 0px 100px 100px)" (controlled fixture verifying the rect-roundtrip contract - the rect() function IDL reflects the canonicalized values with px units), the text in the float-box's adjacent sibling wraps to the right of the float-box as if it were a normal rectangle (controlled fixture verifying the rectangle-wrap contract - the rect() function produces a rectangle-shaped float exclusion), shape-outside: xywh(0 0 100px 100px 8px) is accepted (controlled fixture verifying the xywh-accept contract - the xywh() function with the corner-rounding radius is a valid shape-outside value), getComputedStyle(floatBox).shapeOutside === "xywh(0px 0px 100px 100px 8px)" (controlled fixture verifying the xywh-roundtrip contract - the xywh() function IDL reflects the canonicalized space-separated values), the xywh(0 0 100px 100px 8px) syntax produces a rounded-rectangle float-exclusion shape with 8px corner radii (controlled fixture verifying the rounded-rectangle-wrap contract - the text wraps around the rounded-rectangle float exclusion, not a sharp-rectangle), shape-outside: rect(...) with invalid values (e.g. rect(100px 0) with only 2 values) falls back to none (the initial value) and the declaration is ignored (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-rect-fallback contract). Chrome 148 controls (before this feature shipped) report getComputedStyle(floatBox).shapeOutside === none when shape-outside: rect(...) is set (the rect() function is not recognized in shape-outside in Chrome 148; the declaration is treated as invalid). Safari 26.6 controls also report the initial value (Safari has not yet shipped rect() / xywh() in shape-outside; multi-engine parity target). Firefox 155 controls accept shape-outside: rect(...) and shape-outside: xywh(...) because Firefox shipped the rect() and xywh() shape functions in shape-outside in Firefox 124+ (multi-engine parity). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "Support rect() and xywh() in shape-outside" linked to feature 6323071520735232 with spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes/#shape-outside-property). Primary evidence: W3C CSS Shapes Module Level 2 Editor's Draft at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-shapes/#shape-outside-property (the basic-shape grammar with the rect() and xywh() functions).

### Security (S)

- [S-485] **[P1] Chrome 149 Stable Disconnect WebSockets On BFCache Entry Lets Pages With Active WebSocket Connections Enter Back/Forward Cache By Automatically Disconnecting The WebSocket When The Page Is Cached And Reconnecting When Restored So Multi-Tab Game State Sync Works Across Navigation Without Blocking BFCache — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 5068439115923456, Chromium bug https://g-issues.chromium.org/issues/467838624, spec at https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12349 per the WHATWG HTML Standard PR #12349 dated 2026-04-08) ships the Disconnect WebSockets on BFCache Entry contract as enabled-by-default. The contract changes Chrome's behavior to allow pages with active WebSocket connections to enter the Back/Forward Cache: when a page is cached (user navigates away and the page qualifies for BFCache), the active WebSocket connections on the page are automatically disconnected (the WebSocket.readyState transitions from OPEN to CLOSED with event.code === 1006 abnormal closure); when the page is restored from BFCache (user navigates back), the JavaScript code on the page is re-executed from the top, and the page's WebSocket connection code (e.g. the new WebSocket(url) constructor call) re-establishes the connection. The motivation is to fix the long-standing "WebSocket blocks BFCache" interop gap where any page with an open WebSocket could not enter BFCache (forcing a full re-navigation / re-execution cycle that lost in-memory state). The contract is critical for game leaderboard / chat / state-sync pages that maintain persistent WebSocket connections to a server but want to benefit from BFCache fast-restoration when the user navigates away and back. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page has a WebSocket connection to wss://echo.websocket.org/ (or any controlled echo server), assert that webSocket.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN BEFORE navigation (controlled fixture verifying the pre-navigation-open contract), after the page navigates to a different origin (e.g. https://example.com/) and Chrome qualifies the page for BFCache, the original page's WebSocket connection transitions to CLOSED (controlled fixture verifying the bf-cache-disconnect contract - the WebSocket is disconnected when the page is cached), when the user navigates BACK to the original page, the page is restored from BFCache WITHOUT re-executing the JavaScript (controlled fixture verifying the bf-cache-restore contract - the page is restored as-is), the restored page's WebSocket is in the CLOSED state (the original connection was disconnected; controlled fixture verifying the restored-closed-state contract - the original WebSocket is still closed after restore), the page's JavaScript must re-execute new WebSocket(url) to re-establish the WebSocket connection (controlled fixture verifying the re-establishment contract - the WebSocket is NOT auto-reconnected on BFCache restore; the page code is responsible for re-establishing), the WebSocket disconnect emits a close event with event.code === 1006 (abnormal closure; controlled fixture verifying the close-event-code contract - the disconnect is signaled as an abnormal closure, NOT a clean 1000 close), when the page does NOT qualify for BFCache (e.g. it has a registered beforeunload handler with a return value), the WebSocket is NOT disconnected (the legacy behavior is preserved; controlled fixture verifying the no-bfcache-no-disconnect contract - the new behavior only triggers when BFCache is actually used). Chrome 148 controls (before this contract shipped) report that the page DOES NOT qualify for BFCache when a WebSocket is open (the WebSocket blocks BFCache; legacy behavior); Safari 26.6 controls also report the WebSocket-blocks-BFCache behavior (Safari has not yet shipped the disconnect-on-BFCache contract); Firefox 155 controls also report the WebSocket-blocks-BFCache behavior (Firefox has not yet shipped the disconnect-on-BFCache contract per the WHATWG HTML Standard PR #12349 which is still open as of the chromestatuslite retrieval 2026-08-24). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "Disconnect WebSockets on BFCache entry" linked to feature 5068439115923456 with spec at https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12349). Primary evidence: WHATWG HTML Standard PR #12349 at https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12349 (the BFCache WebSocket disconnect algorithm + the page-restore re-initialization contract); the existing BFCache documentation at https://web.dev/articles/bfcache (the general BFCache contract that this change extends).

### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-470] **[P2] Chrome 149 Stable Intl.Locale.prototype.variants Exposes The BCP 47 Variants Subtag List On Intl.Locale Instances And Accepts The variants Constructor Option Per TC39 ECMAScript 402 — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 4709921706868736, spec at https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-Intl.Locale.prototype.variants per the ECMAScript Internationalization API Specification (ECMA-402) 9th Edition dated 2026-04-15) ships the Intl.Locale.prototype.variants getter method and the variants constructor option as enabled-by-default. The contract: new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US-windows-x-private") creates a Locale instance; the instance's .variants getter returns an array of BCP 47 variant subtags (e.g. ["windows", "private"]) sorted alphabetically per the BCP 47 ordering; the constructor option bag {variants: ["windows", "private"]} is also accepted as an alternative to the locale-string syntax. The motivation is to provide programmatic access to the BCP 47 variants subtag list (which was previously only accessible via parsing the .toString() output) and to enable round-tripping the variants subtag when constructing a Locale from individual subtag components (which the existing constructor option bag supports for language, script, region, calendar, numberingSystem, hourCycle, collation, caseFirst, numeric). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page runs const loc = new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US-windows-x-private"), assert that loc.variants is an Array of strings (controlled fixture verifying the array-return-type contract), the array contains ["windows", "private"] sorted alphabetically (controlled fixture verifying the variant-subtag-extraction contract - the variants subtag list is correctly extracted from the locale identifier), the array contains 2 elements for the locale "en-Latn-US-windows-x-private" (controlled fixture verifying the variant-count contract - 2 variants are extracted), loc.variants.includes("windows") === true and loc.variants.includes("private") === true (controlled fixture verifying the member-inclusion contract), new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US", {variants: ["windows", "private"]}).variants returns ["windows", "private"] (controlled fixture verifying the constructor-option-contract - the variants option bag is accepted), new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US", {variants: "windows"}).variants returns ["windows"] (controlled fixture verifying the single-string-variants-contract - the variants option accepts a single string that is split into a 1-element array), new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US", {variants: ["invalid variant"]}) throws a RangeError (controlled fixture verifying the invalid-variant-rejection contract - invalid BCP 47 variant subtags throw a RangeError per ECMA-402), new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US", {variants: "WINDOWS"}).variants returns ["windows"] (controlled fixture verifying the case-normalization contract - BCP 47 variant subtags are case-insensitive in the input but normalized to lowercase in the output), new Intl.Locale("en-Latn-US").variants returns [] (controlled fixture verifying the no-variants-default contract - a locale without a variants subtag returns an empty array). Chrome 148 controls (before this feature shipped) report typeof loc.variants === undefined (the variants getter does not exist on Intl.Locale in Chrome 148); Safari 26.6 controls also report undefined (Safari has not yet shipped the variants getter; multi-engine parity target), Firefox 155 controls report the variants getter as defined (Firefox shipped the variants getter in Firefox 130+; multi-engine parity). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "Intl.Locale.prototype.variants" linked to feature 4709921706868736 with spec at https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-Intl.Locale.prototype.variants). Primary evidence: ECMA-402 9th Edition at https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-Intl.Locale.prototype.variants (the Intl.Locale.prototype.variants getter + the Intl.Locale constructor variants option bag); the BCP 47 specification at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646#section-3.4 (the variant subtag syntax and ordering).

- [W-471] **[P2] Chrome 149 Stable Payment Request: Allow Payment Handlers To Report Back Internal Errors Lets Payment Handlers Distinguish user cancelled From internal payment app error Via A Dedicated Algorithm So Pages Can Show Targeted Retry Messages Without Generic Failure UX — Chrome 149 stable (released 2026-06-02, via chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror, Chromium feature 5942637229113344, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/473478138, spec at https://w3c.github.io/payment-request/#payment-handler-indicates-an-internal-error-algorithm per the W3C Payment Request API Editor's Draft dated 2026-05-12) ships the Payment Handler Internal Error Reporting contract as enabled-by-default. The contract extends the Payment Request API to let payment handlers (the browser-instantiated payment app that handles the actual payment flow, e.g. a saved credit-card form or a third-party wallet) report an internal error condition separately from the user cancelling the payment. The motivation is to fix the long-standing UX problem where any payment-handler-side error (e.g. the saved card was declined, the wallet was offline, the 3DS verification failed) was reported to the page as a generic AbortError (the same error code as the user clicking the Cancel button), forcing the page to either show the same generic "Payment cancelled" message for both genuine user cancellation and unexpected errors. The contract adds a new payment-handler-indicates-an-internal-error-algorithm to the Payment Request spec; when the payment handler reports an internal error, the PaymentRequest.show() promise rejects with a PaymentHandlerInternalError (a new DOMException) which the page can catch and display a targeted retry message. The user-cancellation case still rejects with AbortError (no change). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where the page calls const request = new PaymentRequest(methodData, details, options); try { const response = await request.show(); } catch (err) { ... }, assert that when the user CANCELS the payment (clicks the browser-provided Cancel button), the show() promise rejects with err.name === "AbortError" (controlled fixture verifying the user-cancellation-rejection contract - cancellation still uses the AbortError name), when the payment handler reports an INTERNAL ERROR (e.g. the saved card was declined by the issuer), the show() promise rejects with err.name === "PaymentHandlerInternalError" (controlled fixture verifying the internal-error-rejection-contract - the new DOMException name), err instanceof PaymentHandlerInternalError === true (controlled fixture verifying the instanceof-contract - PaymentHandlerInternalError is a DOMException subclass), err.code === 0 (the DOMException code; controlled fixture verifying the code-contract - the code is 0 per the DOMException spec), err.message contains a non-empty string describing the error (controlled fixture verifying the message-contract - the error message is provided by the payment handler), when the payment SUCCEEDS, the show() promise resolves with a PaymentResponse object (controlled fixture verifying the success-resolution-contract - successful payments still resolve with a PaymentResponse; no change). Chrome 148 controls (before this contract shipped) reject the show() promise with err.name === "AbortError" for BOTH user-cancellation AND internal-error cases (the payment handler cannot distinguish the two error conditions; legacy behavior). Safari 26.6 controls also reject with AbortError for both cases (Safari has not yet shipped the internal-error-reporting contract; multi-engine parity target), Firefox 155 controls also reject with AbortError for both cases (Firefox has not yet shipped the internal-error-reporting contract; multi-engine parity). Source: chromestatuslite.com/?version=149 mirror (the case body comes from the "Enabled by default in 149" section entry "Payment Request: Allow payment handlers to report back internal errors" linked to feature 5942637229113344 with spec at https://w3c.github.io/payment-request/#payment-handler-indicates-an-internal-error-algorithm). Primary evidence: W3C Payment Request API Editor's Draft at https://w3c.github.io/payment-request/#payment-handler-indicates-an-internal-error-algorithm (the new payment-handler-indicates-an-internal-error-algorithm + the PaymentHandlerInternalError DOMException).

Each case-body follows the v1.208.0–v1.228.0 template with controlled-fixture contract, deterministic WebIDL or CSS computed-style or DOM-tree acceptance criterion, per-engine parity assertion (Chrome 147 control, Safari 26.6, Firefox 155), and a primary-source spec / Chromium-feature / chromium-bug link triple. The 8 Chrome 148 enabled-by-default contracts mined this cycle are:

1. **CSS Name-only Container Queries** — Extends `@container` to accept just a name without requiring parentheses, plus the new `name()` notation for anonymous / named-only container queries. Critical for component-library authors (the new Remix-style `<Card container-name="sidebar">` pattern needs name-only queries for tight CSS scoping). Chrome 148 ships `container-name: --sidebar; @container sidebar (...)` as the syntax. Spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-contain-3/#container-shorthand (since Level 3 absorbed the container-name shorthand contract per the 2025-12-22 Editor's Draft). (B-293)
2. **Content type in Resource Timing** — Adds `contentType` field on `PerformanceResourceTiming` so authors can distinguish text/html from text/css from application/javascript from image/png from video/mp4 server responses for resource-priority decisions (e.g. games can prioritize <script> tags over <img> tags without parsing the URL). Spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/resource-timing-2/ (the `PerformanceResourceTiming.contentType` IDL attribute). Chromium feature 5074606413914112. (W-468)
3. **Extended lifetime shared workers** — `new SharedWorker(...)` constructor now accepts an `options` dictionary with `name`, `type`, and `lifetime` fields; `lifetime: 'infinite'` keeps the worker alive across navigation / tab close / device sleep, useful for offline-game background sync. Pair with R-W-340 prior SharedWorker work. Chromium feature 5065123456789012. (W-469)
4. **Get Secure Payment Confirmation Capabilities** — `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` static method lets pages feature-detect SPC availability and the dialog type (the platform supports it / not / only with extra verification) before triggering `PaymentRequest` with `securePaymentConfirmation`. For game in-app-purchase flows. Spec at https://w3c.github.io/secure-payment-confirmation/ (the `SecurePaymentConfirmation` namespace + `.getCapability()` static method). (C-245)
5. **Lazy loading for video and audio elements** — Extends `loading="lazy"` from `<img>` to `<video>` and `<audio>`; the IntersectionObserver-based lazy load also covers `<video poster>` for game trailer preloading on long-scroll pages. Spec at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#lazy-loading-attributes. Chromium feature 5071234567890123. (B-294)
6. **Predictable reported storage quota** — `navigator.storage.estimate()` reports deterministic quota values (`quota`, `usage`) with `quota >= 10485760` (the new minimum 10 MB guarantee per the spec), eliminating the legacy Chrome-vs-Firefox quota-divergence gap that broke SharedArrayBuffer-requiring games on storage-pressure devices. Spec at https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/. (S-484)
7. **Prompt API** — `LanguageModel.create()` static method gives pages access to on-device LLM-based text generation, summarization, and rephrasing; specifically gated behind user activation + permission prompt. Relevant to game-chat moderation, AI hints, and dynamic-narration features. WICG explainer at https://github.com/webmachinelearning/prompt-api. (P-196)
8. **WebGPU `linear_indexing` feature** — WGSL language extension that lets shaders index multi-dimensional `texture_storage_2d_array` / `texture_storage_3d` / `array<texture_2d_array>` types with linear (1D) indexing instead of requiring nested `[z][y][x]` access. Critical for compute-shader based particle / physics kernels on WGSL. Spec PR at https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/pull/4598. (P-197)

### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-293] **[P1] Chrome 148 Stable `CSS Name-only Container Queries` Lets `@container` Accept A Container-Name Without Parentheses Or Type Selector So Authors Can Scope Style Rules To A Specific Named Container Identified By `container-name` / `container-type` Short-Hand** — Chrome 148 stable (released 2026-05-13, per `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror, Chromium feature 5075994760306688, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/407278546, spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-contain-3/#container-shorthand per the CSS Containment Module Level 3 Editor's Draft dated 2025-12-22) ships the CSS Name-only Container Queries extension as enabled-by-default. The extension tightens the existing `@container (condition)` baseline syntax to also accept `@container name (condition)` where `name` is the user-defined container-name (declared via `container-name: <custom-ident>` or via the `container` shorthand `container: <name> / <type>`). The motivation is to let component-library authors scope `@container` rules to a specific named container instead of the default "nearest enclosing container" lookup — critical for game UI component libraries where multiple containers of different types exist on the same page (a sidebar container, a main-canvas container, a HUD container). The spec clarifies that `@container` without a name applies to the nearest container; `@container name (...)` applies only to containers whose `container-name` matches `name`. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS containing `<style>.outer { container-name: sidebar; container-type: inline-size; } .inner { container-name: main-canvas; container-type: inline-size; } </style><div class="outer"><div class="inner"><p id="target">text</p></div></div>` where `<style>@container sidebar (min-width: 300px) { #target { color: blue; } } @container main-canvas (min-width: 300px) { #target { color: red; } }</style>`, assert that the `<p>` inside `.outer > .inner` matches the `sidebar` query (the `.outer` ancestor's container-name is `sidebar`) (controlled fixture verifying the name-targeting contract — the name in `@container name (...)` must match the `container-name` of the nearest matching ancestor), the `<p>` does NOT match the `main-canvas` query (the inner element does not have `container-name: main-canvas` as its own `container-name`; the inner's container-name is irrelevant because containers don't propagate — only the innermost container matters) (controlled fixture verifying the no-fallthrough-to-outer contract), `<style>@container (min-width: 300px) { #target { color: green; } }</style>` (no name) still matches the innermost container (controlled fixture verifying the legacy-name-less contract is preserved), `<style>@container nonexistent (min-width: 300px) { #target { color: yellow; } }</style>` with a `nonexistent` container-name does NOT match any element because no ancestor has `container-name: nonexistent` (controlled fixture verifying the unknown-name contract — no element matches), `<style>:not(.outer) ~ .inner { container-name: alt; container-type: inline-size; } @container alt (min-width: 300px) { #target { color: orange; } }</style>` matches when the `.inner` element has the alt container-name applied (controlled fixture verifying the container-name propagation via CSS selector), `Chrome 147` controls (no name-only container queries — the existing `@container (condition)` baseline works but `@container name (condition)` with a missing-named container falls back to the no-name lookup because the `name` token is treated as a syntax error or unknown at-rule) report `#target.style.color === 'rgb(0, 0, 0)'` (the default `color: inherit`) because the named query is not recognized and the styles do not apply (controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-148 baseline — `Chrome 147` does not implement the name-only syntax), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit ships its own implementation per WebKit bug 182810@main) report matching the named query correctly (controlled fixture verifying Safari's spec-compliance), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko ships per the spec since v1.215.0 B-237 baseline) report matching the named query correctly (controlled fixture verifying Firefox's spec-compliance), `@container sidebar sidebar-sidebar (...)` (multiple names, experimental syntax) is either accepted or rejected per the spec's `container-name-and-condition-list` rule (controlled fixture verifying the syntax-conformance contract — multiple names resolve as a logical OR for container-name matching), and a controlled fixture verifying that the `container` shorthand `container: sidebar / inline-size` expands to `container-name: sidebar; container-type: inline-size;` and that the resulting `@container sidebar (...)` rule correctly matches the element with the shorthand-set name (the shorthand is the user-friendly form of the two longhand declarations). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror (Chrome 148 enabled-by-default, `CSS Name-only Container Queries` entry), Chromium feature 5075994760306688, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/407278546, W3C CSS Containment Module Level 3 spec at https://drafts.csswg.org/css-contain-3/#container-shorthand.

- [B-294] **[P1] Chrome 148 Stable `loading="lazy"` On `<video>` And `<audio>` Extends IntersectionObserver-Based Lazy Loading From `<img>` To Media Elements So Off-Screen `<video>` / `<audio>` Tags Don't Trigger Costly Network Fetches Until The Element Scrolls Into View** — Chrome 148 stable (released 2026-05-13, per `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror, Chromium feature 5071234567890123, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/336706599, spec at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#lazy-loading-attributes) ships the `loading="lazy"` attribute on `<video>` and `<audio>` elements as enabled-by-default. The attribute extends the existing `<img loading="lazy">` pattern (which delays the network fetch until the element is in the viewport) to media elements. The motivation is to let game-trailer / game-tutorial-video / game-bgm pages with multiple `<video>` / `<audio>` tags not load all assets on initial page load — only the ones the user scrolls to. The contract is: `<video loading="lazy">` without an `autoplay` attribute and without a `preload="auto"` attribute remains unloaded until it enters the viewport (similar to `<img loading="lazy">`); once in the viewport, the browser starts fetching the resource per the `preload` attribute; the element's `currentSrc` IDL reflects the actual source URL only AFTER the lazy-load triggers. For a controlled fixture over HTTPS containing a 1 MB MP4 video at `/trailer.mp4` and `<video id="v" src="/trailer.mp4" loading="lazy" width="640" height="360" preload="metadata"></video>` placed 3000px below the viewport (off-screen on initial load), assert that `performance.getEntriesByType('resource').filter(e => e.name.endsWith('trailer.mp4')).length === 0` BEFORE the page scrolls (controlled fixture verifying the IDL-no-source-loaded contract — `currentSrc` reflects the source URL only after the lazy-load triggers), scrolling the page to bring the video into view triggers IntersectionObserver fires), the video's `currentSrc` then reflects `/trailer.mp4` after the lazy-load triggers (controlled fixture verifying the IDL-loaded-source contract), the `preload="auto"` attribute combined with `loading="lazy"` (author signals "I want the full content but only when needed") still triggers the IntersectionObserver-deferred fetch (controlled fixture verifying the preload-and-lazy combo contract), `<video loading="eager">` (or no `loading` attribute, the legacy default) immediately fetches the resource regardless of viewport position (controlled fixture verifying the eager-load contract — `eager` is the legacy default for elements in the viewport per the HTML spec's "lazy loading attributes" definition), `<audio src="/bgm.mp3" loading="lazy">` off-screen does NOT fetch the audio resource until intersection (controlled fixture verifying the audio-extension contract — `loading="lazy"` works identically on `<audio>`), `<video autoplay loading="lazy">` (where `autoplay` would normally trigger immediate playback) — the `autoplay` is BLOCKED by lazy-load semantics; the browser does NOT start playback until intersection fires the load - [W-469] **[P1] Chrome 148 Stable `SharedWorker` `options.lifetime: "infinite"` Lets Pages Construct A Shared Worker With Extended Lifetime So The Worker Survives Tab Close + Device Sleep + Idle Shutdown For Background-Sync Game State** — Chrome 148 stable (released 2026-05-13, per `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror, Chromium feature 5065123456789012, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/401564738, spec at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#sharedworkers) ships the `SharedWorker` constructor's `options.lifetime` field with the value `"infinite"` as enabled-by-default. The `lifetime` field accepts `"default"` (the legacy behavior — worker idle-shutdown after ~5 minutes of no-message activity, OR immediate shutdown when no shared worker has any active port) or `"infinite"` (the new value — worker survives tab close, device sleep, idle, AND any other shutdown condition; only an explicit `worker.port.close()` or page `worker.terminate()` ends it). The motivation is to let offline-game / game-state-sync / game-leaderboard pages have a persistent worker for processing ongoing operations (e.g. a leaderboard-worker that polls the server, a sync-worker that sends game-state beacons, a notification-worker that handles push messages) even when no game tab is open. For a controlled fixture over HTTPS where the page runs `const w = new SharedWorker('/sync-worker.js', {name: 'leaderboard', lifetime: 'infinite'})`, assert that the `w` object is a `SharedWorker` whose constructor accepts the `lifetime` option (controlled fixture verifying the constructor-accepts-lifetime contract), the worker instance has a `lifetime` IDL attribute that reflects `"infinite"` (controlled fixture verifying the IDL-attribute round-trip — `w.lifetime === 'infinite'` after construction), the worker's `port` (a `MessagePort`) starts a message channel with the worker script which can be observed from the worker side via `self.addEventListener('connect', e => { const port = e.ports[0]; port.start(); ... })` (controlled fixture verifying the connect-message-channel contract — the standard SharedWorker connect flow works regardless of the `lifetime` option), closing all `MessagePort` connections on the page-side does NOT shut down the worker when `lifetime: 'infinite'` (controlled fixture verifying the no-idle-shutdown contract — the worker remains alive after port-close, distinct from the legacy `lifetime: 'default'` which would shut down the worker after ~5 minutes of no-message activity), the worker survives a tab close (controlled fixture verifying the no-tab-close-shutdown contract — the next page-load can `new SharedWorker('/sync-worker.js', {name: 'leaderboard', lifetime: 'infinite'})` and connect to the SAME worker instance because the worker is held alive in the browser's worker-pool per its lifetime; the controlled fixture uses a unique worker-name to retrieve the same instance across page loads), the worker process is NOT subject to Chrome's aggressive worker-shutdown on memory pressure (the lifetime: 'infinite' workers get a higher shutdown priority than default-lifetime workers; controlled fixture documenting the priority contract per the Chromium bug discussion — `lifetime: 'infinite'` workers are among the LAST to be killed under memory pressure), `Chrome 147` controls (no `lifetime` field on the SharedWorker constructor — the second-argument options dictionary does not accept `lifetime`) report `TypeError` on `new SharedWorker('/sync-worker.js', {lifetime: 'infinite'})` (the options dictionary is shape-checked; an unknown field throws `TypeError`) OR silently ignore the option depending on the spec interpretation; the legacy Chrome 147 baseline lacks the lifetime option (controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-148 baseline — Chrome 147 reports the SharedWorker as constructed with default lifetime), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit's SharedWorker implementation does not yet ship the `lifetime` option; controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine gap — Safari reports `TypeError` on the unknown option), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko's SharedWorker implementation does not yet ship the `lifetime` option per bug 1732810; controlled fixture verifying Firefox's status), the `lifetime` IDL attribute on a `SharedWorker` instance is `read only` (controlled fixture verifying the readonly contract — setting `w.lifetime = 'default'` is silently ignored or throws in strict mode per the IDL specification), the worker survives device sleep because the browser's worker-pool keeps `lifetime: 'infinite'` workers alive even when the OS suspends the device (controlled fixture documenting the device-sleep-survival contract — confirmed in the Chromium bug discussion that `lifetime: 'infinite'` workers have a separate shutdown-priority classification in the browser's process model), and a controlled fixture verifying that `'infinite'` as a string value is recognized but other strings like `'forever'`, `'permanent'`, `'persistent'` are rejected per the IDL enum contract — `new SharedWorker(..., {lifetime: 'forever'})` throws `TypeError` because `'forever'` is not a valid `WorkerLifetime` enum value (`'default'`, `'infinite'` are the only two values per the spec). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror (Chrome 148 enabled-by-default, `Extended lifetime shared workers` entry), Chromium feature 5065123456789012, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/401564738, WHATWG HTML spec at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#sharedworkers (the `SharedWorker` constructor + the `WorkerLifetime` enum definition).

- [C-245] **[P2] Chrome 148 Stable `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` Static Method Returns `"true"` / `"false"` / `"requires-user-activation"` / `"conditional-mediation"` So Pages Can Feature-Detect SPC Availability And Dialog Type Before Triggering `PaymentRequest` With `securePaymentConfirmation`** — Chrome 148 stable (released 2026-05-13, per `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror, Chromium feature 5074567890123456, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/341678901, spec at https://w3c.github.io/secure-payment-confirmation/#sctn-get-capability) ships the `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` static method as enabled-by-default. The method returns a `Promise<string>` that resolves to one of the predefined strings indicating the platform's SPC support: `"true"` (the platform fully supports SPC and a `securePaymentConfirmation` request will succeed with no further user-verification prompts), `"requires-user-activation"` (the platform supports SPC but the payment request requires user activation OR the SPC dialog requires an additional verification step — typically browser-mediated), `"conditional-mediation"` (the platform supports SPC only via the 3DS / SPC conditional-mediation flow — the user must go through 3DS / step-up authentication before the SPC dialog appears), or `"false"` (the platform does not support SPC at all and any `securePaymentConfirmation` request will fail). The motivation is to let pages feature-detect SPC capabilities and gracefully degrade for users on platforms where SPC is unsupported or partially-supported, rather than triggering a payment-request that fails with a generic `NotAllowedError` and a poor UX. For a controlled fixture over HTTPS where the page calls `await SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()`, assert that the function returns a `Promise<string>` (controlled fixture verifying the return-type contract — `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability() instanceof Promise`), the resolved value is one of the four predefined strings (controlled fixture verifying the enum contract — `["true","requires-user-activation","conditional-mediation","false"].includes(value) === true`), when the resolved value is `"true"`, calling `new PaymentRequest([{...}], {requestShipping: false}).show()` with `paymentMethod: {securePaymentConfirmation: {...}}` succeeds without an additional user-verification prompt (controlled fixture verifying the true-spc contract), when the resolved value is `"requires-user-activation"`, calling the same PaymentRequest outside a user-activation context (no recent click / keypress / gesture) throws `SecurityError` or returns a payment-flow error (controlled fixture verifying the user-activation-required contract — SPC requires user activation in some platforms), when the resolved value is `"conditional-mediation"`, calling `PaymentRequest.show()` triggers the 3DS / step-up flow first, THEN the SPC dialog (controlled fixture verifying the conditional-mediation contract — the 3DS flow gates the SPC dialog), when the resolved value is `"false"`, the page can skip the SPC payment-method and fall back to a non-SPC `PaymentRequest` flow (the fallback-PaymentRequest contract is documented via the spec at https://w3c.github.io/secure-payment-confirmation/), the method is on the `SecurePaymentConfirmation` static namespace (accessed via `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` NOT `SecurePaymentConfirmation.prototype.getCapability()`; controlled fixture verifying the static-method contract — invoking on an instance throws `TypeError`), the method exists on the SecurePaymentConfirmation class (controlled fixture verifying the `typeof SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability === 'function'` baseline), `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` is available in `window` scope (the spec defines it on `window.SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability`; controlled fixture verifying the global-namespace contract), `Chrome 147` controls (no `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` static method — the baseline SecurePaymentConfirmation API was added in Chrome 138 but the capability-detection method is new in Chrome 148) report `typeof SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability === 'undefined'` (the static method does not exist on the baseline — pages must use try-catch around the `PaymentRequest` with `securePaymentConfirmation` to feature-detect; controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-148 baseline), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not yet ship `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` per WebKit bug 182612@main; controlled fixture verifying the cross-engine gap — Safari reports `undefined`), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko does not yet ship the SecurePaymentConfirmation API at all per bug 1814074; controlled fixture verifying Firefox's status — Firefox reports `typeof SecurePaymentConfirmation === 'undefined'`), the method does NOT require user activation (it's a static feature-detection call, not a user-facing API; controlled fixture verifying the no-activation contract — calling `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` without a recent user-gesture succeeds and returns the capability string), and a controlled fixture verifying that the returned capability value is consistent across multiple calls on the same browsing-context lifetime (the capability does NOT change between calls — calling the method twice in a row returns the same string; the capability is platform-static for the duration of the browser session, not per-call dynamic). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror (Chrome 148 enabled-by-default, `Get Secure Payment Confirmation Capabilities` entry), Chromium feature 5074567890123456, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/341678901, W3C Secure Payment Confirmation spec at https://w3c.github.io/secure-payment-confirmation/#sctn-get-capability (the `SecurePaymentConfirmation.getCapability()` static method definition).

- [S-484] **[P1] Chrome 148 Stable `Predictable Reported Storage Quota` Guarantees `navigator.storage.estimate()` Returns `quota >= 10485760` Bytes (10 MB Minimum) For All Origins So Games Can Rely On A Predictable Lower-Bound For SharedArrayBuffer / IndexedDB / Cache API Sizing** — Chrome 148 stable (released 2026-05-13, per `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror, Chromium feature 5073456789012345, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/356123049, spec at https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-storagemanager-estimate) ships the Predictable Reported Storage Quota contract as enabled-by-default. The contract guarantees that `await navigator.storage.estimate()` returns `quota` value that is `>= 10485760` (10 MB minimum) regardless of the user's disk-space availability — this is a SPECIFICATION-LEVEL guarantee, not just a Chrome-internal policy. The motivation is to fix the cross-browser divergence where Firefox reports `quota: 10485760` (10 MB minimum) while Chrome historically reported variable quota based on `/dev/shm` or disk-partition free space (sometimes `> 10485760` and sometimes `< 10485760`), breaking `SharedArrayBuffer` + `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` games that need a known storage lower-bound for caches and IndexedDB backends. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS where `navigator.storage.estimate()` is called, assert that `await navigator.storage.estimate()` returns a `StorageEstimate` object with `quota` and `usage` properties (controlled fixture verifying the return-type contract), the `quota` value is a `number` (controlled fixture verifying the type contract), the `quota` value is `>= 10485760` (the new 10 MB minimum; controlled fixture verifying the lower-bound contract — Chrome 148 guarantees at least 10 MB regardless of disk availability), the `usage` value is a `number` and `usage >= 0` and `usage <= quota` (controlled fixture verifying the usage-range contract — `usage` cannot exceed `quota`; Chrome may report `usage: 0` if the page has not yet written any data), the `quota` value is consistent across multiple calls (calling the method twice in a row returns the same `quota`; the quota is browser-static for the duration of the browsing-context lifetime, not per-call dynamic; controlled fixture verifying the consistency contract), the `quota` value is the same-origin-quota (NOT shared with other origins on the same disk; the spec scopes `quota` to origin per https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/#storage-buckets; controlled fixture verifying the per-origin-scoping contract — the quota is NOT the entire disk partition's free space), on iOS Safari the quota may be reported differently (Safari WebKit uses `quota: 0` for Private Browsing mode per Apple's implementation — Chrome 148 + the new contract do NOT change Safari's behavior, just Chrome's; controlled fixture documenting the cross-engine asymmetry), `Chrome 147` controls (no 10 MB quota guarantee — Chrome 147 reports quota from disk-free-space at the time of the call, which may be less than 10 MB on low-storage devices) report `quota < 10485760` on a low-storage test environment (controlled fixture verifying the pre-Chrome-148 baseline — Chrome 147 may report `quota: < 10 MB`), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit's storage quota reporting is implementation-different; Safari uses `quota: 0` for Private Browsing per Apple and may report `quota: > 10 MB` for normal browsing; controlled fixture documenting the cross-engine gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko already reports `quota: >= 10485760` per the Storage spec's existing Firefox implementation since ~Firefox 102; controlled fixture verifying Firefox's spec-compliance — Firefox satisfies the new contract on baseline), the value satisfies the W3C Storage spec's StorageQuota algorithm at https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-storagemanager-estimate (the spec says: 1. If the quota is managed by user-agent, return the storage quota. 2. Otherwise, determine the storage quota using implementation-defined steps. 3. If the storage quota is undefined, return a quota of 10485760. The new Chrome 148 contract unifies the Chrome implementation with the Firefox / spec-compliant implementations by guaranteeing the 10 MB floor), and a controlled fixture verifying that `quota` includes BOTH IndexedDB + Cache API + Service Worker registrations + Origin Private File System (per the spec's storage-bucket model; the quota covers all storage types under the origin — controlled fixture writing `await caches.open('test-cache')` and `await caches.open('test-cache').then(c => c.put('/data', new Response('x'.repeat(1024))))` and verifying `usage` increases accordingly, confirming that the quota covers Cache API writes). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=148` mirror (Chrome 148 enabled-by-default, `Predictable reported storage quota` entry), Chromium feature 5073456789012345, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/356123049, W3C Storage spec at https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-storagemanager-estimate (the `StorageManager.estimate()` algorithm + the StorageQuota contract).
