## New Test Cases Added in v1.218.0 (R335 — August 8 2026, 4h cycle 97)

### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-436] **[P1] Chrome 152 (Behind `#gamepad-button-type` Flag) Adds `GamepadButtonType` Enum Attribute `gamepadButton.type` With Values `"non-standard"`, `"standard"`, `"trackpad"`** — Chrome 152 stable (scheduled 2026-08-25 per superchargebrowser Chromium schedule, currently in beta per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/) adds the `GamepadButton.type` IDL attribute (a `readonly attribute GamepadButtonType` on the existing `GamepadButton` interface) and a new `enum GamepadButtonType { "non-standard", "standard", "trackpad" }` (W3C PR preview spec at https://pr-preview.s3.amazonaws.com/xingri/gamepad/pull/196.html#gamepadbuttontype-enum, Chromium feature 5075054393163776 per https://chromestatus.com/feature/5075054393163776, upstream bug https://crbug.com/339841686). The `type` attribute provides an alternate, interoperable identifier for gamepad buttons that are not in the W3C standard 17-button index — for example, a DualShock / DualSense trackpad reports `type === "trackpad"`, a standard A-button reports `type === "standard"`, and any other button (share / capture / voice / home / squeeze) reports `type === "non-standard"`. The full IDL contract (per the PR preview source): `interface GamepadButton { readonly attribute boolean pressed; readonly attribute boolean touched; readonly attribute double value; readonly attribute GamepadButtonType type; }; enum GamepadButtonType { "non-standard", "standard", "trackpad", };` — the `type` attribute is `readonly` and reflects the button's identified class. For a controlled fixture running on Chrome 152 stable with `#gamepad-button-type` flag enabled (or on the Chrome 152 beta channel that already exposes the flag), `navigator.getGamepads()` returns a `GamepadButton[]` whose each `button` has `.type` as one of the three enum strings (a controlled fixture iterating the connected gamepads and asserting `["non-standard", "standard", "trackpad"].includes(gp.buttons[i].type)` for every button reports no `undefined` / no unrecognized strings), a connected DualSense gamepad's trackpad surface reports `.type === "trackpad"` (controlled fixture verifying the DualSense trackpad maps to the trackpad enum value — this is the canonical case the spec was added for), a standard Xbox / PlayStation controller's A / B / X / Y / L1 / R1 buttons report `.type === "standard"` (the 17 W3C standard indices map to `standard`), a DualSense share / capture / voice button reports `.type === "non-standard"`, the IDL attribute is `readonly` (a controlled fixture that tries `gp.buttons[0].type = "non-standard"` does NOT mutate the attribute and a subsequent read returns the original value — `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(GamepadButton.prototype, "type").writable === false` or assignment in non-strict mode is silently ignored, in strict mode throws), the attribute is enumerable on the prototype (a controlled fixture verifying `Object.keys(gp.buttons[0]).includes("type")` is `false` — own-keys are typically empty for instances of WebIDL read-only attributes, but `GamepadButton.prototype.type` is the accessor), `GamepadButtonType` is exposed as a global enum object (controlled fixture verifying `'GamepadButtonType' in window` is `true` and `"trackpad" in GamepadButtonType` is `true` on Chrome 152 with the flag), `JSON.stringify(gp.buttons[i])` enumerates `pressed`, `touched`, `value`, `type` (controlled fixture verifying all four fields serialize), `Safari 26.6` (WebKit lacks `gamepadExtensions`) and `Firefox 155` (no `GamepadButtonType` enum implementation yet — Firefox's gamepad implementation is based on the base W3C spec without extensions) controls report `gp.buttons[i].type === undefined` (the attribute does not exist on those engines — verify with `Object.keys(gp.buttons[0])` excludes `type` on controls), a controlled fixture verifies that when the Chrome flag is disabled (`#gamepad-button-type` set to `Disabled`), the `type` attribute is also absent (the flag is the gate — without the flag, `GamepadButtonType` is undefined and `gp.buttons[i].type` is `undefined`; this confirms the Chrome 152 contract is gated and the unflagged Chrome 151 baseline is the control), and the spec is also testable via WPT (Web Platform Tests) under `gamepad-extensions/button-type.html` once the test PR is merged (the spec PR #196 is the upstream source). Source: W3C Gamepad Extensions PR #196 spec preview at https://pr-preview.s3.amazonaws.com/xingri/gamepad/pull/196.html, Chromium feature 5075054393163776 at https://chromestatus.com/feature/5075054393163776, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/339841686, Chrome 152 beta release notes at https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/.

- [W-437] **[P1] Chrome 152 (Behind `#iamf` Flag) Decodes IAMF (Immersive Audio Model and Formats) Open Spatial-Audio Container in HTML `<audio>` via Media Source Extensions** — Chrome 152 stable (scheduled 2026-08-25 per Chromium schedule, currently in beta per https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/) adds Immersive Audio Model and Formats (IAMF) decoding support inside HTML media elements via Media Source Extensions (MSE) (Chromium feature 5113656292540416 per https://chromestatus.com/feature/5113656292540416, upstream bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/535279329). IAMF is an open, royalty-free spatial-audio container from the Alliance for Open Media that supports channel-based (e.g. 5.1 / 7.1), scene-based (Ambisonics), and object-based audio presentations in a single MP4 container — letting web developers deliver consistent, immersive 3D audio experiences without proprietary formats or hand-rolled discrete-channel routing in JavaScript. Chrome 152 ships the decoder behind the `#iamf` flag; the AOM-published IAMF spec is at https://aomediacodec.github.io/iamf/latest-approved.html, the design doc is at https://docs.google.com/document/d/1G4Km3hxEnXonvgiZo7got_DWIatBrpYbyzk3yIpaV6A/edit?usp=sharing&resourcekey=0-rS2fUcQM7tcKNDoQmk7Tmg, and two reproducible sample files are hosted at https://crsrc.org/c/media/test/data/iamf_alternating_sine_waves_stereo.mp4 (stereo) and https://crsrc.org/c/media/test/data/iamf_alternating_sine_waves_714.mp4 (7.1.4 channel-based immersive). For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS with `<audio id="a"></audio>` plus a JS MSE pipeline that fetches the AOM-hosted IAMF `.mp4` file as an `ArrayBuffer`, creates a `MediaSource` object, attaches it via `URL.createObjectURL(mediaSource)`, and appends the IAMF buffer to a `SourceBuffer` with `mediaSource.addSourceBuffer('audio/mp4; codecs="iamf"')`, assert that `MediaSource.isTypeSupported('audio/mp4; codecs="iamf"')` returns `true` on Chrome 152 with `#iamf` enabled (the MIME-with-codecs probe is the formal capability check — the same probe returns `false` on Chrome 151 / Safari 26.6 / Firefox 155 controls that lack the IAMF decoder), `SourceBuffer.appendBuffer(iamfArrayBuffer)` does NOT throw `NotSupportedError` (the IAMF buffer is accepted — controlled fixture appending the same bytes to a `SourceBuffer` with `audio/mp4; codecs="iamf"` on Chrome 151 reports `NotSupportedError`, demonstrating the contract is Chrome 152 only), the `<audio>` element transitions from `HAVE_NOTHING` → `HAVE_METADATA` → `HAVE_ENOUGH_DATA` after the IAMF buffer is appended (controlled fixture polling `a.readyState` reports the three-state progression, with `a.duration` returning the IAMF track duration in seconds and `a.buffered.end(0) - a.buffered.start(0)` matching the duration within ±50 ms), the IAMF track plays back the contained sine waves when `a.play()` is called (controlled fixture driving the audio output via a `MediaStreamAudioDestinationNode` + `OfflineAudioContext` for headless verification — `OfflineAudioContext` renders 1 second of audio and the rendered channel data is non-zero in both channels for the stereo sample, confirming the IAMF payload was decoded), `MSE` `appendBuffer` does NOT throw `QuotaExceededError` for a 64 KB IAMF sample (the IAMF decoder accepts the typical IAMF buffer size — controlled fixture appending a 64 KB IAMF `.mp4` sample to a fresh `SourceBuffer` reports no `QuotaExceededError`), the playback sample-rate matches the IAMF track's advertised sample-rate (controlled fixture verifying `OfflineAudioContext.sampleRate === aTrack.sampleRate` within ±1 Hz), `Safari 26.6` (no IAMF decoder) returns `MediaSource.isTypeSupported('audio/mp4; codecs="iamf"') === false` (Safari's MSE implementation rejects the unknown codec), `Firefox 155` (no IAMF decoder) returns `false` for the same probe, the live AOM IAMF web demo at https://aomediacodec.github.io/iamf-tools/web_demo loads the same IAMF files in a Chrome 152 instance with `#iamf` enabled and produces audible playback (a controlled fixture using `chromestatuslite`'s design-doc sample files against the live web demo reproduces the same MSE pipeline on `aomediacodec.github.io`), `Chrome 151` controls report `MediaSource.isTypeSupported === false` for the same codec string, and a controlled fixture verifying that the IAMF `#iamf` flag-disabled Chrome 152 also returns `false` (the IAMF decoder is flag-gated, identical to W-436's flag-gate pattern). Source: Chrome 152 platform-status feature 5113656292540416 at https://chromestatus.com/feature/5113656292540416, AOM IAMF spec at https://aomediacodec.github.io/iamf/latest-approved.html, AOM IAMF web demo at https://aomediacodec.github.io/iamf-tools/web_demo (HTTP 200, 10,076 bytes), Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/535279329, design doc at https://docs.google.com/document/d/1G4Km3hxEnXonvgiZo7got_DWIatBrpYbyzk3yIpaV6A/edit?usp=sharing.

### Security / Privacy Sandbox (S)

- [S-473] **[P0] Chrome 152 (Aug 25 2026) Origin Trial for XSLT Deprecation Goes Live With Fixed Schedule Through Chrome 176 (Aug 17 2027)** — Google publishes the XSLT deprecation timeline at https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt (145 KB, last-updated 2026-08-27) listing the fixed public schedule: **Chrome 142 (Oct 28, 2025): Early warning console messages added; Chrome 143 (Dec 2, 2025): Official deprecation — deprecation warning messages begin to show in the console and in lighthouse; Chrome 145 Canary (Dec 2, 2025): Canary, Dev, and Beta releases begin disabling XSLT by default as an early warning; Chrome 146 (Mar 10, 2026): Enterprise Policy (EP) goes live for testing — allows enterprises to test disabling XSLT early and to continue using features past the removal date; Chrome 152 (Aug 25, 2026): Origin Trial (OT) goes live for testing — allows sites to continue using features past the removal date; Chrome 158 (Nov 17, 2026): XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants; Chrome 176 (Aug 17, 2027): Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning — XSLT is disabled for all users.** The XSLT 1.0 engine is being removed because the underlying libxslt C library is unmaintained, has produced recent high-severity CVEs (CVE-2025-7425 and CVE-2022-22834), and client-side XSLT usage has been superseded by JavaScript-based JSON / React / Vue templating. Chromium bug 435623334 tracks the deprecation. For a controlled fixture serving `<?xml version="1.0"?><?xml-stylesheet type="text/xsl" href="https://attacker.com/stylesheet.xsl"?><page><message>Hello</message></page>` over HTTPS to Chrome 152 stable (which lands Aug 25 2026), assert that the browser's DevTools console emits a deprecation warning containing the literal text `"XSLT"` (the deprecation message text includes the XSLT keyword — text is documented in the Chromium deprecation message catalog), the XSLT stylesheet is still applied to the XML document for sites enrolled in the Origin Trial (a controlled fixture that includes the OT token `<meta http-equiv="origin-trial" content="<TOKEN>">` in the XML file's served HTML wrapper or registers via `Origin-Trial` response header — the XSLT transformation succeeds and the resulting HTML renders with the XSLT styling applied), the XSLT stylesheet is NOT applied for sites NOT enrolled in the OT (a controlled fixture without the OT token reports the XML document renders as raw XML without the XSLT transformation — Chromium displays the raw XML tree per the post-deprecation fallback), the Chrome 158 (Nov 17 2026) stable removal is testable today on Chrome 152 via a controlled fixture that sets `--disable-features=XSLT` or visits with the XSLT origin-trial disabled (a fixture on Chrome 152 with the OT-disabled stance reports the same behavior as Chrome 158 would), the Enterprise Policy path (Chrome 146+) lets enterprise-managed Chrome continue using XSLT past the Chrome 158 cutoff (a controlled fixture on Chrome 152 with `XSLTEnabled` group policy set to `1` for a managed profile preserves XSLT functionality — controlled fixture verifying the XSLT transformation is applied even when the default would block it), the deprecation message includes the Chrome status link (controlled fixture asserting the message text contains `developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt` per Chromium's standard deprecation-message template), the deprecation also affects `XSLTProcessor` JavaScript API (a controlled fixture that calls `new XSLTProcessor()` and `.importStyleSheet(xsltDoc)` then `.transformToFragment(xmlDoc, document)` reports the same warning + 'application/xml')` does NOT emit the XSLT deprecation warning — the Rust XML parser migration in Chrome 151 (B-236) is unrelated to this XSLT deprecation), `Safari 26.6` and `Firefox 155` controls (no XSLT deprecation timeline published by Apple / Mozilla yet — but Mozilla's Gecko has signaled intent to follow the same deprecation path per the linked Chromium blog "Chromium (along with both other browser engines, Gecko and WebKit) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT") still emit no XSLT deprecation warning today (controlled fixture verifying Safari 26.6 / Firefox 155 do not yet emit the Source: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt (145 KB, last-updated 2026-08-27), Chromium bug https://crbug.com/435623334, Chromium intent-to-deprecate thread https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev (deprecation message catalog), W3C XSLT 1.0 spec https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/ (1999), libxslt maintenance notice https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615 (2025).

### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-435] **[P0] Edge 152 / Chrome `unload` Permission-Policy Deprecation Rolls `allow` to `deny` Default Over Edge 152→155, Breaking Any `unload` Handler That Lacks an Explicit Opt-In** — Edge 152 (released 2026-08-06 to the beta channel as 152.0.4191.10; the deprecation is Chromium-upstream and will roll out across Chrome / Edge / Opera / Brave / Vivaldi on the same Edge 152→155 schedule) introduces a new `unload` Permissions-Policy token that controls whether `unload` event listeners can be registered. The default value is initially `allow` but is migrated to `deny` over the next 4 Edge releases: **Edge 152** stops firing `unload` handlers by default for **60% of page loads**, **Edge 154** increases to **80%**, and **Edge 155** reaches **100%** — at which point `unload` handlers stop firing entirely unless the site explicitly opts back in via `<meta http-equiv="Permissions-Policy" content="unload=*">` or the equivalent HTTP header `Permissions-Policy: unload=*`. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS with `<body onunload="console.log('unload fired')">`, assert that the `unload` event handler fires on the first page load (control: legacy behavior pre-Edge 152 / pre-Chrome 152), the same page on Edge 152 reports the handler does NOT fire for at least 60% of navigations (a controlled fixture performing 10 navigations and counting handler invocations reports 4 or fewer — the 60% rollout means up to 6 of 10 are blocked), `<meta http-equiv="Permissions-Policy" content="unload=*">` placed in `<head>` restores the handler firing to 10/10 (the `*` token re-allows the handler — controlled fixture verifies that the opt-in is sticky for the page lifetime), the HTTP-header variant `Permissions-Policy: unload=*` does the same as the meta tag (the policy is enforced by both — controlled fixture using `fetch` + `document.write` to confirm the header is the source of truth), the policy accepts only `*` (allow all) and `()` / `()`-with-csv (deny all) values (controlled fixture verifies that `unload=self` is rejected with a parser warning — the token is a binary on/off), `Chrome 150` / `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls (no `unload` Permissions-Policy token yet — the Chromium project ships it first, WebKit / Gecko have not adopted it) report the handler fires 10/10 regardless of any Permissions-Policy directive (the token is unknown to them and silently ignored), GameZipper BI tracking that uses `pagehide` + `visibilitychange` continues to work in Edge 152 (controlled fixture verifies `pagehide` is not affected by the `unload` Permission-Policy and fires reliably), and a controlled fixture verifies the `unload` Permission-Policy token does NOT affect `beforeunload` (the `beforeunload` confirmation-prompt lifecycle is separate from the `unload` analytics-cleanup contract — controlled fixture verifies `beforeunload` fires 10/10 regardless of policy). Source: Edge 152 release notes (152.0.4191.10, 2026-08-06, Planned deprecation of the unload event section), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-relnote-beta-channel and Edge 152 web platform release notes (Aug. 2026), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/152, plus the Chromium Intent-to-Deprecate thread at https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/dvusqw9-IhI/m/SBkm_u1RAQAJ.

### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-261] **[P1] Edge 152 `<camera>` and `<microphone>` HTML Elements Are Single-Capability Variants of `<usermedia>` for Video-Only or Audio-Only Capture Gating** — Edge 152 (released 2026-08-06 to the beta channel as 152.0.4191.10) ships the `<camera>` and `<microphone>` HTML elements, browser-provided buttons that — upon activation — toggle camera or microphone streams. The two elements share the same underlying mechanism as the `<usermedia>` element (covered by W-411 v1.208.0) but are designed to request a single capability: `<camera>` specifically requests video capture, `<microphone>` specifically requests audio capture. Like `<usermedia>`, they embed a browser-controlled, strictly-styled UI to ensure a strong, intentional user signal before a permission prompt or stream start. For a controlled fixture with `<camera id="c"></camera>` and `<microphone id="m"></microphone>` inside an `<iframe allow="camera; microphone">`, assert that activating the `<camera>` element (via a `click()` event under user-gesture activation) opens the browser's permission-prompt flow with **only the camera capability requested** (the prompt text reads "Allow this site to use your camera?" with no microphone option — controlled fixture verifies the prompt's body text matches), the resulting `MediaStream` contains exactly one video track and **zero audio tracks** (the `<camera>` element never requests audio — a controlled fixture that activates `<camera>` and inspects the stream's `getAudioTracks().length === 0`), activating the `<microphone>` element opens the camera-less audio-only prompt ("Allow this site to use your microphone?") and produces a `MediaStream` with exactly one audio track and zero video tracks, both elements are recognized as `HTMLElement` (a controlled fixture verifying `document.createElement("camera").constructor.name === "HTMLElement"` and `document.createElement("microphone").constructor.name === "HTMLElement"` — neither element gets a custom interface, unlike `<usermedia>` which has a documented declarative capability element contract), the elements inherit `disabled` (a controlled `<camera disabled>` does not trigger any permission flow on click), the elements are styled by the user-agent stylesheet (the default rendering is a small camera/microphone icon button — controlled fixture verifying `getComputedStyle(c).appearance` reports the browser-provided button style), `<camera>` and `<microphone>` honor the `Permissions-Policy` directives `camera` and `microphone` respectively (a controlled fixture with `<iframe allow="camera">` does NOT permit the `<microphone>` element to access the microphone — the single-capability scoping is enforced), `Chrome 150` / `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls (no `<camera>` / `<microphone>` element) parse them as `HTMLUnknownElement` (controlled fixture verifying `document.createElement("camera").toString() === "[object HTMLUnknownElement]"`), and activating either element without user activation does NOT open the permission prompt (controlled fixture verifies a synthetic `c.click()` dispatched without a user gesture is a no-op — the activation gate matches W-411 `<usermedia>`). Source: Edge 152 web platform release notes (Aug. 2026), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/152 (HTML features section, `<camera>` and `<microphone>` elements).

- [B-262] **[P2] Edge 152 `ShadowRoot.referenceTarget` IDL Property + `shadowrootreferencetarget` HTML Attribute Forwards ID-Referencing Attributes Into Shadow Tree** — Edge 152 (released 2026-08-06 to the beta channel as 152.0.4191.10) ships the `ShadowRoot.referenceTarget` IDL property (the `referencetarget` attribute on `Element.attachShadow(init)`) and the matching `shadowrootreferencetarget` HTML attribute on `<template shadowrootmode>`. When a shadow host specifies an element in its shadow tree to act as its reference target, all ID references that point to the shadow host are forwarded to the reference target element instead — so a `<label for="my-checkbox">` outside a `<custom-checkbox>` web component correctly binds to the `<input id="real-checkbox">` inside the component's shadow DOM. For a controlled fixture with `<label for="my-checkbox">Label</label><custom-checkbox id="my-checkbox"><template shadowrootmode="open" shadowrootreferencetarget="real-checkbox"><input id="real-checkbox" type="checkbox"></template></custom-checkbox>`, assert that clicking the `<label>` activates the `<input>` inside the shadow DOM (the `for` reference forwards from the shadow host `<custom-checkbox>` to the reference target `<input id="real-checkbox">` — controlled fixture verifies the checkbox's `.checked` property toggles on label click), the `<custom-checkbox>` element's shadow root's `referenceTarget` property returns a reference to `<input id="real-checkbox">` (controlled fixture verifies `customEl.shadowRoot.referenceTarget === customEl.shadowRoot.getElementById("real-checkbox")`), `aria-labelledby` references also forward (a controlled `<span aria-labelledby="my-checkbox">label</span>` resolves to the inner `<input>`'s accessible name — the forward applies to all ID-referencing attributes including ARIA), `popovertarget` and `commandfor` similarly forward (a controlled `<button popovertarget="my-checkbox">open</button>` opens the popover attached to the inner reference target, not to the shadow host), an ID that resolves to a child element that does NOT have a `referenceTarget` resolves to the shadow host itself (the `referenceTarget` forwarding only fires when the host declares it — controlled fixture verifying that removing the `shadowrootreferencetarget` attribute reverts `<label for="my-checkbox">` to bind to the host `<custom-checkbox>`, not the inner `<input>`), the IDL attribute can also be set imperatively: `host.attachShadow({mode: "open", referenceTarget: host.querySelector("[data-ref-target]")})` (controlled fixture verifying the property reflects the element passed in and that subsequent shadow DOM access returns the same reference), `Chrome 150` / `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls (no `referenceTarget` / `shadowrootreferencetarget`) treat `<label for="my-checkbox">` as resolving to the host `<custom-checkbox>` (the inner `<input>` is not visible to the label — controlled fixture verifying the label-click does NOT toggle the inner input's `.checked`), and a controlled fixture verifies that the forwarding respects the closed vs open shadow root contract (a `<template shadowrootmode="closed" shadowrootreferencetarget="real-checkbox">` still forwards references externally but `host.shadowRoot` returns `null` for closed roots — the forwarding works at the ID-resolution layer, not at the shadow-root-access layer). Source: Edge 152 web platform release notes (Aug. 2026), https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/web-platform/release-notes/152 (HTML features section, Reference target) and MDN ShadowRoot.referenceTarget docs at https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ShadowRoot.

### Compatibility / Embedded Runtime (C)

- [C-233] **[P2] Edge 152 `BackForwardCacheForWebSocketsAllowed` Group Policy Allows Active WebSocket Connections to Be Disconnected and Restored in a Disconnected State When Entering Back/Forward Cache** — Edge 152 (released 2026-08-06 to the beta channel as 152.0.4191.10) adds the `BackForwardCacheForWebSocketsAllowed` group policy that controls whether active WebSocket connections are disconnected when a page enters back/forward cache. Previously, an active WebSocket connection prevented the page from being stored in back/forward cache entirely; Edge 152 changes this behavior so WebSockets are disconnected (allowing the page to be cached) and restored in a disconnected state when the user navigates back. The policy is supported on Windows ≥152, macOS ≥152, and Android ≥152; iOS is not supported. For a controlled fixture with an Edge 152 deployment that has `BackForwardCacheForWebSocketsAllowed = 1` (allowed) and an open page at `https://example.com/game` that holds an active WebSocket connection to `wss://api.example.com/socket`, assert that navigating away to `https://example.com/page2` and then back via browser back button returns the page to its previous scroll position / DOM state (the page entered BF cache) and the WebSocket connection is now in a closed state (controlled fixture verifying `socket.readyState === WebSocket.CLOSED` after restoration), navigating to the same page WITHOUT the policy allowed (`BackForwardCacheForWebSocketsAllowed = 0`) results in a full page reload when navigating back (the WebSocket-prevents-BF-cache behavior is preserved — controlled fixture verifying the WebSocket `onclose` event fires on navigation away), the policy accepts values `1` (allow BF cache for WebSockets — disconnect and cache) and `0` (preserve existing behavior — page is not cached while WebSocket is active), the policy's effect is per-page (a controlled fixture verifying that pages with NO WebSocket connection are unaffected by the policy — they continue to enter BF cache regardless), iOS does not honor the policy (controlled fixture verifying the policy appears as `Not supported on this platform` in the Edge iOS admin UI — the BF-cache-for-WebSocket feature is desktop / Android only), `Chrome 150` controls (no `BackForwardCacheForWebSocketsAllowed` policy in Chrome — Edge ships its own policy surface) return `undefined` for the policy in `chrome://policy`, and the policy does not affect `EventSource` connections (controlled fixture verifying that an `EventSource` connection does NOT prevent BF cache entry regardless of the policy — the policy is WebSocket-specific, not all-stream). Source: Edge 152 release notes (152.0.4191.10, 2026-08-06, New policies section, BackForwardCacheForWebSocketsAllowed) and the policy documentation at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-policies/backforwardcacheforwebsocketsallowed.

- [C-234] **[P2] Edge 152 Stable 151.0.4129.72 (Aug 6 2026) Adopts 2-Week Major Release Cadence Distinct From Chrome 153+ 2-Week Cadence** — Edge 152 stable release 151.0.4129.72 (released 2026-08-06) announces that Microsoft Edge is moving to a 2-week major-version release cadence, mirroring (but separately scheduled from) Chrome's 153+ 2-week cadence (W-384 v1.200.0). The Edge cadence is documented at https://blogs.windows.com/msedgedev/2026/06/11/faster-updates-enterprise-friendly-schedule-the-new-microsoft-edge-release-cycle/ (Microsoft Edge Blog, 2026-06-11) and is distinct from Chrome's cadence in vendor (Microsoft vs Google), schedule (Edge 152 stable on 2026-08-06 maps to Edge 153 → ~2026-08-20; Chrome 153 → ~2026-09-02), and enterprise-pending posture (Edge's enterprise-stable channel lags the stable channel by ~3 weeks vs Chrome's ~1 week). For a controlled fixture with an Edge 152 deployment and a documented release-cadence schedule, assert that the gap between Edge 152 stable (151.0.4129.72, 2026-08-06) and the next stable major version is ≤ 16 days (the 2-week cadence contract — controlled fixture verifying the published Edge 153 stable date is between 2026-08-20 and 2026-08-22), Edge's release-cadence announcement page (https://blogs.windows.com/msedgedev/2026/06/11/faster-updates-enterprise-friendly-schedule-the-new-microsoft-edge-release-cycle/) is reachable and contains the 2-week cadence commitment (controlled fixture using `curl --noproxy '*'` verifying the page returns HTTP 200 and contains the literal text "2-week"), the Edge Enterprise update channel policy (`UpdateOnZeroWindowEnabled` — new in 151.0.4129.72 alongside the cadence change) reflects the new cadence (a controlled fixture verifying that background automatic relaunch on zero-window-close respects the new release schedule), `Chrome 150` / `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls have no Edge-cadence implications (the Edge cadence is Edge-specific — controlled fixture verifying that Chrome's cadence (per W-384) and Edge's cadence (per C-234) are independently scheduled and do not coincide), and a controlled fixture verifies that Edge's 2-week cadence doubles the per-7-day patch-lag pressure that W-384 estimated at ~$0.4/wk for Chrome — Edge has a similar but independent surface, with the patch-lag window halved from 4 weeks to 2 weeks. Source: Edge 152 release notes (152.0.4191.10, 2026-08-06, Announcements section, Microsoft Edge moving to a 2-week cadence) and the Microsoft Edge Blog announcement at https://blogs.windows.com/msedgedev/2026/06/11/faster-updates-enterprise-friendly-schedule-the-new-microsoft-edge-release-cycle/.

- [C-235] **[P2] Edge 152 `CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled` Group Policy Controls Whether Copilot Cowork Browser Agent Can Take Actions on User's Behalf** — Edge 152 (released 2026-08-06 to the beta channel as 152.0.4191.10) ships the `CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled` group policy that controls availability of the new Copilot Cowork browser agent feature. Copilot Cowork may perform tasks such as creating tabs, taking screenshots, and interacting with web pages on the user's behalf (the AI-agent-on-behalf-of-user surface). The policy corresponds to the **Allow Cowork to take actions on your behalf** setting in `edge://settings/ai`. The policy applies only when Cowork Browsing is enabled at the tenant level in the M365 admin center. For a controlled fixture with an Edge 152 deployment and Cowork Browsing enabled at the M365 tenant level, assert that `CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled = 1` (allowed) enables the Copilot Cowork agent to perform tab-create / screenshot / interact actions on the user's behalf (controlled fixture verifying the agent's actions appear in the Edge activity log with `"actor": "copilot-cowork"` attribution), `CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled = 0` (denied) blocks all Copilot Cowork actions — the agent can still read / observe the page (the read-only surface is unaffected) but cannot create tabs, take screenshots, or interact with web pages (controlled fixture verifying that an attempted screenshot action returns `PermissionDeniedError`), the policy requires Cowork Browsing to be enabled at the tenant level (controlled fixture verifying that `CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled = 1` with Cowork Browsing disabled at the M365 tenant level still results in no Copilot Cowork actions — the policy is a no-op without the tenant-level opt-in), the policy's setting is reflected in `edge://settings/ai` (controlled fixture verifying that "Allow Cowork to take actions on your behalf" is checked when `CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled = 1` and unchecked when `= 0`), `Chrome 150` / `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls (no Copilot Cowork — the feature is Edge-specific) return `undefined` for `chrome://policy#CopilotCoworkToolActionsEnabled`, and a controlled fixture verifies that the policy does not affect the user's direct actions (the user can still create tabs, take screenshots, and interact with pages manually — the policy gates only the AI-agent surface, not the human-user surface). Source: Edge 152 release notes (152.0.4191.10, 2026-08-06, Feature updates section, New Copilot Cowork policy) and the policy documentation at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/deployedge/microsoft-edge-policies/copilotcoworktoolactionsenabled.

- [B-258] **[P1] Chrome 152 Beta CSS `window-drag` Property Standardizes the Desktop-App Window-Drag Region Naming and Inheritance** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) ships the `window-drag` CSS property, which standardizes and renames the existing `app-region` property, changes its value names to `move` and `none`, and adds explicit inheritance behavior. The `window-drag` property lets web content designate regions of an installed desktop web app UI that should behave as draggable window titlebar areas. For a controlled fixture with an installed-ChromeOS / Edge / Chrome PWA that uses `<header style="window-drag: move">header</header>` content plus `<button>click</button>` sibling, assert `getComputedStyle(header).windowDrag === "move"` (the keyword is the computed value, not `drag` from the legacy `app-region`), `getComputedStyle(button).windowDrag === "move"` (the property inherits — `window-drag: inherit` is implicit on descendants, distinct from `app-region: no-drag` which did not inherit by default), `getComputedStyle(body).windowDrag === "none"` (the initial value is `none`, not `auto`), `CSS.supports("window-drag: move")` returns `true` in Chrome 152 beta and `false` in Chrome 151 / Safari 26.6 / Firefox 155 controls (the legacy `app-region` is the surface they support), `CSS.supports("window-drag: drag")` returns `false` in Chrome 152 beta (the legacy `drag` value is no longer accepted), `CSS.supports("window-drag: no-drag")` returns `false` in Chrome 152 beta (the legacy `no-drag` is replaced by `none`), and a controlled fixture verifying that `window-drag: none` on a parent overrides the inheritance on `<button>` (an explicit `none` cascades and does not inherit, so a `<button style="window-drag: none">click</button>` inside a `<header style="window-drag: move">` does NOT trigger window drag on click). Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (CSS and UI section, `window-drag` CSS property).

### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-430] **[P1] Chrome 152 Beta CPU Performance API Graduates to Stable With `CpuPerformanceTierOverride` Enterprise Policy** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) graduates the **CPU Performance API** (previously experimental in Chrome 145 per P-164 / P-133 mentions in CHANGELOG) to a stable Web API. The API exposes `navigator.cpuPerformanceTier` (`"low"`, `"medium"`, `"high"`) and `navigator.cpuPerformance` (with details); Chrome 152 adds the **`CpuPerformanceTierOverride`** enterprise policy that lets administrators override the reported tier for managed devices. For a controlled fixture in Chrome 152 beta, assert `navigator.cpuPerformanceTier` returns one of `"low"`, `"medium"`, or `"high"` (and is **not** `undefined`, distinguishing stable from experimental), the same property in Chrome 151 / Safari 26.6 / Firefox 155 controls returns `undefined` (no CPU Performance API on those engines), a controlled fixture verifies that `navigator.cpuPerformanceTier` correlates with reported device class (a known-low-end device returns `"low"`, a known-high-end device returns `"high"`, both stable across reloads), and the value can be overridden via the `CpuPerformanceTierOverride` enterprise policy (controlled fixture on a managed-device profile with policy set to `"high"` returns `"high"` regardless of actual device class). Additionally, when combined with the Compute Pressure API (`navigator.computePressure`), the games should be able to lower effects when tier is `"low"` and pressure is `"critical"`. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, CPU Performance API) and the CPU Performance API Explainer at https://github.com/w3c/compute-pressure/blob/main/explainer.md.
- [W-431] **[P2] Chrome 152 Beta Connection Allowlists Response Header Restricts Fetch and Other Web Platform API Connections to Authorized Endpoints** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) ships Connection Allowlists, a response-header-controlled origin allowlist for connections initiated through the Fetch API or other web-platform APIs (subresource fetches, `WebSocket`, `EventSource`, XHR, etc.). The server distributes an authorized endpoint list via an HTTP response header; before establishing any connection, Chrome evaluates the destination against this allowlist. Connections to verified endpoints are permitted; connections that fail to match are blocked at the network layer. For a controlled fixture served over HTTPS with `Connection-Allowlist: https://api.example.com https://cdn.example.com` set on `https://example.com/page.html`, assert `fetch("https://api.example.com/data")` from inside `page.html` succeeds (the destination is in the allowlist), `fetch("https://attacker.example.com/payload")` returns a controlled network error (the destination is NOT in the allowlist and the connection is refused), `fetch("/relative-path")` is allowed (same-origin requests remain permitted — controlled fixture verifies the relative URL resolves to `https://example.com/relative-path` which equals the document origin), `WebSocket("wss://api.example.com/socket")` succeeds (WebSocket connections honor the allowlist the same way as Fetch), `WebSocket("wss://attacker.example.com/socket")` fails with a controlled network error, the allowlist is enforced on the worker global scope (a controlled `new Worker("worker.js")` from `page.html` cannot `fetch("https://attacker.example.com/payload")` — the allowlist inherits into the worker), the allowlist header is per-page (a controlled fixture served WITHOUT the header allows all connections, demonstrating the opt-in nature), the header accepts a space-separated list of origins, `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls (no Connection Allowlists support) silently allow all connections regardless of the header (the header is unknown to them and ignored), and the allowlist does not affect the implicit same-origin document navigation (clicking `<a href="/internal">` continues to work; only cross-origin resource fetches are gated). Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, Connection Allowlists) and the Connection Allowlists proposal explainer at https://github.com/WICG/connection-allowlists.

### Performance (P)

- [P-186] **[P1] Chrome 152 Beta CSS Color 5 `alpha()` Function Takes an Origin Color and Modifies Only the Alpha Channel for Relative Transparency** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) ships the CSS Color 5 `alpha()` function, which takes an origin color and modifies only the alpha channel — letting web developers set transparency relative to an existing color value. The function accepts a color and an optional alpha percentage: `alpha(<color>, <alpha-percentage>)` returns the color with the alpha channel replaced by the new percentage. For a controlled fixture with `<style>.a { color: rgb(255, 0, 0); background: alpha(currentColor, 50%); }</style><div class="a" id="a"></div>`, assert `getComputedStyle(a).backgroundColor` returns `rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)` (the `red` color with alpha `0.5`), `alpha()` works with named colors (`alpha(rebeccapurple, 25%)` returns `rgba(102, 51, 153, 0.25)`), `alpha()` works with hex values (`alpha(#ff0000, 50%)` returns `rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)`), `alpha()` works with `color-mix()` (`background: alpha(color-mix(in oklab, red, blue), 80%)` returns the mixed color with alpha `0.8`), `alpha()` can be combined with the existing `color-mix(in oklab, red, alpha(currentColor, 50%))` and similar nested expressions, `CSS.supports("color: alpha(rgb(0, 0, 0), 50%)")` returns `true` in Chrome 152 beta and `false` in Chrome 151 / Safari 26.6 / Firefox 155 controls (the `alpha()` function is new to CSS Color 5 and not yet supported in stable Chrome), `getComputedStyle` reports the resolved color via `Color` IDL value (controlled fixture using `element.computedStyleMap().get("background-color")` returns a `CSSColorValue` with the alpha-modified color — distinguishable from the original color), the function accepts `from <color>` syntax variant: `alpha(from red alpha 0.5)` returns `rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)` (the `from` keyword lets the alpha be replaced without specifying the RGB channels), an `alpha()` whose origin color is invalid (e.g. `alpha(not-a-color, 50%)`) makes the whole property invalid (the rule is dropped, no fallback), and `alpha()` works with `currentColor` (controlled fixture where the page text color is `currentColor` and the background uses `alpha(currentColor, 25%)` returns the text color with 25% alpha). Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (CSS and UI section, Relative alpha colors — CSS Color 5 alpha() function).
- [P-187] **[P2] Chrome 152 Beta `OpaqueRange` Represents Live Text Spans Within Form-Control Values for Range-Like Operations** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) ships `OpaqueRange`, an object that represents a live span of text within a form control's value (a `<textarea>` or text-based `<input>`), so web developers can work with value text using range-like APIs. `OpaqueRange` supports operations such as `getBoundingClientRect()`, `getClientRects()`, integration with the CSS Custom Highlight API for inline suggestions / highlights / anchored popovers, and preserves encapsulation by exposing only value offsets (returning `null` for `startContainer` and `endContainer`). For a controlled fixture with `<textarea id="t">hello world</textarea>`, assert `const range = t.createRangeReference(0, 5)` returns an `OpaqueRange` (a controlled `console.log(range.constructor.name)` outputs `"OpaqueRange"` in Chrome 152 beta and `undefined` in controls), the range's `getBoundingClientRect()` returns a `DOMRect` whose width is approximately the pixel width of the `"hello"` substring at line 1 of the textarea (within a fixed pixel tolerance — the rect's top is the textarea's first line top), `range.getClientRects()` returns a list of `DOMRect` instances (one rect per line when the range spans multiple lines), `range.startOffset === 0` and `range.endOffset === 5` (the offsets reflect the value-text positions), `range.startContainer` and `range.endContainer` are `null` (the encapsulation contract — the range exposes only offsets, not DOM nodes), the range is live: a controlled fixture where the textarea value is mutated (`t.value = "hi world"; t.dispatchEvent(new Event("input"))`) updates the range's effective text without invalidating the range object (the range's `getBoundingClientRect()` returns the rect for `"hi wo"` after the mutation), `range.cloneRange()` returns another `OpaqueRange` with the same offsets (controlled fixture verifies the clone is independent of the original — modifying the original's offsets does not affect the clone), the range integrates with the CSS Custom Highlight API (`new Highlight(range); document.cssHighlights.add(highlight)` plus `::highlight(my-highlight) { background: yellow }` styles the range's text), `Safari 26.6` / `Firefox 155` controls (no `OpaqueRange`) return a different type for `t.createRangeReference(0, 5)` — either `undefined` (the method does not exist) or a plain object, and the size of the value-text that triggers an OOM is bounded (a controlled fixture with a 50 MB textarea value can create an `OpaqueRange` without crashing — heap delta ≤ 4x the parsed-string size, matching the v1.208.0 B-236 Rust XML parser heap bound). Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, OpaqueRange) and the Custom Highlight API integration in the CSS Custom Highlight API spec.

## New Test Cases Added in v1.216.0 (R333 — August 6 2026, 4h cycle 95)

### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-259] **[P1] Chrome 152 Beta Unframed Display Mode for Isolated Web Apps Removes Window Borders and Title Bars, Gated by `DefaultWindowManagementSetting` Policy** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) lets an installed IWA opt into the unframed display mode (CSS `display-mode: unframed`), which removes standard window borders and title bars and supports custom branding and menu hierarchies. The behavior is controlled by the `DefaultWindowManagementSetting`, `WindowManagementAllowedForUrls`, and `WindowManagementBlockedForUrls` enterprise policies. For a controlled fixture running inside an IWA shell that opts into `display-mode: unframed` via its manifest, assert that `matchMedia('(display-mode: unframed)').matches === true` when the IWA is in unframed mode (the media query is the CSS-side contract — the same media query that the W3C Display Modes spec defines for PWA display-mode), the OS chrome (window borders, title bars) is absent in unframed mode (controlled fixture verifies the window's outer-bounds rectangle equals the inner-bounds rectangle — no OS-chrome height delta), the IWA can render a custom menu hierarchy via a `<button>` element positioned at `top: 0, left: 0` (the absence of OS chrome means the IWA's UI starts at `y: 0` of the window, not `y: OS-chrome-height`), `WindowManagementAllowedForUrls` overrides the default to allow the URL to enter unframed mode without user prompt (the policy is per-origin — when set, the user gesture for window management is bypassed), `WindowManagementBlockedForUrls` blocks the URL from entering unframed mode regardless of any other permission state (the policy is a hard override — even an IWA installed with the proper manifest is denied unframed mode), `DefaultWindowManagementSetting` controls the baseline behavior (prompt / allow / block) for URLs not covered by the per-origin allow/block lists (the same three-tier policy composition as C-232 sub apps), Safari 26.6 / Firefox 154 controls (no unframed display mode for IWA) return `matchMedia('(display-mode: unframed)').matches === false` for any URL (the display-mode is unframed-specific to Chrome's IWA surface), and a controlled fixture verifies that toggling between `display-mode: standalone` and `display-mode: unframed` in the manifest updates the `matchMedia` result on next launch (the media query is bound to the install-time manifest — runtime switching requires re-install), demonstrating the manifest-bound contract. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, Unframed display mode for Isolated Web Apps).
- [B-260] **[P2] Chrome 152 Beta Notification Attribution for PWAs on macOS Routes PWA Notifications to the PWA's Own Name and Icon in Notification Center** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) attributes notifications from installed Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) on macOS to the PWA itself — using its own name and icon in Notification Center — rather than to Google Chrome. As a side effect, the `requireInteraction` field is no longer supported for PWA notifications on macOS because notification persistence is now controlled per-app by macOS settings, and the Badging API requires notification permissions for the app badge to display. For a controlled fixture with a PWA installed on macOS that calls `serviceWorker.showNotification('Hello', {body: 'World'})` (or `registration.showNotification` from the service worker), assert that the resulting notification in macOS Notification Center is attributed to the PWA's display name (not "Google Chrome") and shows the PWA's manifest icon (not the Chrome browser icon), `registration.showNotification('Hello', {requireInteraction: true, ...})` ignores the `requireInteraction: true` flag (the field is silently dropped — macOS controls persistence via its own per-app settings), `navigator.setAppBadge(1)` requires that the PWA has been granted notification permission (the Badging API is now permission-gated; without `Notification.permission === 'granted'`, `setAppBadge` rejects with `NotAllowedError`), an MDM configuration profile is needed to pre-grant notification permission for the PWA's bundle ID (the `NotificationsAllowedForUrls` Chrome policy pre-grants for Chrome but a separate macOS MDM profile is needed for the PWA's specific bundle ID — without both, the PWA's notifications fall back to the Chrome attribution), the PWA's notifications still respect `Notification.permission` requests via `Notification.requestPermission()` (the permission UI is the system permission dialog, not Chrome's), Safari 26.6 (no Chrome PWA installation attribution on macOS — Safari uses its own add-to-dock flow) and Firefox 154 controls (no Chrome PWA installation) report `Notification.permission` per their own implementations without the Chrome PWA attribution path, and a controlled fixture verifies that uninstalling the PWA removes its notifications from Notification Center (notification lifetime is tied to the PWA install, not Chrome), demonstrating the per-app identity contract. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, Notification attribution for PWAs on macOS).

### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-432] **[P1] Chrome 152 Beta `getDisplayMedia` Adds `audioPreference` Attribute to `DisplayMediaStreamOptions` for Audio-Capture Hint** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) adds an `audioPreference` attribute to the `DisplayMediaStreamOptions` dictionary used in `navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia()`, which lets web applications signal to the browser that audio sharing is preferred along with video capture. For a controlled fixture with `navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia({video: true, audioPreference: "prefer"})` invoked under a user-gesture activation and a mocked `MediaDevices` implementation, assert that the resulting `MediaStream` either includes an audio track (the user selected a tab/screen with audio and the preference was honored) or has no audio track but the call succeeds with `video: true, audio: false` effective capture (when the chosen surface has no audio, the preference is a hint not a hard requirement — the browser may elect to capture video-only rather than reject), `audioPreference: "deny"` produces a `MediaStream` with no audio track regardless of the chosen surface's audio capability (the user-gesture capture flow respects the preference; a tab/screen with audio is still captured without audio when the preference is `deny`), the default value of `audioPreference` (omitted) preserves the legacy behavior (no preference change — the capture flow follows the `audio: boolean` flag), `DisplayMediaStreamOptions.audioPreference` is enumerable in Object.keys and reflects the string value passed in, `audioPreference` accepts only `"prefer"` / `"deny"` (unknown strings either fall back to the default or throw a `TypeError` per the dictionary's string-enum contract), Safari 26.6 / Firefox 154 controls (no `audioPreference` attribute on `DisplayMediaStreamOptions`) treat the attribute as an ignored extra property (the call succeeds and the option is silently dropped, demonstrating no breakage on cross-browser implementations), and a controlled fixture verifies that `audioPreference: "prefer"` is honored on user-facing surfaces that have audio (e.g. a tab with playing media) versus ignored on surfaces without audio (e.g. a window with no audio track), demonstrating the hint-not-mandate contract. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Media section, `audioPreferred` capture in getDisplayMedia API).
- [W-433] **[P2] Chrome 152 Beta WebGPU Adds Optional `subgroup-size-control` Feature for Explicit Subgroup Size Selection in Compute Shaders** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) adds an optional GPU feature `subgroup-size-control` to `GPUAdapter.features` and `GPUDevice.features` that lets WGSL compute shaders explicitly set the subgroup size via `enable subgroups; enable subgroupsizecontrol; override-subgroup-size: 4;` (or 8 / 16 / 32 / 64). For a controlled fixture with a WebGPU-capable adapter that supports `subgroup-size-control`, assert that `adapter.features.has("subgroup-size-control") === true` when the underlying hardware exposes the capability (the feature is opt-in via `requiredFeatures: ["subgroup-size-control"]` on `requestDevice()`), a WGSL shader with `enable subgroups; enable subgroupsizecontrol; override-subgroup-size: 32;` compiles and a `workgroupSize(32)` `subgroupAdd` returns the expected per-subgroup reduction result (the `subgroupAdd` reduction honors the explicitly requested size of 32 even if the underlying hardware's native subgroup size is 64 or 128), `adapter.limits.subgroupMinSize` and `adapter.limits.subgroupMaxSize` reflect the supported bounds (e.g. `subgroupMinSize: 4, subgroupMaxSize: 64` on Vulkan-class hardware; the chosen `override-subgroup-size` must be within this range), a WGSL shader that uses `override-subgroup-size` without `enable subgroupsizecontrol` fails WGSL validation (the `override-subgroup-size` attribute is gated by the `subgroupsizecontrol` enable-extension), a `requestDevice({requiredFeatures: ["subgroup-size-control"]})` call on an adapter without that feature rejects with `GPUDevice` creation failure (the feature is a true capability, not silently granted), Safari 26.6 / Safari TP 249 controls (subgroups exist per W-428 but `subgroup-size-control` is Chrome 152 beta only) reject the `subgroupsizecontrol` enable-extension as unknown, and a controlled fixture verifies that the runtime-selected subgroup size affects `subgroupBallot` / `subgroupBroadcast` semantics (a 32-subgroup broadcast returns a 32-lane ballot; a 64-subgroup broadcast returns a 64-lane ballot — the size is observable in `subgroupSize`). Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, WebGPU Subgroup Size Control).
- [W-434] **[P2] Chrome 152 Beta Window Shape API Lets ChromeOS Isolated Web Apps Set Non-Rectangular Window Geometry via `window.chromeos.isolatedWebApp.setShape`** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) ships the Window Shape API on ChromeOS, accessed via `window.chromeos.isolatedWebApp.setShape(rects)`, which lets an installed Isolated Web App (IWA) customize the non-rectangular shape of the window by passing an array of `DOMRect` (or `{x, y, width, height}`) rectangles describing the visible regions of the window. For a controlled fixture running inside an IWA shell on ChromeOS, assert that `window.chromeos.isolatedWebApp?.setShape([{x: 0, y: 0, width: 200, height: 100}, {x: 250, y: 0, width: 100, height: 50}])` succeeds when the window is in the unframed display mode (the API is gated by the unframed mode and by the `window-management` permission; the call returns a resolved `Promise<void>`), `setShape([])` resets the window to a single rectangle matching the window's current bounding box (the empty array is the explicit reset — useful for toggling custom-shape off), `setShape` rejects with `NotAllowedError` when the window is in framed display mode (the API requires unframed display mode — framed windows cannot have a non-rectangular shape because they have OS chrome), `setShape` rejects with `NotAllowedError` when the IWA has not been granted the `window-management` permission (the API is permission-gated per the Permissions Policy `window-management` directive), a `setShape` call with rectangles outside the window's bounding box clamps to the bounding box (a `{x: -100, y: 0, width: 500, height: 200}` call with a 200×200 window is clamped to `{x: 0, y: 0, width: 200, height: 200}` — no overflow), `setShape` reflects in the window's `Window.boundingBox` / `matchMedia('(display-mode: unframed)')` queries (the window remains unframed and the bounding box tracks the union of the rectangles), Safari 26.6 / Firefox 154 controls (no `window.chromeos.isolatedWebApp` namespace, no Window Shape API) return `undefined` for `window.chromeos` (the API is ChromeOS-only and IWA-only), and a controlled fixture verifies that `setShape` is observable in the resulting window's screen-capture shape (a window with two rectangles is captured as two regions — the area between them is transparent / not captured), demonstrating the visual-geometry contract. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, Window Shape API).

### Performance (P)

- [P-188] **[P1] Chrome 152 Beta `MediaCapabilities.decodingInfo` Adds `encryptionScheme` Attribute to `KeySystemTrackConfiguration` for EME Encryption Scheme Capability Query** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) extends the `KeySystemTrackConfiguration` dictionary used in `navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo()` with an `encryptionScheme` attribute that lets web applications query whether a specific encryption scheme such as `'cenc'` (AES-CTR) or `'cbcs'` (AES-CBCS with subsample encryption) is supported by the underlying Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) implementation. For a controlled fixture with a synthetic `MediaCapabilities` instance, assert that `navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo({type: "media", video: {contentType: "video/mp4; codecs="avc1.42E01E"", encryptionScheme: "cenc", robustness: ""}, keySystemConfiguration: {keySystem: "com.widevine.alpha", videoCapabilities: [{contentType: "video/mp4; codecs="avc1.42E01E"", encryptionScheme: "cenc"}]}})` returns a `MediaCapabilitiesInfo` whose `.supported` reflects the EME implementation's actual `cenc` capability (the fixture asserts the returned value's `.supported` boolean matches what Chrome's EME Widevine implementation actually reports — true for Widevine-cleared fixture, false for unsupported configurations), `navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo({... encryptionScheme: "cbcs" ...})` returns the corresponding `cbcs` capability and a separate `.supported` boolean (the `cenc` vs `cbcs` distinction is preserved — fixtures that ask only for `cenc` must not silently return the `cbcs` capability and vice versa), the dictionary reports `KeySystemTrackConfiguration.encryptionScheme` as part of its serialization (the attribute is enumerable and reflects the value passed in), `navigator.mediaCapabilities.decodingInfo({... encryptionScheme: "foo" ...})` for an unknown encryption scheme string returns a `MediaCapabilitiesInfo` with `.supported === false` and a `MediaCapabilitiesException` is thrown when the dictionary fails validation (unknown values fall back to not-supported), Safari 26.6 / Firefox 154 controls (no `encryptionScheme` attribute on `KeySystemTrackConfiguration`) treat the same dictionary as if `encryptionScheme` were absent (the call succeeds and returns the same value as without the attribute, demonstrating graceful degradation), and a controlled fixture verifies that omitting `encryptionScheme` (backward-compatible default) yields the same `.supported` boolean as omitting `robustness` (the previous attribute for capability scoping), demonstrating that `encryptionScheme` is an additional dimension rather than a replacement. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Media section, `MediaCapabilities encryptionScheme`).

### Security / Privacy Sandbox (S)

- [S-472] **[P0] Chrome 152 Beta Removes the Private Aggregation API Following the Third-Party Cookies Maintained Announcement, Affecting Shared Storage and Protected Audience Call Sites** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) removes the Private Aggregation API following Chrome's announcement that the current approach to third-party cookies will be maintained. The Private Aggregation API was only exposed through the Shared Storage and Protected Audience APIs, which are also planned to be deprecation-removed. For a controlled fixture with a Shared Storage or Protected Audience worklet, assert that `privateAggregation.contributeToHistogram(...)` (the previously-available worklet-scoped function) is now `undefined` (the API is removed from the global scope — worklet scripts that previously called it now throw `ReferenceError`), Shared Storage `Worklet` scripts that call `privateAggregation.contributeToHistogram({bucket, value})` fail at parse / script-evaluation time with `ReferenceError: privateAggregation is not defined` (the removal is at the script-eval level — the worklet does not load), Protected Audience `AuctionWorklet` scripts that previously called `privateAggregation.contributeToHistogram` similarly fail at evaluation (the API is not polyfilled back), `navigator.sharedStorage?.worklet?.addModule('...')` still resolves for backward compatibility but the loaded worklet no longer has access to `privateAggregation` (the Shared Storage surface remains, but the aggregation primitive is gone — call sites that depended on aggregation must migrate to a different telemetry channel), `navigator.runAdAuction({...})` Protected Audience calls that previously expected aggregation results from the auction's `reportResult` no longer receive aggregation results (the `reportResult` callback can still run, but `forDebuggingOnly.privateAggregation.contributeToHistogram` inside it is `undefined`), Chrome 151 / Chrome 150 controls (Private Aggregation still available before removal) expose `privateAggregation` in Shared Storage and Protected Audience worklets — running the same fixture against Chrome 151 returns the aggregation result, demonstrating the removal contract, Safari 26.6 / Firefox 154 controls (no Shared Storage / Protected Audience — those APIs are Chromium-only Privacy Sandbox APIs) return `undefined` for `navigator.sharedStorage` and `navigator.runAdAuction` (the APIs do not exist outside Chrome), and a controlled fixture verifies that the Shared Storage `selectURL` and Protected Audience auction flows still run and return their non-aggregation outputs (the auction logic is intact — only the aggregation primitive is removed), demonstrating the targeted removal contract. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Deprecations and removals section, Remove Private Aggregation API).

### Compatibility / Embedded Runtime (C)

- [C-232] **[P2] Chrome 152 Beta Isolated Web Apps (IWA) Sub Apps Let Multiple Apps Share a Single IWA Installation With Distinct Identities and Enterprise Policies** — Chrome 152 beta (released 2026-07-30 to the beta channel) lets developers create multiple sub apps under a single Isolated Web App (IWA) installation via the `DefaultSubAppsWithoutPromptsSetting`, `SubAppsWithoutPromptsAllowedForOrigins`, and `SubAppsWithoutPromptsBlockedForOrigins` enterprise policies. For a controlled fixture with an installed IWA bundle that declares two sub apps in its manifest, assert that each sub app appears in the OS desktop shelf with its own distinct name and icon (the parent IWA's identity is shared, but each sub app has its own OS integration — the icon is sourced from the sub app's manifest, not the parent), a sub app can declare its own file-type association (e.g. `.foo`) and the OS routes that file type to the sub app rather than the parent IWA (the file handler is per-sub-app, not global to the IWA), `SubAppsWithoutPromptsAllowedForOrigins` permits an origin to install sub apps without a per-app user prompt (the policy is per-origin — when set, the prompt for the listed origin is suppressed), `SubAppsWithoutPromptsBlockedForOrigins` denies sub app installation from a listed origin (the policy blocks installation regardless of any other permission state), `DefaultSubAppsWithoutPromptsSetting` controls the default behavior (prompt / allow / block) for sub apps not covered by the per-origin allow/block lists (the three-tier policy composition: per-origin overrides default which overrides the user-prompt baseline), sub app installation calls `navigator.subApps?.add({name, icon, ...})` (the proposed Web API) and resolves with a `SubApp` instance when the parent IWA has been granted the permission (the `subApps` API is permission-gated), Safari 26.6 / Firefox 154 controls (no IWA / no sub apps concept) return `undefined` for `navigator.subApps` (the API does not exist outside Chrome's IWA surface), and a controlled fixture verifies that uninstalling the parent IWA removes all sub apps (sub app lifecycle is tied to the parent — no orphan sub apps are left in the OS shelf), demonstrating the install-tree contract. Source: Chrome 152 beta release notes, https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-152-beta/ (Web APIs section, Isolated Web Apps (IWA) Sub apps).
