- [B-271] **[P2] Chrome 154 Stable CSS4 `text-decoration-skip-spaces` Property Controls Whether Text-Decoration Lines (Underlines / Overlines / Line-Throughs) Skip Over Whitespace Characters With `auto` / `none` / `start` / `end` / `left` / `right` / `space-first` / `space-last` Values** — Chrome 154 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=154`) ships the `text-decoration-skip-spaces` CSS property from CSS Text Decoration Level 4: the property controls whether text-decoration lines (underlines / overlines / line-throughs) skip over whitespace characters in the decorated text. The motivation is to allow authors to prevent decorations from being drawn under spaces — visually more appealing than the legacy "underline-everything" behavior where a `text-decoration: underline` decoration extends under every space and creates long visual gaps in justified text. The values are: `auto` (skip decoration on word separators, per language-specific word-separator rules — the default), `none` (do NOT skip, draw decoration through all characters including spaces), `start` / `end` (skip the first / last space adjacent to a word boundary), `left` / `right` (skip the first / last space adjacent to the left / right edge, depending on writing direction), and `space-first` / `space-last` (skip only the first / last space in a sequence of spaces). The four WPT fixtures at `http://wpt.live/css/css-text-decor/text-decoration-skip-spaces-001.html` through `004.html` give controlled-fixture acceptance criteria. For a controlled fixture serving `<p id="t" style="text-decoration: underline; text-decoration-skip-spaces: none;">Hello World</p>` over HTTPS where the underline decoration is rendered, assert that the default `auto` value skips decoration on word-separator whitespace (controlled fixture verifying that the underline decoration between "Hello" and "World" is shorter than the full inter-word distance — i.e. the decoration does NOT extend under the space), `text-decoration-skip-spaces: none` does NOT skip decoration on whitespace (controlled fixture verifying the underline decoration between "Hello" and "World" is the full inter-word distance — i.e. the decoration DOES extend under the space, matching the legacy behavior), `text-decoration-skip-spaces: start` skips the first space adjacent to a word boundary (controlled fixture verifying the decoration skips the first space but draws through any subsequent spaces), `text-decoration-skip-spaces: end` skips the last space adjacent to a word boundary (controlled fixture verifying the decoration draws through leading spaces but skips the last space), `text-decoration-skip-spaces: space-first` skips only the first space in a sequence (controlled fixture verifying the decoration skips the first space but draws through the second / third space in a sequence like "A  B"), `text-decoration-skip-spaces: space-last` skips only the last space in a sequence (controlled fixture verifying the decoration draws through leading spaces but skips the last space in "A  B"), the property works in CSS shorthand form `text-decoration: underline skip-spaces-none` (controlled fixture verifying the shorthand parses correctly and the resulting `text-decoration-skip-spaces` computed value is `none`), `@supports (text-decoration-skip-spaces: none)` returns `true` on Chrome 154 stable (controlled fixture verifying the `@supports` probe is the capability gate), `Chrome 153` controls (no `text-decoration-skip-spaces` property; the legacy default is `auto` per the original CSS Text Decoration Level 3 contract) report `getComputedStyle(t).textDecorationSkipSpaces === ""` (the property is not present on the Chrome 153 baseline), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari has partial CSS Text Decoration Level 4 support — the `text-decoration-skip-spaces` property may or may not be exposed depending on the Safari version) report mixed coverage, `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox has partial CSS Text Decoration Level 4 support; Firefox shipped `text-decoration-skip-ink` earlier than `text-decoration-skip-spaces`) report mixed coverage. Spec reference: CSS Text Decoration Level 4 at `https://www.w3.org/TR/css-text-decor-4/#text-decoration-skip-spaces-property` documents the property grammar; the WPT fixtures at `http://wpt.live/css/css-text-decor/text-decoration-skip-spaces-001.html` through `004.html` give controlled-fixture acceptance criteria. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the computed-style assertion for each of the 7 property values + the shorthand form + the `@supports` probe + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 154 stable for the live-fire part.

- [B-272] **[P2] Chrome 154 Stable `<install>` HTML Element Lets Authors Declaratively Prompt Users To Install A Web App With Optional `src` And `referrerpolicy` Attributes For Cross-Origin Installation Prompts (Graduating From Edge 152 Origin Trial)** — Chrome 154 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=154`, chromestatus feature `5152834368700416`, samples at `https://liahiscock.github.io/PWA/WebInstall/element-store.html` + `https://kbhlee2121.github.io/pwa/web-install/only-elements.html`) ships the `<install>` HTML element as enabled-by-default after graduating from the Edge 152 origin trial. The element is a browser-controlled button-like element that, when activated by the user, installs the web app associated with the page's manifest. The element optionally accepts two attributes that allow installation of content from a different origin: (a) `src` attribute — when present, the element installs the manifest at the URL specified by `src` (a different origin from the current page), enabling cross-origin app installation prompts; (b) `referrerpolicy` attribute — when present, controls the referrer policy sent when fetching the manifest at `src`, defaulting to `no-referrer`. For a controlled fixture serving `<install id="inst">Install App</install>` over HTTPS where the page is installable (has a manifest at `/manifest.webmanifest` with `name`, `short_name`, `icons`, `start_url`, and `display` fields), assert that the `<install>` element renders as a browser-controlled button (controlled fixture verifying `getComputedStyle(inst).display !== "none"` and the element is focusable / clickable — `inst.matches(':hover')` and `inst.matches(':focus')` work as expected), clicking the element triggers the install flow (controlled fixture verifying the browser shows an install dialog — `window.beforeinstallprompt` is NOT fired because the declarative `<install>` element does NOT trigger the JS event; the install flow is handled entirely declaratively by the browser), the `<install>` element with no `src` attribute installs the current page's manifest (controlled fixture verifying the install flow resolves to the current origin's manifest at `/manifest.webmanifest`), the `<install>` element with `src="https://other-origin.example/manifest.webmanifest"` attribute installs a different origin's manifest (controlled fixture verifying the install flow resolves to the cross-origin manifest at the specified `src` URL — this is the primary use case for app stores that want to install third-party PWAs), the `referrerpolicy` attribute on `<install>` controls the referrer sent with the `src` manifest fetch (controlled fixture verifying `referrerpolicy="no-referrer"` causes the manifest fetch to omit the Referer header, and `referrerpolicy="origin"` causes the manifest fetch to send only the origin), `<install>` is rendered as an `HTMLElement` (controlled fixture verifying `inst instanceof HTMLElement === true` — the element does NOT have a custom interface), `Chrome 153` controls (no stable `<install>` element; the feature was Edge 152 OT) parse `<install>` as `HTMLUnknownElement` (controlled fixture verifying `document.createElement('install') instanceof HTMLUnknownElement === true` — the element is not yet recognized as a custom element on Chrome 153), `Safari 26.6` controls (no `<install>` element) parse `<install>` as `HTMLUnknownElement`, `Firefox 155` controls (no `<install>` element) parse `<install>` as `HTMLUnknownElement`. Spec reference: the explainer doc at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rGvLhD4SR8Y9M1wVmqgyesPNkbZGU7HOqlttjEFJ5Vo/edit?tab=t.tmx19oox759l#heading=h.j3tt49hqiuck` documents the element contract + the cross-origin installation semantics; the sample at `https://kbhlee2121.github.io/pwa/web-install/only-elements.html` gives a working demo of the declarative install flow. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the declarative install flow + the `src` cross-origin manifest fetch + the `referrerpolicy` attribute round-trip + the `HTMLUnknownElement` parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 154 stable for the live-fire part.

### Security / Privacy Sandbox (S)

- [S-475] **[P0] Chrome 154 Stable Removes The `<fencedframe>` HTML Element (Step 1: Stub — No JS Calls Throw) And The `window.fence` APIs (Step 2: Complete Removal) Following Protected Audience + Shared Storage Deprecation** — Chrome 154 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=154`, Chromium IDL source at `https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/fenced_frame/fenced_frame_config.idl`, blink-dev Intent-to-Deprecate thread for Protected Audience at `https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/k_nubsMb97g/m/awPD4IGLBAAJ`, blink-dev Intent-to-Deprecate thread for Shared Storage at `https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/uh5Ke6qyegc/m/WFTFnhyJBAAJ`) ships the M154 step-1 stub of the fenced-frame element AND the M154 step-2 complete removal of the `window.fence` APIs as part of the broader Privacy Sandbox deprecation (the Protected Audience API and Shared Storage API are being deprecated and removed, and since fenced frames can only be navigated using the `urn:uuid` in a `FencedFrameConfig` (which can only be created via `runAdAuction` and `selectURL`), removing PA + selectURL means fenced frames can no longer be navigated, so removing the fenced-frame element + `window.fence` APIs is the safe cleanup). The plan as published is: (a) **M154**: Keep the fenced-frame element and its associated IDL dependencies as **stubs** — i.e. `fenced-frame-element.config.setSharedStorageContext()` does NOT throw (it's a no-op stub), but the element no longer actually creates a fenced frame; (b) **M154**: In the same milestone, **completely remove `window.fence`** APIs — `window.fence.setReportEventDataForAutomaticBeacons()` / `window.fence.reportEvent()` / etc. all return `undefined`; (c) **M155 Canary/Beta**: Begin a controlled rollout of the stub FF HTML element removal via a field trial — the element starts resolving to `HTMLUnknownElement` for a small percentage of users; (d) **M155 Stable**: Assuming no regressions after 1% stable, request additional approval for full removal. The deprecation is gated by the broader Privacy Sandbox removal; the chromium bug tracks the deprecation at `https://crbug.com/435623334` (same bug tracker as S-473 XSLT deprecation timeline, but the deprecation target is different). For a controlled fixture serving `<fencedframe id="ff" mode="opaque-ads" src="https://attacker.example/"></fencedframe>` over HTTPS, assert that the `<fencedframe>` element exists as a stub on Chrome 154 stable (controlled fixture verifying `document.createElement('fencedframe')` returns an element whose `.constructor.name === "HTMLElement"` — the element is parsed but is now a stub), `fencedframe.config.setSharedStorageContext("test")` does NOT throw on Chrome 154 stable (controlled fixture verifying the stub no-throw contract — the call returns `undefined` silently per the M154 step-1 plan), `window.fence` is `undefined` on Chrome 154 stable (controlled fixture verifying the M154 step-2 complete removal — `typeof window.fence === "undefined"` and `typeof window.fence.setReportEventDataForAutomaticBeacons === "undefined"`), `window.fence` was previously available on Chrome 153 stable (controlled fixture noting the Chrome 153 baseline has `typeof window.fence === "object"` with methods like `setReportEventDataForAutomaticBeacons` / `reportEvent` / `getNestedConfigs` — the M154 step-2 removal closes this surface), the fenced-frame element does NOT actually navigate to the `src` URL on Chrome 154 stable (controlled fixture verifying the element renders as an empty / stub DOM — the navigation path is broken because `FencedFrameConfig` can no longer be created via `runAdAuction` or `selectURL`), the deprecation does NOT remove the `<iframe>` element (controlled fixture verifying `<iframe>` continues to function normally — `<iframe src="https://example.com">` navigates as expected, the removal is fenced-frame-specific), `Chrome 154` controls (no stable Chrome 154 yet for cross-version check, but Chrome 153 baseline has `typeof window.fence === "object"` and the fenced-frame element navigates correctly) demonstrate the pre-removal state, `Safari 26.6` controls (no `<fencedframe>` element ever shipped in Safari; no `window.fence` ever shipped in Safari) report `document.createElement('fencedframe') instanceof HTMLUnknownElement === true` and `typeof window.fence === "undefined"` (Safari was never a target for fenced frames), `Firefox 155` controls (no `<fencedframe>` element; no `window.fence`) report the same parity as Safari. Spec reference: the Chromium IDL source at `https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/fenced_frame/fenced_frame_config.idl` documents the stub no-throw contract; the blink-dev Intent threads document the broader Privacy Sandbox deprecation context. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the M154 step-1 stub no-throw contract + the M154 step-2 complete removal of `window.fence` + the `<fencedframe>` element no-navigation behavior + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 154 stable for the live-fire part.

### Compatibility / Cross-Browser (C)

- [C-236] **[P2] Chrome 154 Stable Web Install API `navigator.install()` (3 Signatures: 0 Args / 1 Arg / 2 Args) Lets A Website Install Either Itself Or Another Origin's Web App After Graduating From Edge 152 Origin Trial** — Chrome 154 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=154`, chromestatus feature `5183481574850560`, sample at `https://kbhlee2121.github.io/pwa/web-install/index.html` + `https://microsoftedge.github.io/Demos/pwa-pwastore`) ships the Web Install API as enabled-by-default after graduating from the Edge 152 origin trial. The API provides 3 signatures that are all experimented with in parallel: (a) `navigator.install()` with 0 args — installs the current document's web app (the page that called `navigator.install()`); (b) `navigator.install(url)` with 1 arg — installs the web app at the specified URL, which can be either a same-origin URL (different page on the same site) or a different-origin URL (cross-origin install); (c) `navigator.install(url, options)` with 2 args — installs the web app at the specified URL with options like `referrerPolicy` or `installDescription`. The 0-arg signature is a "current document install"; the 1-arg and 2-arg signatures are "background document install". The motivation is to give authors a JS-driven alternative to the `beforeinstallprompt` event-based installation flow — particularly for app stores that want to install third-party PWAs without navigating away from the current page. For a controlled fixture serving a PWA-installable page (has a manifest at `/manifest.webmanifest` with `name`, `short_name`, `icons`, `start_url`, `display`) over HTTPS with a user-gesture activation handler, assert that the `navigator.install` method exists (controlled fixture verifying `typeof navigator.install === "function"`), `navigator.install()` with 0 args returns a `Promise<boolean>` that resolves to `true` when the user accepts the install prompt (controlled fixture verifying the install flow — the browser shows a confirmation dialog, and after the user accepts, `navigator.install()` resolves to `true`), `navigator.install()` rejects with `NotAllowedError` when called WITHOUT a user-gesture activation (controlled fixture verifying the activation gate — `try { navigator.install(); } catch(e) { e.name === "NotAllowedError" }` when called from a non-activation handler), `navigator.install("https://other-origin.example/")` with 1 arg returns a `Promise<boolean>` that resolves to `true` when the user accepts the cross-origin install prompt (controlled fixture verifying the cross-origin install flow — the browser fetches the manifest at the specified URL and prompts for installation), `navigator.install("https://other-origin.example/", {referrerPolicy: "no-referrer"})` with 2 args controls the referrer policy sent when fetching the cross-origin manifest (controlled fixture verifying the manifest fetch omits the Referer header when `referrerPolicy: "no-referrer"` is specified), `navigator.install` does NOT throw when the page is NOT installable (controlled fixture verifying the API returns a `Promise` that rejects with a meaningful error — e.g. `NotSupportedError` or `NotInstallableError` — rather than throwing synchronously), `Chrome 153` controls (no stable Web Install API; the feature was Edge 152 OT) report `typeof navigator.install === "undefined"` (the method does not exist on the Chrome 153 baseline), `Safari 26.6` controls (no Web Install API; Safari has no equivalent declarative install API beyond the `beforeinstallprompt` event) report `typeof navigator.install === "undefined"`, `Firefox 155` controls (no Web Install API; Firefox has no equivalent declarative install API beyond `beforeinstallprompt`) report `typeof navigator.install === "undefined"`. Spec reference: the explainer doc at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/12nSXJLm8mW0gWZ_yjlXfrV8r9gwJliVt4WVa-209-KA/edit?tab=t.0` documents the 3 signatures + the current-document vs background-document install semantics; the sample at `https://kbhlee2121.github.io/pwa/web-install/index.html` gives a working demo of all 3 signatures. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the 3-signature round-trip + the user-gesture activation gate + the cross-origin manifest fetch + the not-installable page rejection + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 154 stable for the live-fire part.

### Performance (P)

- [P-190] **[P1] Chrome 154 Stable IndexedDB: SQLite Backend Step 2 Of Multi-Phase Rollout Rewrites IDB On Top Of SQLite To Replace LevelDB + Flat-Files Hybrid (No Web API Change — Only Affects New Data Stores)** — Chrome 154 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=154`, chromestatus feature `5126896685809664`, docs at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/1S9Rx67BmCZIP7tpasKaQ2FlV4TL1Z15DitR2kRZs9nw/edit?usp=sharing` + `https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-N4NqdYjqaWEbfVPYnCg2Ho1u4YK48pUoQ_tSy9SUg8/edit?usp=sharing`, sample at `https://evanstade.github.io/web-storage-demos/idb-txn-scopes`) ships step 2 of the multi-phase IndexedDB backend migration to SQLite. The migration rewrites Chromium's IndexedDB implementation on top of SQLite to replace the prior implementation that uses a hybrid of LevelDB (for key-value data) and flat files (for indexing). There is **no change to the Web API** — the `indexedDB` interface, `IDBFactory` / `IDBDatabase` / `IDBObjectStore` / `IDBTransaction` / `IDBIndex` interfaces, and the `IDBRequest` event flow all remain the same. The migration is expected to improve reliability (SQLite has decades of production hardening vs. LevelDB's narrower scope) and, to a lesser extent, performance (especially for large object stores). The rollout is multi-phase: step 1 (already shipped) was the in-memory i.e. incognito contexts rollout (chromestatus feature `5126896685809664` parent); step 2 (this cycle) is the *new data stores* rollout — the first time a user visits a site, or after clearing site data, new IDB data will be stored in a backend that uses SQLite; existing data stored in LevelDB is unimpacted; step 3 (future) will consist of migrating existing data from LevelDB stores to SQLite stores. For a controlled fixture serving `<script>const open = indexedDB.open('test-db', 1); open.onupgradeneeded = (e) => { e.target.result.createObjectStore('store', {keyPath: 'id'}); }; open.onsuccess = (e) => { const db = e.target.result; const tx = db.transaction('store', 'readwrite'); tx.objectStore('store').put({id: 1, value: 'test'}).onsuccess = () => { console.log('OK'); }; };</script>` over HTTPS where the page has NO prior storage (cleared site data), assert that the Web API round-trip succeeds identically (controlled fixture verifying the API contract is unchanged — `indexedDB.open` resolves with an `IDBDatabase`, `db.transaction` returns an `IDBTransaction`, the `put()` `IDBRequest` fires `success` event), the new IDB data store is stored in the SQLite backend (controlled fixture verifying via DevTools — the IDB data store at `~/.config/google-chrome/Default/IndexedDB/` shows SQLite file format `.sqlite3` rather than the legacy `.ldb` LevelDB format; this is a DevTools-level assertion requiring Chrome internal access, not a Web API probe), the migration is transparent to the Web API (controlled fixture verifying the same `put` / `get` / `delete` / `cursor` / `index` operations all work identically — no behavior change visible to web pages), the existing LevelDB data is NOT migrated automatically (controlled fixture verifying that a pre-Chrome-154 IDB store with data continues to function — the existing data is unimpacted and will be migrated in step 3), clearing site data (`indexedDB.deleteDatabase('test-db')` + reopen) creates a new SQLite-backed store (controlled fixture verifying the migration applies to new stores only — `deleteDatabase` removes both the LevelDB file and any stub SQLite file, and a subsequent `open()` creates a fresh SQLite-backed store), the migration does NOT affect the `navigator.storage.estimate()` quota reporting (controlled fixture verifying the quota is reported identically — `navigator.storage.estimate()` returns the same `{usage, quota}` values before and after the migration), `Chrome 153` controls (no SQLite backend; uses the legacy LevelDB + flat-files hybrid) demonstrate the pre-migration state (controlled fixture noting that the legacy implementation works identically from a Web API perspective but the storage backend is LevelDB), `Safari 26.6` controls (no SQLite IDB backend migration; Safari uses its own IDB implementation) report no parity changes, `Firefox 155` controls (no SQLite IDB backend migration; Firefox uses its own IDB implementation) report no parity changes. Spec reference: the docs at `https://docs.google.com/document/d/1S9Rx67BmCZIP7tpasKaQ2FlV4TL1Z15DitR2kRZs9nw/edit?usp=sharing` documents the storage differences between LevelDB and SQLite that IDB users should be aware of (e.g. SQLite enforces stricter typing on key-value pairs); the sample at `https://evanstade.github.io/web-storage-demos/idb-txn-scopes` gives a working demo of transaction-scope usage that works identically on both backends. Acceptance gate: the controlled fixture verifies the Web API round-trip + the new-store SQLite backend assertion (via DevTools) + the cross-engine parity assertion in a single Playwright session running on Chrome 154 stable for the live-fire part.

## New Test Cases Added in v1.220.0 (R337 — August 10 2026, 4h cycle 99)

v1.220.0 = R337 Dynamic Test Intelligence cron — 8 new, machine-verifiable test cases from 2026-08-10 research. v1.220.0 mines the unmined surface of Google Chrome 153 that v1.219.0 R336 deliberately skipped because v1.219.0 prioritized the freshly-opened 17 enabled-by-default features (10 of which got case bodies: W-438/W-439/W-440/W-441/W-442 + B-264/B-265/B-266/B-267 + S-474) plus the previously-skipped Chrome 152 flagged + deprecation surface (W-436, W-437, S-473). The remaining 7 enabled-by-default entries were deferred because the v1.219.0 budget of 10 cases was already full — specifically the Web Install API (5183481574850560), the Web app HTML install element (5152834368700416), the WebAudio Configurable render quantum (5078190552907776), and the Capability elements `<camera>` and `<microphone>` (5153829504024576) are origin-trial-scope per the skill's "Defer case bodies for experimental-only features until they graduate to stable" rule and remain deferred. The two true stable-surface contracts v1.219.0 deferred are: (a) **Expose CSSStyleValue hierarchy to Worker contexts** (feature 5114591051907072) — the CSS Typed OM's CSSStyleValue / CSSKeywordValue / CSSNumericValue / CSSUnitValue / CSSUnparsedValue interfaces are now exposed to `Worker` global scopes, aligning Blink with Firefox and Safari that already shipped per the W3C TR; (b) **XML parsing in Rust for non-XSLT scenarios** (feature 5309598397497344) — Chrome 153 re-launches the Rust XML parser for `DOMParser` + `XMLHttpRequest.responseXML` + standalone-SVG-image + external-SVG-image paths, complementing the Chrome 151 disabled-rollout and the Chrome 152 XSLT deprecation. Additionally v1.220.0 mines the 3 Chrome 153 **flagged** features that v1.219.0 deferred per the "flag → stable graduation" rule, plus the JS Self-Profiling Markers origin trial that v1.219.0 deferred as origin-trial-scope: (c) **SpeechRecognitionResult Timestamps (WebSpeech API)** (feature 5811907077472256, behind `#web-speech-timestamp` flag) — adds `audioStartTime` / `audioEndTime` `DOMHighResTimeStamp` attributes to `SpeechRecognitionResult`; (d) **Spell Check Custom Dictionary API** (feature 6185007701557248, behind `#spell-check-custom-dictionary` flag) — per-document transient spell-check dictionary supplemented to the browser's built-in dictionaries; (e) **Support Long Animation Frames API in Web Workers** (feature 5387465121726464, behind `#soft-navigation-heuristics` adjacent flag, more precisely `#long-animation-frames-in-worker`) — extends LoAF to dedicated workers, reporting `PerformanceObserver` `long-animation-frame` entries from inside the worker for event-loop-blocking tasks; (f) **JS Self-Profiling Markers** (feature 5201297767792640, origin trial) — adds an optional `marker` field to each `ProfilerSample` identifying the type of browser activity running when the sample was taken (`script` / `gc` / `style` / `layout` / `paint` / `other`); (g) a long-running edge case for the WebAudio Configurable render quantum (`AudioContextOptions.renderSizeHint` accepting the `"default"` / `"hardware"` `AudioContextRenderSizeCategory` enum OR a positive integer) — now graduating from Edge 152 origin trial to Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, allowing web audio games to trade render-quantum size for latency; (h) the **`SVG`-standalone-image and `SVG`-external-image XML parsing edges** of the Rust re-implementation that the original v1.219.0 deferred XML-parsing case body did not exhaust. The 5 required broad queries returned the same persistent failure pattern as v1.207.0 R324 through v1.219.0 R336 (no fresh SearXNG, no fresh DDG HTML content) — the single viable fallback chain (direct `curl --noproxy '*'` to `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` plus the W3C CSS Typed OM 1 spec + the W3C Long Animation Frames API spec + the W3C Web Audio API spec + the Chromium bugs 466303347 / 534781956 / 534893134 / 528037568 / 428005649 / 40800459) was used to mine the surface. Adjacent but distinct surfaces verified: B-268 Worker-context CSSStyleValue is the **Worker-exposure** contract distinct from any prior CSS Typed OM case (the v1.214.0–v1.219.0 cycle never covered the Worker exposure); B-269 Rust XML parser is the **non-XSLT path** distinct from S-473 XSLT deprecation timeline (B-269 is the parser migration, S-473 is the XSLT deprecation schedule) and distinct from v1.208.0 B-236 Chrome 151 Rust XML parser migration (which was the disabled launch — Chrome 151 disabled it on launch, Chrome 153 is the re-launch with the same Rust parser but extended scope); W-443 SpeechRecognitionResult Timestamps is the **per-result timestamp** contract distinct from any prior Web Speech API case (the v1.200.0–v1.219.0 cycle never covered the Web Speech API; W-443 is the first contract targeting the `SpeechRecognitionResult` interface); W-444 Spell Check Custom Dictionary is the **per-document transient dictionary** contract distinct from any prior spell-check case (the v1.214.0–v1.219.0 cycle never covered Spell Check); W-445 Worker-LoAF is the **Worker-side LoAF exposure** distinct from v1.209.0 P-183 Chrome 151 main-thread LoAF co-emit (W-445 is the Worker-side coverage, P-183 is the main-thread `long-animation-frame` entry contract); W-446 JS Self-Profiling Markers is the **marker-field extension** distinct from the JS Self-Profiling API baseline (W-446 is the marker-field addition on top of the existing JS Self-Profiling API); W-447 WebAudio renderSizeHint is the **`AudioContextOptions.renderSizeHint` constructor option** distinct from any prior WebAudio option (the v1.213.0–v1.219.0 cycle never covered the configurable render quantum); P-189 Rust XML SVG edge cases are the **SVG-image-parsing edge** distinct from B-269's generic DOMParser / XHR path (P-189 covers the `image/svg+xml`-content-type edge). The case-body template matches v1.208.0–v1.219.0: each case has a controlled fixture, a deterministic acceptance criterion (worker-context IDL exposure, WGSL parser validation, WebAudio IDL constructor option, Fetch abort-reason equality, TC39 Iterator helper round-trip, SpeechRecognition attribute round-trip, Spell Check dictionary round-trip, PerformanceObserver entry dispatch, ProfilerSample marker field round-trip, etc.), a parity control against Safari 26.6 / Firefox 155 / Chrome 152 where applicable, and a primary-source URL anchored to the `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror + the relevant W3C / WICG / WHATWG / Chromium spec PR. ### Browser Compatibility / CSS (B)

- [B-268] **[P1] Chrome 153 Stable Exposes CSSStyleValue Hierarchy (CSSStyleValue / CSSKeywordValue / CSSNumericValue / CSSUnitValue / CSSUnparsedValue) To Worker Global Scopes So Off-Main-Thread Web-Audio / Game-Logic Code Can Construct Typed CSS Values Without DOM Access** — Chrome 153 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 5114591051907072, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/534781956, spec https://www.w3.org/TR/css-typed-om-1/#stylevalue-subclasses) ships the CSS Typed OM Worker-exposure contract: the W3C CSS Typed OM Level 1 spec already declared `[Exposed=(Window, Worker, PaintWorklet, LayoutWorklet)]` on the `CSSStyleValue` base interface and its subclasses, but Blink only exposed `CSSStyleValue` to Workers (via the basic constructor / `parse` static method / `toString` stringification behavior) — the subclass constructors `CSSKeywordValue`, `CSSNumericValue`, `CSSUnitValue`, `CSSUnparsedValue` were `undefined` inside DedicatedWorker / SharedWorker / ServiceWorker global scopes, unlike Firefox and Safari that already shipped the full hierarchy per spec. Chrome 153 stable closes this interop gap. For a controlled fixture that loads `new Worker(URL.createObjectURL(new Blob(["self.postMessage('ready')"], {type: 'text/javascript'})))` over HTTPS, then issues from the main thread a `worker.postMessage({action:'probe'})` that runs `self.importScripts('data:text/javascript,var v=new CSSKeywordValue(\"auto\"); self.postMessage({k:v.constructor.name,t:typeof v.value});')` inside the 26.6` controls (already compliant per the W3C spec) report `{k:"CSSKeywordValue", t:"string"}` (controlled fixture verifying Safari's existing behavior matches the new Chrome 153 contract — the fix is parser disabled) report the same behavior — Chrome 151 was disabled-on-launch so the Rust parser was effectively rolled back to legacy. `Chrome 152` controls (Rust parser not yet re-launched) also ### Web Platform / Browser (W)

- [W-443] **[P2] Chrome 153 Flagged (Behind `#web-speech-timestamp` Flag) Adds `audioStartTime` / `audioEndTime` `DOMHighResTimeStamp?` Attributes On `SpeechRecognitionResult` So Web-Speech Transcription Can Be Mapped To Audio Timeline** — Chrome 153 (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 5811907077472256, Chromium bug https://crbug.com/528037568, spec https://github.com/WebAudio/web-speech-api/pull/192) ships the WebSpeech API timestamps feature behind the `#web-speech-timestamp` flag: the `SpeechRecognitionResult` interface gains two new `readonly attribute DOMHighResTimeStamp?` fields, `audioStartTime` and `audioEndTime`, that map the transcribed text segment to the source audio's timeline, enabling developers to determine on-device transcription latency and synchronize captions / animations / game events with audio playback. The `DOMHighResTimeStamp` is measured against the same time origin as `performance.now()` so it composes with the existing performance-observer infrastructure. For a controlled fixture serving a WAV audio file over HTTPS via `getUserMedia({audio:true})` (with a known-duration test tone) and `new SpeechRecognition()` with `interimResults=true` and `continuous=true`, assert that the `audioStartTime` attribute on each `SpeechRecognitionResult` is a `DOMHighResTimeStamp` (a number, not `null`, not `undefined`) (controlled fixture verifying the attribute exists and has the right type per the spec PR contract — `result.audioStartTime === typeof 'number'`), the `audioEndTime` attribute on each `SpeechRecognitionResult` is a `DOMHighResTimeStamp` ≥ `audioStartTime` (controlled fixture verifying the time range is non-empty — the end-time is at-or-after the start-time, otherwise the recognition is malformed), the difference `audioEndTime - audioStartTime` approximates the segment's audio duration in seconds (controlled fixture verifying the mapping is roughly correct — a 2-second audio segment reports `audioEndTime - audioStartTime ≈ 2.0`), the `audioStartTime` / `audioEndTime` for `final` results (`result.isFinal === true`) are stable across re-emit (the same final result is not re-emitted with different times; controlled fixture verifying the stability contract), the `audioStartTime` / `audioEndTime` for `interim` results may change as the recognition model refines its hypothesis (controlled fixture verifying the interim-results contract — interim results may have times that change as more audio is processed, final results do not), the timestamps are relative to `performance.timeOrigin` (the document's time origin, not the audio device's time origin; controlled fixture verifying the relative-time-origin contract via `result.audioStartTime < performance.now()` and `result.audioStartTime > 0`), `Chrome 152` controls (no SpeechRecognition timestamps feature) report `result.audioStartTime === undefined` and `result.audioEndTime === undefined` (the attributes do not exist on the Chrome 152 baseline — `SpeechRecognitionResult` has only `transcript` + `confidence` + `isFinal` fields per the pre-existing W3C Web Speech API spec), `Chrome 153` controls WITHOUT the `#web-speech-timestamp` flag enabled also report `undefined` (the feature is gated behind the flag — the attributes only appear when the flag is enabled), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit's Web Speech API is implementation-different — Safari ships a different Web Speech API surface than the W3C TR; controlled fixture verifying the W3C-PR-compatibility gap — Safari may not expose `SpeechRecognitionResult.audioStartTime` per Safari's own API surface), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox ships Web Speech API behind a flag — `dom.web_speech_api.enabled`; controlled fixture verifying Firefox reports `undefined` for the timestamps when the flag is off, may report timestamps when on), a controlled fixture verifying that `result.audioStartTime` and `result.audioEndTime` are exposed on `event.results[i]` for the `result` event handler (the new attributes propagate through the standard `result` event), and a controlled fixture verifying that the timestamps integrate with the existing `Performance.now()` round-trip (a game loop reading `performance.now()` and a SpeechRecognition handler reading `result.audioStartTime` can compare them in the same time-origin — no cross-time-origin mismatch). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (Chrome 153 flagged, "SpeechRecognitionResult Timestamps (WebSpeech API)" entry), Chromium bug https://crbug.com/528037568, Web Speech API spec PR https://github.com/WebAudio/web-speech-api/pull/192 (the IDL addition).

- [W-444] **[P2] Chrome 153 Flagged (Behind `#spell-check-custom-dictionary` Flag) Adds Spell Check Custom Dictionary API With `SpellChecker.customDictionary` And Per-Document `add()` / `remove()` / `has()` / `clear()` Methods So Pages Can Suppress Spell-Check False Positives Without User Action** — Chrome 153 (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 6185007701557248, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/428005649, spec https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/tree/main/spell-check-dictionary, sample WPT fixture https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/web_tests/wpt_internal/spell-check-custom-dictionary/add-remove-words-manual.html) ships the Spell Check Custom Dictionary API behind the `#spell-check-custom-dictionary` flag: a per-document transient dictionary that supplements the browser's built-in spell-checking dictionaries; pages add words via `SpellChecker.customDictionary.add(word)` and remove via `remove(word)`; words in the custom dictionary are not flagged as spelling errors by the browser's spell checker (suppressing false-positives in game-input fields, custom vocabulary, brand names, technical jargon). The dictionary is per-document (transient — does not persist across page reloads) and does NOT modify the browser's built-in dictionaries. For a controlled fixture serving `<html spellcheck="true"><body><textarea spellcheck="true">My customterm mispelled.</textarea></body></html>` over HTTPS where the browser's built-in spell checker would normally flag "customterm" and "mispelled" as spelling errors, assert that the `SpellChecker` interface is exposed on Chrome 153 with the flag enabled (controlled fixture verifying `typeof SpellChecker === "function"` and `typeof SpellChecker.customDictionary === "object"`), `SpellChecker.customDictionary.add("customterm")` returns a `Promise<boolean>` that resolves to `true` (controlled fixture verifying the add method accepts the word and reports success), after the `add`, the spell-check operation on the textarea does NOT flag "customterm" (controlled fixture running `document.querySelector('textarea').attachShadow({mode:'open'}).innerHTML = '<div spellcheck="true">customterm</div>'` and verifying the spell-check underline is not present — the custom dictionary suppresses the false-positive), `SpellChecker.customDictionary.has("customterm")` returns `true` after the `add` (controlled fixture verifying the lookup method), `SpellChecker.customDictionary.remove("customterm")` returns a `Promise<boolean>` that resolves to `true` (controlled fixture verifying the remove method succeeds for an existing word), after the `remove`, the spell-check operation flags "customterm" again as a spelling error (controlled fixture verifying the remove restores the original spell-check behavior — the dictionary is truly transient), `SpellChecker.customDictionary.clear()` empties the dictionary (controlled fixture verifying `add("a"); add("b"); add("c"); clear();` reports `has("a") === false` and `has("b") === false` and `has("c") === false`), the dictionary is per-document — reloading the page empties it (controlled fixture verifying `add("persisttest"); location.reload()` reports `has("persisttest") === false` after reload — the transient contract per the spec), `Chrome 152` controls (no Spell Check Custom Dictionary) report `typeof SpellChecker === "undefined"` (the interface is not exposed — the API does not exist on Chrome 152 baseline), `Chrome 153` controls WITHOUT the `#spell-check-custom-dictionary` flag also report `undefined`, `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit's spell-check API is implementation-different — Safari uses different APIs like `Editor.customDictation`; controlled fixture verifying the W3C-PR-compatibility gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox ships spell-check via `editor.spellCheck()` extensions or via internal APIs; controlled fixture verifying Firefox reports `undefined` for `SpellChecker`), the dictionary does NOT affect the browser's global spell-check (e.g. the OS-level spell-check in form fields outside the page's DOM — controlled fixture verifying the per-document scope), and a controlled fixture verifying that the dictionary does not affect programmatic `getSpellingErrors()` checks on other parts of the page (an `<input value="mispelled">` is still flagged as a spelling error because the custom dictionary only contains `"mispelled"` if explicitly added — the add operation is the only way to suppress a specific word). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (Chrome 153 flagged, "Spell Check Custom Dictionary API" entry), Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/428005649, Igalia explainer at https://github.com/Igalia/explainers/tree/main/spell-check-dictionary, sample WPT fixture at https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/web_tests/wpt_internal/spell-check-custom-dictionary/add-remove-words-manual.html.

- [W-445] **[P2] Chrome 153 Flagged (Behind `#long-animation-frames-in-worker` Flag) Extends Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API To Dedicated Workers So Event-Loop-Blocking Tasks Inside Workers Are Reported As `PerformanceObserver` `long-animation-frame` Entries With Per-Script Attribution** — Chrome 153 (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 5387465121726464, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/534893134, spec https://w3c.github.io/long-animation-frames/) ships the Long Animation Frames API in Web Workers (dedicated workers initially) behind the `#long-animation-frames-in-worker` flag: a long task that blocks a worker's event loop is now reported as a `long-animation-frame` entry that is observable from inside the worker via `PerformanceObserver`, with the usual per-script attribution (`scripts` field containing the URLs of the scripts that ran during the long task). The browser-side motivation is to surface congested moments in worker event loops — currently LoAF only reports on the main thread and is anchored to rendering frames, so worker-side long tasks that block the worker event loop are invisible to developers. For a controlled fixture that creates a `new Worker(URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([`...long-task-code...`], {type:'text/javascript'})))` over HTTPS, where the worker code runs a 100 ms synchronous loop (`const start = performance.now(); while (performance.now() - start < 100) {}`) and the page registers `new PerformanceObserver((list) => { self.postMessage({type:'loaf', entries: list.getEntries().map(e => ({name: e.name, duration: e.duration, startTime: e.startTime, entryType: e.entryType})) }); }).observe({type:'long-animation-frame', buffered: true})` inside the worker, assert that the worker receives a `loaf` message with at least one entry having `entryType === 'long-animation-frame'` (controlled fixture verifying the LoAF entry is dispatched inside the worker on Chrome 153 with the flag enabled), the entry's `duration` is ≥ 50 ms (the LoAF long-task threshold) and ≤ 150 ms (the 100 ms synchronous loop plus scheduler overhead) (controlled fixture verifying the duration range matches the synchronous-loop contract), the entry's `scripts` field contains at least one `WindowOrWorkerGlobalScope`-resolved URL (the synchronous loop runs in the worker's main script, so the URL should be the `blob:` URL of the worker source; controlled fixture verifying the per-script attribution), `Chrome 152` controls (no LoAF in workers — LoAF is `[Exposed=Window]` only per the spec, Chrome 152 does not widen it to `DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope`) report no entries (the `PerformanceObserver` callback never fires inside the worker — `list.getEntries().length === 0`; controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 152 baseline lacks the worker-exposure), `Chrome 153` controls WITHOUT the `#long-animation-frames-in-worker` flag also report no entries (the feature is gated behind the flag), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit's LoAF implementation is per-spec main-thread only; controlled fixture verifying Safari does not expose LoAF in workers — `PerformanceObserver` with `type:'long-animation-frame'` inside a worker is a no-op), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox has not yet shipped LoAF in workers; controlled fixture verifying Firefox reports no entries), the entry is dispatched at the worker's `WorkerGlobalScope` not the main page's `Window` (controlled fixture verifying the entry is captured by the worker's observer, not a separate observer registered in the main page — the entry should not appear in the main page's observer because the long task ran in the worker), the entry respects the existing LoAF privacy thresholds (`renderTime`, `styleAndLayoutStart` are not exposed; only `startTime`, `duration`, `blockingDuration`, `firstUIEventTimestamp`, `scripts` are exposed per the spec; controlled fixture verifying the privacy contract), and a controlled fixture verifying that a long task in `SharedWorkerGlobalScope` is NOT reported in the initial Chrome 153 release (the spec target is Dedicated Worker first, Shared Worker is follow-up work per the Chromium bug; controlled fixture with `new SharedWorker(...)` running a 100 ms loop reporting no LoAF entries). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (Chrome 153 flagged, "Support Long Animation Frames API in Web Workers" entry), Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/534893134, W3C Long Animation Frames API spec at https://w3c.github.io/long-animation-frames/, design doc at https://docs.google.com/document/d/13tERlM0Cd8gKUDC01-lQeW4oNllKs4AKdEGw41bnH4k/edit?usp=sharing.

- [W-446] **[P2] Chrome 153 Origin Trial (OT Token Required) JS Self-Profiling API Optional `marker` Field On `ProfilerSample` Identifies Browser Activity Type Running When Sample Was Taken (`script` / `gc` / `style` / `layout` / `paint` / `other`)** — Chrome 153 (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 5201297767792640, origin trial, Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40800459, spec https://github.com/WICG/js-self-profiling/pull/89, docs https://github.com/WICG/js-self-profiling/blob/main/markers.md) ships the JS Self-Profiling Markers feature as an origin trial: each `ProfilerSample` in the JS Self-Profiling API trace gains an optional `marker` field that identifies the type of browser activity running when the sample was taken. Without the markers, a trace shows gaps between stacks that cannot be interpreted — with markers, developers can attribute that time to browser work happening outside their JavaScript, for example distinguishing script execution from style recalculation, layout, or a garbage collection pause. The marker enum values are `"script"`, `"gc"`, `"style"`, `"layout"`, `"paint"`, and `"other"`. For a controlled fixture that requests the JS Self-Profiling API via `const profiler = new Profiler({sampleInterval: 10, maxBufferSize: 10000}); profiler.addEventListener("samplebufferfull", () => { ... })` inside an OT-enrolled page, assert that each `ProfilerSample` has a `marker` field whose value is one of the six enum strings (controlled fixture verifying the marker-field contract — `["script","gc","style","layout","paint","other"].includes(sample.marker) === true`), a controlled fixture that does intensive CSS work (`document.body.style.cssText = \`...10000 rules...\``) reports samples with `marker === "style"` (controlled fixture verifying the style-marker attribution — the profiler correctly identifies the CSS-parse work as style, not script), a controlled fixture that does intensive layout work (`for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) document.body.offsetHeight`) reports samples with `marker === "layout"` (controlled fixture verifying the layout-marker attribution), a controlled fixture that triggers a garbage collection (allocates large arrays until GC fires) reports samples with `marker === "gc"` (controlled fixture verifying the GC-marker attribution), a controlled fixture that does pure JavaScript computation (no DOM, no CSS) reports samples with `marker === "script"` (controlled fixture verifying the script-marker attribution — the default for JavaScript work), the marker is OPTIONAL — samples without a recognized browser-activity type have `marker === undefined` (controlled fixture verifying the optional contract — the spec says the marker is optional because not every sample can be attributed to a known browser activity), `Chrome 152` controls (JS Self-Profiling API baseline exists but no marker field; the JS Self-Profiling API is `[Exposed=Window]` and opt-in via the OT) report `sample.marker === undefined` for all samples (controlled fixture verifying the Chrome 152 baseline lacks the marker field — only the basic Profiler API is exposed), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit does not ship the JS Self-Profiling API; controlled fixture verifying `typeof Profiler === "undefined"` for the WICG-proposal-compatibility gap), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox ships the JS Self-Profiling API behind the `dom.profiler.enabled` pref; controlled fixture verifying Firefox's existing API surface may or may not include the marker field per Firefox's own implementation status), the origin trial requires an OT token in the `Origin-Trial` HTTP response header (controlled fixture verifying that pages WITHOUT the OT token see `typeof Profiler === "undefined"` per the OT-gating contract — the API is gated by OT enrollment for the marker-field extension, the baseline API also requires OT), and a controlled fixture verifying the marker composes with the existing `stack` field — `sample.stack` reports the JavaScript call stack at sample time, and `sample.marker` reports the browser activity type, allowing developers to distinguish "GC happened while my function was on the stack" vs "my function was actively executing" via the combined stack-and-marker view. Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (Chrome 153 origin trial, "JS Self-Profiling Markers" entry), Chromium bug https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40800459, WICG JS Self-Profiling spec PR https://github.com/WICG/js-self-profiling/pull/89, docs https://github.com/WICG/js-self-profiling/blob/main/markers.md.

- [W-447] **[P2] Chrome 153 Stable (Graduating From Edge 152 Origin Trial) `AudioContextOptions.renderSizeHint` Lets Web-Audio Game Authors Specify Custom Render-Quantum Size To Trade Latency For CPU** — Chrome 153 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 5078190552907776, spec https://webaudio.github.io/web-audio-api/#dom-audiocontextoptions-rendersizehint) ships the WebAudio Configurable Render Quantum feature as enabled-by-default after graduating from the Edge 152 origin trial. The new `AudioContextOptions.renderSizeHint` field accepts either the `AudioContextRenderSizeCategory` enum value `"default"` (render quantum size 128, the legacy default) or `"hardware"` (the User-Agent picks a good render quantum size for the current configuration) OR an `unsigned long` integer (the explicit render quantum size to use). The motivation is to let web-audio games / DAWs / interactive music apps tune the render-quantum size for their latency / CPU trade-off — a smaller render-quantum (e.g. 64 frames at 48 kHz = 1.33 ms) reduces audio latency but increases CPU overhead; a larger render-quantum (e.g. 1024 frames = 21.3 ms) reduces CPU but increases latency. For a controlled fixture over HTTPS, assert that `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: 64})` constructs an `AudioContext` whose internal render quantum is 64 (controlled fixture verifying the explicit-integer form — `audioContext.renderQuantumSize === 64` or equivalent internal slot per the spec's `[[render quantum size]]` private slot contract), `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: "default"})` constructs an `AudioContext` whose render quantum is 128 (the legacy default — controlled fixture verifying the default-enum form), `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: "hardware"})` constructs an `AudioContext` whose render quantum is the User-Agent's choice (Chrome 153 picks 128 on most hardware; controlled fixture verifying the hardware-enum form returns a non-empty render quantum that is a positive integer multiple of a power of 2 per the W3C spec's "Supported Render Quantum Sizes" section), `new OfflineAudioContext({numberOfChannels: 1, length: 44100, sampleRate: 44100, renderSizeHint: 256})` constructs an `OfflineAudioContext` whose render quantum is 256 (controlled fixture verifying the offline-context form — same `renderSizeHint` field is exposed in `OfflineAudioContextOptions`), a render-quantum size that is not a power of 2 (e.g. `renderSizeHint: 100`) throws `NotSupportedError` (controlled fixture verifying the spec's "Supported Render Quantum Sizes" constraint — only powers of 2 in a User-Agent-defined range are accepted), the `AudioContextRenderSizeCategory` enum is exposed globally with values `"default"` and `"hardware"` (controlled fixture verifying the enum's TypeScript-style contract — `AudioContextRenderSizeCategory.Default === "default"` and `AudioContextRenderSizeCategory.Hardware === "hardware"`), `Chrome 152` controls (no configurable render quantum — `renderSizeHint` is `undefined` per the legacy constructor signature) report `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: 64})` silently ignores the `renderSizeHint` field (Chrome 152 constructs an `AudioContext` with the legacy 128-quantum regardless of the `renderSizeHint` value — controlled fixture verifying the field is silently dropped), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit may support `renderSizeHint` per WebKit's own implementation status; controlled fixture verifying `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: 64}).renderQuantumSize === 64` if supported, undefined if not), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox does not yet ship `renderSizeHint`; controlled fixture verifying `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: 64}).renderQuantumSize === 128` — the field is silently ignored on Firefox baseline), the smaller render-quantum (64 frames) reduces `audioContext.baseLatency` (controlled fixture verifying `audioContext.baseLatency < audioContext.baseLatency` for the legacy 128-quantum — the smaller quantum yields lower base latency per the spec's `baseLatency` calculation: `baseLatency = renderQuantumSize / sampleRate`), a render-quantum size of 0 or negative throws `TypeError` (controlled fixture verifying the input-validation contract — `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: 0})` throws `TypeError` with a message containing "renderSizeHint" or similar), and a controlled fixture verifying the audio-output sample rate (`audioContext.sampleRate`) is unaffected by `renderSizeHint` (changing the render quantum does NOT change the sample rate — they are orthogonal audio-config dimensions; controlled fixture verifying `new AudioContext({renderSizeHint: 64, sampleRate: 48000}).sampleRate === 48000`). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, "WebAudio: Configurable render quantum" entry), W3C Web Audio API spec at https://webaudio.github.io/web-audio-api/#dom-audiocontextoptions-rendersizehint (the `renderSizeHint` IDL field and the `AudioContextRenderSizeCategory` enum).

### Performance (P)

- [P-189] **[P2] Chrome 153 Stable Rust-Based XML Parser Handles SVG Standalone / External Image Edge Cases Without XSLT So Embedding SVG Assets In Games Doesn't Hit The Legacy Parser** — Chrome 153 stable (Aug 2026, via `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153`, feature 5309598397497344, paired with B-269) ships the SVG-specific edge cases of the Rust XML parser migration: (a) **SVG standalone images** (top-level navigation to `image/svg+xml` documents via `window.location.href = "/game-icon.svg"` or `<a href="/game-icon.svg">` direct-link), and (b) **SVG external images** (embedding an SVG asset as an `<img src="/game-icon.svg">` external-image resource in a main HTML document). These two SVG-specific paths were deferred in v1.219.0 B-269's generic DOMParser / XHR coverage because they have distinct rendering-pipeline integration (SVG-standalone-image is rendered by the navigation / view subsystem, SVG-external-image is rendered by the image-decoding subsystem) and require separate controlled-fixture acceptance. For a controlled fixture serving `/game-icon.svg` over HTTPS with `Content-Type: image/svg+xml` and content `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="100"><circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red"/></svg>`, assert that `window.location.href = "/game-icon.svg"` followed by `document.documentElement.localName === "svg"` (controlled fixture verifying the top-level SVG navigation is parsed by the Rust parser — the document's root element is the SVG `svg` element per the standalone-image path), the standalone SVG `<circle>` element is queryable via `document.querySelector("circle").getAttribute("fill") === "red"` (controlled fixture verifying the SVG-specific selectors work — Rust parser preserves the SVG element tree correctly), the standalone SVG renders with `document.documentElement.getBoundingClientRect()` returning 100x100 px (controlled fixture verifying the SVG viewport contract — the `width="100" height="100"` attributes are honored), a controlled fixture serving `<html><body><img src="/game-icon.svg" id="svg-img"></body></html>` reports `img.complete === true` after the SVG loads (controlled fixture verifying the external-image path — the SVG is decoded by the image-decoding subsystem and the `<img>` element's `complete` flag is set), the external SVG is queryable via `fetch(img.src).then(r => r.text()).then(t => new DOMParser().parseFromString(t, "image/svg+xml"))` returning a non-null SVG document whose root `.localName === "svg"` (controlled fixture verifying the Rust parser handles the SVG-parse correctly when the SVG arrives via image-decoding pipeline), the Rust parser preserves SVG-namespaced elements (`<svg:foreignObject>` parses with `.namespaceURI === "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"`; controlled fixture verifying the SVG-namespace contract), the Rust parser rejects malformed SVG with `DOMException` `SyntaxError` (controlled fixture verifying the strictness contract — `<svg><circle></svg>` is rejected because `<circle>` is not closed, unlike legacy parsers that might recover), `Chrome 152` controls (no Rust parser for SVG-image paths; SVG parsing falls back to the legacy parser) report equivalent behavior for the user-visible API surface (controlled fixture verifying the legacy parser handles SVG-image paths correctly — no behavioral regression is introduced by the Rust migration), `Safari 26.6` controls (Safari WebKit's SVG parser handles standalone + external images via libsvg2 + libxml2 — separate codebase) report equivalent SVG-rendering behavior (controlled fixture verifying Safari's existing behavior matches the new Chrome 153 contract for the user-visible API surface), `Firefox 155` controls (Firefox Gecko's SVG parser handles standalone + external images via Gecko's image-decoding subsystem) report equivalent behavior (controlled fixture verifying Firefox's existing behavior matches), the Rust parser handles SVG `<style>` element with embedded CSS (controlled fixture serving `<svg><style>circle { fill: blue; }</style><circle/></svg>` and verifying `document.querySelector("circle").style.fill === "blue"` per the SVG-style-element contract — Rust parser preserves the embedded CSS parsing), the Rust parser handles SVG `<script>` element (controlled fixture serving `<svg><script>window.__svgScriptRan = true;</script></svg>` and verifying the script executes; the SVG parser runs `<script>` elements per the SVG spec), the Rust parser handles SVG `<use>` element with cross-document references (`<use href="/other.svg#element-id"/>`; controlled fixture verifying the cross-document reference contract — Rust parser resolves external-document references correctly), and a controlled fixture verifying the Rust parser handles SVG-as-image with explicit `width`/`height` attributes (`<img src="/icon.svg" width="32" height="32">` and `img.getBoundingClientRect().width === 32` per the SVG-as-image sizing contract). Source: `chromestatuslite.com/?version=153` mirror (Chrome 153 enabled-by-default, "XML parsing in Rust for non XSLT scenarios" entry, sub-bullet "SVG standalone images" and "SVG external images"), Chromium bug https://crbug.com/466303347, W3C XML 1.0 spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/xml, W3C SVG 2 spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/.
